body_text:
`ViewerComparator.getLabel` unwraps a `DecoratingLabelProvider` and sorts by the undecorated label (Bug 364735). It does not unwrap a `DecoratingStyledCellLabelProvider`. That is the label provider of every `CommonViewer`, which sets a `NavigatorDecoratingLabelProvider` derived from it. For those viewers the comparator sorts by the decorated text.

The `DecorationScheduler` computes decorations in a background job. The job writes them into the result cache through `internalPutResult` while the UI thread may be sorting. The label of an element then changes between two comparisons of one `Arrays.sort`, and TimSort throws:

```
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract!
    at java.base/java.util.TimSort.mergeHi(TimSort.java:903)
    at java.base/java.util.TimSort.mergeAt(TimSort.java:520)
    at java.base/java.util.TimSort.mergeForceCollapse(TimSort.java:461)
    at java.base/java.util.TimSort.sort(TimSort.java:254)
    at java.base/java.util.Arrays.sort(Arrays.java:1234)
    at org.eclipse.jface.viewers.TreePathViewerSorter.sort(TreePathViewerSorter.java:105)
    at org.eclipse.jface.viewers.AbstractTreeViewer.getSortedChildren(AbstractTreeViewer.java:685)
    at org.eclipse.jface.viewers.AbstractTreeViewer.updateChildren(AbstractTreeViewer.java:2907)
    at org.eclipse.jface.viewers.AbstractTreeViewer.internalRefreshStruct(AbstractTreeViewer.java:2032)
    ...
    at org.eclipse.ui.navigator.CommonViewer.refresh(CommonViewer.java:370)
```

A trace in the sorter of our product caught the label change in a Common Navigator with 120 Git-shared projects during a build:

```
label of P/plcSample105 changed during one sort from 'plcSample105' to '> plcSample105 [plcSample105 master]'
```

A second effect: the EGit dirty prefix `> ` sorts before letters, so dirty projects move to the top of a group once their decoration is cached.

**To Reproduce**

1. Common Navigator with at least 32 elements under one parent, all shared with EGit so that their labels carry text decorations. TimSort checks the contract from 32 elements upward.
2. Change the Git state of many elements at once, for example by touching a file in each project. The decorations are then recomputed while the viewer refreshes.
3. The failure depends on timing. It needs a decoration result to arrive during one sort, so it does not happen on every refresh.

**Expected behavior**

`ViewerComparator` sorts by the undecorated label for the styled decorating providers as it does for `DecoratingLabelProvider`.

**Proposed fix**

In `ViewerComparator.getLabel`, read the undecorated text of a `DelegatingStyledCellLabelProvider` through its styled string provider:

```java
if (prov instanceof DelegatingStyledCellLabelProvider delegating) {
	StyledString text = delegating.getStyledStringProvider().getStyledText(e1);
	name1 = text == null ? null : text.getString();
} else if (prov instanceof ILabelProvider lprov) {
	if (lprov instanceof DecoratingLabelProvider dprov) {
		lprov = dprov.getLabelProvider();
	}
	name1 = lprov.getText(e1);
} else {
	name1 = e1.toString();
}
```

**Environment**

- Eclipse Platform 4.38 (org.eclipse.jface 3.38.100, org.eclipse.ui.navigator 3.13.300). `ViewerComparator.getLabel` in master has the same code.
- Java 21, Windows 11.

I noticed a possible HTTP/2 codec server performance regression after moving from Vert.x `5.0.12` to Vert.x `5.1.0`.

This is only about the **HTTP/2 codec implementation**, not the multiplex implementation.

Environment:

```text
Ubuntu Linux
Java 21
native epoll transport
```

Benchmark shape:

```text
h2load -n 5000000 -c 8 -m 128 -t 8 http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

Minimal h2c server returning a small fixed body.

Rough numbers on my machine:

```text
5.0.12:
  usually around 2.15M req/s
  often up to ~2.20M

5.1.0:
  usually around 2.02M–2.10M
```

So the difference looks roughly like a 5–8% throughput drop in this synthetic HTTP/2 hot-path benchmark, and h2load reported request latency also gets worse.

I collected async-profiler CPU/allocation profiles. Allocation did not look significantly worse overall. CPU looked like a distributed overhead increase around the new HTTP/2 request/response path, especially around:

```text
HttpRequestHeaders validate/sanitize
HttpRequestHead / HttpResponseHead
HttpServerRequestImpl / HttpServerResponseImpl
DefaultHttp2ServerStream.writeHead
request dispatch / stream close handling
```

My current understanding is that this may be related to the HTTP/2 codec path now going through the generic HTTP stream/request/response model, while HTTP/1 still has specialized `Http1ServerRequest` / `Http1ServerResponse` classes.

Question: would it make sense for the HTTP/2 codec server path to also have a specialized request/response fast path, similar to HTTP/1, while keeping the generic stream model for HTTP/2 multiplex and HTTP/3?

I am not asking to revert the 5.1 HTTP stream architecture. I wanted to ask whether this performance tradeoff is intentional/acceptable, or whether a specialized HTTP/2 codec path would be considered if it can be done cleanly.

### Version

io.vertx:vertx-core:4.5.30

### Context

When using Vertx, with PemTrustOptions for example, during the execution of the code, Vertx tries to load all the application properties from the quarkus classpath using the FileResolverImpl.

When this file is an absolute path reference, an exception is thrown. When a relative file is used, it works, but will represent other issues in the code.

Refering to line [147](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blame/5a9bafbc965e5082ad6e6fdb2867fea2d66a0226/vertx-core/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/file/impl/FileResolverImpl.java#L147)

This method also scans the entire classloader and starts to resolve all files.
But the resolve will generate an incorrect `subResource` reference in line [267](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blame/5a9bafbc965e5082ad6e6fdb2867fea2d66a0226/vertx-core/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/file/impl/FileResolverImpl.java#L267)

### Steps to reproduce

(minimal DemoResolve project in attachment [demoResolve.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30701396/demoResolve.zip))

1. Project containing only 1 resource file `application.yml` in `src/main/resources`
2. Test containing 1 `@QuarkusTest`
3. The test will try to resolve the (absolute) `/application.yml` file
4. Run test > gives exception

When changing 
`fileResolver.resolveFile("/application.yml");`
to 
`fileResolver.resolveFile("application.yml");`
it does not give an exception.

Problem lies in the fact that in this example, QuarkusTest writes an empty application.properties to a temp workfolder (e.g. `%TEMP%/startup-override9955225914473382599`)
The absolutePath will then find the startup folder (url) but reference is with a fileName '/' instead of `url.getPath()` which results in:
`//application.properties` > does not exist
instead of

`%TEMP%/startup-override9955225914473382599/application.properties` 



### Do you have a reproducer?

_No response_

body_text:
Hi,

Currently, I am using Vert.x 4.5.28, and due to the characteristics of my project and environment, I need to balance requests across all available connections.

I have seen that the default (and currently only) option is the LIFO selector in `SharedClientHttpStreamEndpoint`. This made me wonder whether it would be possible to configure the connection pool strategy for the HttpClient through `HttpClientOptions`.

For example, `HttpClientOptions` could expose an option to configure a `BiFunction<PoolWaiter<HttpClientConnection>, List<PoolConnection<HttpClientConnection>>, PoolConnection<HttpClientConnection>>` , which would be passed to `HttpClientImpl` and then to `SharedClientHttpStreamEndpoint`.

This would allow users to provide their own connection selector implementations when required.

If you think this makes sense, I would be happy to help by creating a PR with the necessary changes.

Thanks!

### Describe the feature

`HttpServerOptions.setStrictThreadMode(true)` only benefits HTTP/1 today: HTTP/2 server streams
ignore the option and every write goes through the per-stream outbound message queue, even when the
stream is bound to the connection event-loop and can only be written from it. Such a stream could
relay its writes to the connection directly, like HTTP/1 does, and reject writes made from another
thread. This applies to both the codec and the multiplex server implementations.

body_text:
### Version

5.1.8 (same code on `master` at 911ff73, `VertxConnection` line 94), Netty 4.2.18, JDK 27.

### Context

Every `VertxConnection` not in strict thread mode creates an `InternalMessageChannel`. Its `OutboundMessageQueue` builds a `MessagePassingQueue.MpSc`, which calls `PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue()`. That is Netty's `MpscUnboundedArrayQueue(1024)`: the first 1025-slot chunk is allocated eagerly and kept for the life of the connection.

```java
// VertxConnection.java:94
this.outboundMessageQueue = strictThreadMode ? new DirectOutboundMessageQueue() : new InternalMessageChannel(executor);
// MessagePassingQueue.MpSc
super(PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue(), consumer, lowWaterMark, highWaterMark);
// Netty PlatformDependent$Mpsc.newMpscQueue()
new MpscUnboundedArrayQueue(1024)   // sipush 1024
```

The uncontended path does not use that queue. `MessagePassingQueue.add` keeps the element in the `overflow` field when `wip` goes 0 → 1; `queue.add` runs only when another element is already in flight (a racing producer, or the consumer refused an element). The default high-water mark is 16.

### Size (JOL 0.17, JDK 27)

Retained size of one instance (`GraphLayout.parseInstance(x).totalSize()`); the first column is JDK 27's default (compact object headers on), the second is `-XX:-UseCompactObjectHeaders`:

| instance | bytes (COH) | bytes (no COH) |
|---|---:|---:|
| `new OutboundMessageQueue<>(null)` (as built per connection) | 4,776 | 4,800 |
| `PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue()` (`MpscUnboundedArrayQueue(1024)`) | 4,680 | 4,696 |
| `new MpscUnboundedArrayQueue<>(16)` (Netty-shaded) | 648 | 664 |
| `PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue(16, 1 << 30)` (`MpscChunkedArrayQueue`) | 656 | 672 |
| JCTools 4.0.5 `MpscGrowableArrayQueue(16, 1 << 30)` | 656 | 672 |
| JCTools 4.0.5 `MpscLinkedQueue` | 408 | 424 |
| `PlatformDependent.newSpscQueue()` (`SpscLinkedQueue`) | 408 | 424 |
| `java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedQueue` | 32 | 48 |

About 575 B of each JCTools array queue is the padded queue object itself, so a smaller chunk still costs about 650 B.

### In an application

This came up in a benchmark: a Quarkus 4 (Vert.x 5.1.8) HTTP/1.1 server with keep-alive connections, ParallelGC.
- **Class histogram, 1,024 vs 16,384 connections:** live heap grew by about 11 KB per connection. 4,352 B per connection of that was `Object[]`, alongside exactly one shaded `MpscUnboundedArrayQueue` per connection.
- **At 4,096 connections, `setStrictThreadMode(true)`:** the queue instances went from 4,104 to 8, and the live heap (`jmap -histo:live`, mid-run) from 63.9 MB to 45.3 MB, with 0 errors.

Strict mode is `@Unstable` and only applies when every write happens on the event loop, so it is not a general answer.

### Alternatives

1. **Allocate the queue lazily** (a sketch, not implemented). Only the contended path needs it. The first producer that has to `queue.add` creates it and publishes it with a CAS; producers that lose the race use the winner's queue. The consumer only polls the queue after an element was added to it, so it always sees a non-null queue. Connections whose writes never race pay nothing.
2. **Use a smaller chunk, sized to the high-water mark.** Use `PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue(16, 1 << 30)`, which Netty already exposes (`MpscChunkedArrayQueue`, effectively unbounded), or the shaded `MpscUnboundedArrayQueue(16)`. Either way it's about 650 B instead of about 4.7 KB. Further chunks are linked in on demand only when more than one chunk's worth is queued. `MpscGrowableArrayQueue(16, 1 << 30)` (not in Netty's shaded set) starts at the same size and doubles.
3. **Use a linked MPSC queue (`MpscLinkedQueue`, or `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`).** The empty footprint is 32–408 B, at the cost of one node allocation per queued element, which again only happens on the contended path.

Option 1 removes the per-connection cost for the common case. Option 2 is the smallest code change.

### Reproducer (JOL)

```java
// classpath: vertx-core 5.1.8, netty-common 4.2.18, jol-core 0.17
System.out.println(GraphLayout.parseInstance(new io.vertx.core.internal.concurrent.OutboundMessageQueue<Object>(null)).totalSize()); // 4776
System.out.println(GraphLayout.parseInstance(io.netty.util.internal.PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue()).totalSize());                // 4680
System.out.println(GraphLayout.parseInstance(io.netty.util.internal.PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue(16, 1 << 30)).totalSize());     // 656
```

That is Netty's `MpscUnboundedArrayQueue(1024)`: the first 1025-slot chunk is allocated eagerly and kept for the life of the connection.

```java
// VertxConnection.java:94
this.outboundMessageQueue = strictThreadMode ? new DirectOutboundMessageQueue() : new InternalMessageChannel(executor);
// MessagePassingQueue.MpSc
super(PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue(), consumer, lowWaterMark, highWaterMark);
// Netty PlatformDependent$Mpsc.newMpscQueue()
new MpscUnboundedArrayQueue(1024)   // sipush 1024
```

The uncontended path does not use that queue. `MessagePassingQueue.add` keeps the element in the `overflow` field when `wip` goes 0 → 1; `queue.add` runs only when another element is already in flight (a racing producer, or the consumer refused an element). The default high-water mark is 16.

### Size (JOL 0.17, JDK 27)

Retained size of one instance (`GraphLayout.parseInstance(x).totalSize()`); the first column is JDK 27's default (compact object headers on), the second is `-XX:-UseCompactObjectHeaders`:

| instance | bytes (COH) | bytes (no COH) |
|---|---:|---:|
| `new OutboundMessageQueue<>(null)` (as built per connection) | 4,776 | 4,800 |
| `PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue()` (`MpscUnboundedArrayQueue(1024)`) | 4,680 | 4,696 |
| `new MpscUnboundedArrayQueue<>(16)` (Netty-shaded) | 648 | 664 |
| `PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue(16, 1 << 30)` (`MpscChunkedArrayQueue`) | 656 | 672 |
| JCTools 4.0.5 `MpscGrowableArrayQueue(16, 1 << 30)` | 656 | 672 |
| JCTools 4.0.5 `MpscLinkedQueue` | 408 | 424 |
| `PlatformDependent.newSpscQueue()` (`SpscLinkedQueue`) | 408 | 424 |
| `java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedQueue` | 32 | 48 |

About 575 B of each JCTools array queue is the padded queue object itself, so a smaller chunk still costs about 650 B.

### In an application

This came up in a benchmark: a Quarkus 4 (Vert.x 5.1.8) HTTP/1.1 server with keep-alive connections, ParallelGC.
- **Class histogram, 1,024 vs 16,384 connections:** live heap grew by about 11 KB per connection. 4,352 B per connection of that was `Object[]`, alongside exactly one shaded `MpscUnboundedArrayQueue` per connection.
- **At 4,096 connections, `setStrictThreadMode(true)`:** the queue instances went from 4,104 to 8, and the live heap (`jmap -histo:live`, mid-run) from 63.9 MB to 45.3 MB, with 0 errors.

Strict mode is `@Unstable` and only applies when every write happens on the event loop, so it is not a general answer.

### Alternatives

1. **Allocate the queue lazily** (a sketch, not implemented). Only the contended path needs it. The first producer that has to `queue.add` creates it and publishes it with a CAS; producers that lose the race use the winner's queue. The consumer only polls the queue after an element was added to it, so it always sees a non-null queue. Connections whose writes never race pay nothing.
2. **Use a smaller chunk, sized to the high-water mark.** Use `PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue(16, 1 << 30)`, which Netty already exposes (`MpscChunkedArrayQueue`, effectively unbounded), or the shaded `MpscUnboundedArrayQueue(16)`. Either way it's about 650 B instead of about 4.7 KB. Further chunks are linked in on demand only when more than one chunk's worth is queued. `MpscGrowableArrayQueue(16, 1 << 30)` (not in Netty's shaded set) starts at the same size and doubles.
3. **Use a linked MPSC queue (`MpscLinkedQueue`, or `ConcurrentLinkedQueue`).** The empty footprint is 32–408 B, at the cost of one node allocation per queued element, which again only happens on the contended path.

Option 1 removes the per-connection cost for the common case. Option 2 is the smallest code change.

### Reproducer (JOL)

```java
// classpath: vertx-core 5.1.8, netty-common 4.2.18, jol-core 0.17
System.out.println(GraphLayout.parseInstance(new io.vertx.core.internal.concurrent.OutboundMessageQueue<Object>(null)).totalSize()); // 4776
System.out.println(GraphLayout.parseInstance(io.netty.util.internal.PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue()).totalSize());                // 4680
System.out.println(GraphLayout.parseInstance(io.netty.util.internal.PlatformDependent.newMpscQueue(16, 1 << 30)).totalSize());     // 656
```

### Version
5.2.2 (also `master` and `4.x` — `Http1xUpgradeToH2CHandler`)

### Context
When an HTTP/1.1 request carries `Upgrade: h2c`, `Http1xUpgradeToH2CHandler.channelRead` converts the HTTP/1.1 headers into `DefaultHttp2Headers` with

```java
headers.add(header.getKey().toLowerCase(), header.getValue());   // vertx-core/.../http2/codec/Http1xUpgradeToH2CHandler.java:113
```

`String.toLowerCase()` follows the JVM default locale. On a JVM whose default locale is Turkish (`tr-TR` — the default on any Turkish OS/user account; `-Duser.language=tr -Duser.country=TR` reproduces it anywhere) every header name containing an uppercase `I` (`If-None-Match`, `If-Modified-Since`, `If-Match`, `X-Request-ID`, `X-Correlation-ID`, `X-API-Key`, `Idempotency-Key`, `Last-Event-ID`, …) becomes `ıf-none-match` (dotless ı, U+0131). Netty's `DefaultHttp2Headers` rejects the non-token byte, so after `101 Switching Protocols` has already been written the server fails the connection and the client hangs.

### Do you have a reproducer?
Yes — a Vert.x server with `new HttpServerOptions().setHttp2ClearTextEnabled(true)` and a Vert.x client with `new HttpClientOptions().setProtocolVersion(HttpVersion.HTTP_2).setHttp2ClearTextUpgrade(true)` sending `If-None-Match: "abc"` and `X-Request-ID: 1`, run with `-Duser.language=tr -Duser.country=TR` (vert.x 5.2.2, Netty 4.2.19):

```
en-US: SERVER saw request version=HTTP_2 path=/probe  header name=[if-none-match]  header name=[x-request-id]  CLIENT response status=200
tr-TR: io.netty.handler.codec.http2.Http2Exception: invalid header name [ıf-none-match]
          at io.netty.handler.codec.http2.DefaultHttp2Headers$2.validateName(DefaultHttp2Headers.java:62)
          at io.vertx.core.http.impl.http2.codec.Http1xUpgradeToH2CHandler.lambda$channelRead$0(Http1xUpgradeToH2CHandler.java:113)
       CLIENT failed: java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException
```

### Extra
`Locale.ROOT` is already the house style elsewhere (`VertxTestBase` folds the transport name with `Locale.ROOT`). Fix is `header.getKey().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)` (same line on `4.x`), plus a regression test that performs an h2c upgrade with an `If-None-Match` header under a `tr-TR` default locale. I have the branch ready.

body_text:
### Description

There are various places were we are inconsistent or frankly, silly, in our IO patterns for vector search.

- [ ] All our *flat formats should load vectors with `normal` MMAP. It is debatable on if we want to prefetch here. But, making these `normal` makes the most sense. You will generally be searching blocks of these at a time, and read aheads will help significantly.
- [ ] Non-quantized vectors should load via `random` MMAP, and access to them should take advantage of prefetching. Generally, access of the non-quantized vectors only occurs during merging and rescoring. Specifically, in rescoring, we should consider prefetching heavily, and possibly prefetching across segments before attempts at scoring (to account for scenarios when a segment only has one vector we care about, then per-segment prefetching is basically useless). 
- [ ] Quantized vectors & indexing structures should always be `normal` MMAP. Basically, we always want to load as much as possible as we know those vectors will be used and the index structure will always be used. Random here likely only hurts us in the end.
- [ ] Quantized and index files should be easily set to pre-load in the directory. I am not 100% sure if we want to do this by default or not (e.g. if we see a `.veq` that is used in an HNSW field, load it). But, at a minimum, we need to make this experience better (like, who the crap actually knows that they should load `vex` and `veq` and sometimes `veb`...we need to do this better).
- [ ] For DiskBBQ, we need to consider more aggressive pre-fetching of postings lists, right now we only prefetch a single postings list at a time. Our scoring is at times so fast, especially for short lists, we still spend time waiting on IO. Let's fix that.


I hope it goes without saying, we should benchmark to validate each of my assertions.

### Elasticsearch Version

9.3.0, most probably it affects older versions.

### Installed Plugins

_No response_

### Java Version

_bundled_

### OS Version

OSX

### Problem Description

We have the following test:

```sql
sortAsc
from ul_logs | sort bytes_in nulls first, id | limit 12;

       @timestamp:date  |      bytes_in:ul                       |     bytes_out:ul   |      id:i     |    status:k
2017-11-10T20:35:55.000Z|null                                    |null                |41             |Error
2017-11-10T19:51:38.000Z|null                                    |null                |90             |Error
2017-11-10T23:22:36.000Z|null                                    |null                |101            |Error
2017-11-10T20:35:57.000Z|0                                       |2507200025082562692 |70             |OK
2017-11-10T00:27:03.000Z|0                                       |18223615477147360166|71             |OK
2017-11-10T00:27:46.000Z|0                                       |11206857258468587792|72             |OK
2017-11-10T00:00:22.000Z|0                                       |11060623717086222747|80             |OK
2017-11-10T00:01:20.000Z|74330435873664882                       |4875216609683497742 |82             |OK
2017-11-10T21:34:49.000Z|[154551962150890561, 154551962150890564]|4317649615355527138 |42             |Error
2017-11-10T20:21:58.000Z|154551962150890564                      |9382204513185396493 |63             |OK
2017-11-10T00:01:45.000Z|[154551962150890564, 754822992931077409]|12647826153259487490|85             |OK
2017-11-10T20:06:49.000Z|195161570976258241                      |15395084776572180858|88             |Error
;
```

This type of query gets translated to a `LuceneTopNSourceOperator` in the data nodes:

```
Local execution plan for data: |  
-- | --
DriverFactory(instances = 1, type = DATA_PARALLELISM) |  
\_LuceneTopNSourceOperator[dataPartitioning = AUTO, maxPageSize = 9362, limit = 12, needsScore = false, sorts = [{"bytes_in":{"order":"asc","missing":"_first","unmapped_type":"unsigned_long"}},{"id":{"order":"asc","missing":"_last","unmapped_type":"integer"}}]] |  
\_ValuesSourceReaderOperator[fields = [bytes_in, id]] |  
\_ProjectOperator[projection = [0, 1, 2]] |  
\_ExchangeSinkOperator
```

but this is not returning data in the correct order because the nulls don't get sorted correctly.

The only reason we get correct results for this query is that both the node_reduce phase and the coordinator resort with a `TopNOperator`.

It's unclear to me whether this is a Lucene bug or a bug in the compute operator.

### Steps to Reproduce

If we use a smaller limit we can reproduce:

```sql
sortAsc
from ul_logs | sort bytes_in nulls first, id | limit 4;
```

with:

```sh
./gradlew ":x-pack:plugin:esql:qa:server:single-node:javaRestTest" --tests "org.elasticsearch.xpack.esql.qa.single_node.EsqlSpecIT" -Dtests.method="test {csv-spec:unsigned_long.SortAsc}"
```

should return:

```
@timestamp:datetime      | bytes_in:unsigned_long | bytes_out:unsigned_long | id:integer | status:keyword
2017-11-10T20:35:55.000Z | null                   | null                    | 41         | Error
2017-11-10T19:51:38.000Z | null                   | null                    | 90         | Error
2017-11-10T23:22:36.000Z | null                   | null                    | 101        | Error
2017-11-10T20:35:57.000Z | 0                      | 2507200025082562692     | 70         | OK
```

but instead yields the results:

```
@timestamp:datetime      | bytes_in:unsigned_long | bytes_out:unsigned_long | id:integer | status:keyword
2017-11-10T20:35:55.000Z | null                   | null                    | 41         | Error
2017-11-10T20:35:57.000Z | 0                      | 2507200025082562692     | 70         | OK
2017-11-10T00:27:03.000Z | 0                      | 18223615477147360166    | 71         | OK
2017-11-10T00:27:46.000Z | 0                      | 11206857258468587792    | 72         | OK
```

### Why is this happening

When loading unsigned int values from Lucene we use `LongValuesComparatorSource`. This treats nulls as `Long.MinValue`:

```java
        final long lMissingValue = (Long) missingObject(missingValue, reversed);
```

but min value for Long is -2^63, which is how we encode an unsigned 0 into a long: 

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/8d51a8af0d8886dec46971b6b4bdf7fee4a77c60/x-pack/plugin/mapper-unsigned-long/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/unsignedlong/UnsignedLongFieldMapper.java#L861

So nulls and 0s are the same when reading from Lucene, hence why we break the tie with the id column

body_text:
Currently the `CHUNK` function defaults to a specific token size when chunking content, regardless of whether the backing field is a pre-chunked `semantic_text` field or not. 

Consider changing the default behavior to return existing `semantic_text` chunks by default when a `semantic_text` field is used with `CHUNK`. This would be overridden by also passing in explicit chunking settings.

body_text:
### Description

Unlike Retrievers and DFS: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/139445 

Unlike ESQL: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/140177

The `knn` query is treated like a regular 'ole query. Meaning, every shard gets called for `doToQuery` and then individual rewritten and thus, tada, we rescore per shard. 

We should strive to reduce the amount of rescoring done with the `knn` query. This will be tricky, I am not 100% what it will look like. 

If we could get rescoring to be done per NODE instead of per shard on the node that would be glorious.

However, I might settle for dynamically adjusting the amount of rescoring done if we notice that there are many shards (e.g. if there are 3 shards, and we are doing 3x oversampling, many reduce to 1x oversampling...). I suspect however, this may still be problematic as the drop in recall might not be acceptable (e.g. are we really gathering more K and rescoring them? Shards are randomly distributed...how would this actually work...)

This is a tough one.

body_text:
### Description

Right now, we have the query bits hard-coded for DiskBBQ indices. Specifically:

 - 4bit queries for 1 & 2 bit indices
 - 4 bit queries for 4 bit indices
 - 7 bit queries for 7 bit indices (soon).

We know for larger vector sizes, that even lower query bits than 4 for 1 & 2 bits would be acceptable and provide a significant qps improvement.

We should think about what it looks like to expose this query hint/configuration and how we can give it to users without making it too flexible and confusing.

`ESVectorUtil.squareDistanceBulk` currently has scalar and panama implementations. A native implementation would most likely be even faster, making use of the bulk-with-offsets native call.

However, the vectors are currently represented as a non-contiguous `float[][]` in `KMeansLocal` and `NeighborHood`. Bulk-with-offsets expects all the scoring vectors to be presented as a contiguous `MemorySegment`, and there could be too many vectors to allocate a single contiguous `float[]`.

Just calling the single vector native function in a loop is slower than the panama implementation, so we would need an explicit native bulk implementation.

Instead, we could split it up into blocks of ?100 contiguous floats, which could then be scored together. We might need to group the node offsets together too, so we're not jumping around between blocks.

Tasks:

1. Verify the expected performance gain through using bulk-with-offsets over the Panama `squareDistanceBulk`
2. Create a structure storing contiguous blocks of floats in a `float[][]` ready for bulk scoring
3. Propagate this structure through the code, keeping/optimizing the relevant node offsets together with each vector block.
4. Call `Similarities.squareDistanceF32BulkWithOffsets` to do the native scoring on each block
5. Profit!

This issue was created out of a small number of remaining work from https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/108385 that was deemed not necessary for a tech preview, essentially all the items from the "_Things to circle back to after tech preview_" section in the aforementioned ticket.

**Vector-only dispatch.**
Special handling for block values that can be vectorized has been disabled in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/138390; it was a no-op. At some point, we'd like to enable it back and actually have it implemented for performance reasons as the vector path won't have to check for nulls, or mult-ivalues.

Currently, the t-digest field, like the histogram field, just accepts whatever data the user sends.  We should consider reencoding this with the digest settings the field was defined with.  This would protect against users mistakenly loading very large fields into what is meant to be a compact format. 

I think there are two options we can adopt: 
- Always re-encode the data; this incurs a memory and compute cost on every ingest, which may not be useful if the user sent the right thing in the first place
- Apply some heuristic, such as `if (centroids.length) > compression * 10)`, which makes a reasonable guess about the shape of the sketch and only re-encodes if the supplied data looks very different from that guess.

Currently when a value trips `ignore_above`, and the index is using synthetic source, the flattened field mapper stored the value in a separate stored field ([FlattenedFieldParser.javaL141](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/45a1ec7035e9c5fbc050487983c3131c188aa96b/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/index/mapper/flattened/FlattenedFieldParser.java#L141)).
However, when we're using binary doc values (`doc_values.cardinality = HIGH`), we can just store the field in doc values as usual, since there is no length limit on binary doc values.

Relates to https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/141610#discussion_r2760800604.

body_text:
## Description

PromQL trigonometric functions (e.g. `atanh`, `acos`, `asin`) currently throw an `ArithmeticException` when given out-of-range inputs. For example, `atanh(2)` throws rather than returning `NaN`.

In PromQL, these functions are expected to return `NaN` for out-of-range inputs instead of raising errors. This difference affects compatibility with Prometheus behavior.

## Current behavior

```
atanh(2) → ArithmeticException: Atanh input out of range
```

## Expected PromQL behavior

```
atanh(2) → NaN
```

## Affected functions

- `atanh` (input outside [-1, 1])
- `acos` (input outside [-1, 1])
- `asin` (input outside [-1, 1])
- Potentially other trigonometric functions with domain restrictions

## Proposal

Either create PromQL-specific variants of these functions that return `NaN`, or add a wrapping mechanism that catches `ArithmeticException` and returns `NaN` when invoked from a PromQL context.

PromQL trigonometric functions (e.g. `atanh`, `acos`, `asin`) currently throw an `ArithmeticException` when given out-of-range inputs. For example, `atanh(2)` throws rather than returning `NaN`.

In PromQL, these functions are expected to return `NaN` for out-of-range inputs instead of raising errors. This difference affects compatibility with Prometheus behavior.

## Current behavior

```
atanh(2) → ArithmeticException: Atanh input out of range
```

## Expected PromQL behavior

```
atanh(2) → NaN
```

## Affected functions

- `atanh` (input outside [-1, 1])
- `acos` (input outside [-1, 1])
- `asin` (input outside [-1, 1])
- Potentially other trigonometric functions with domain restrictions

## Proposal

Either create PromQL-specific variants of these functions that return `NaN`, or add a wrapping mechanism that catches `ArithmeticException` and returns `NaN` when invoked from a PromQL context.

### Description

On stateless search nodes we eagerly populate the `BitsetFilterCache` (assuming `load_fixed_bitset_filters_eagerly` is `true`).

This will be done for whichever segments happen to have open readers on the local node, which will vary over time as the segments move in and out of the local disk cache. That means that the amount of memory that is needed in the `BitsetFilterCache` is variable and dependent on which segments have been "recently" searched (where "recently" might not be very recent, if we haven't needed to evict from the disk cache).

In some cases we've seen the cache consume ~3GiB of heap on a node with 4GiB of total heap. Retaining these Bitsets in memory is useful because they are necessary for joins (nested fields) but not if they consume so much heap that the node becomes unstable.

In stateless we already accept that segments can be evicted from the disk cache, which closes the reader and evicts their Bitsets from the `BitsetFilterCache`. So we already do not guarantee that every segment has its Bitsets cached, even when `load_fixed_bitset_filters_eagerly` is `true`. We should extend that to heap management: allow evicting Bitsets from the bitset cache when needed to keep heap usage reasonable, even if the segment reader is still open (because the segment is still on disk).

Related:
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/28857
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/105791

body_text:
### Description

With Cosine and normalized dot product, we normalize all the vectors. Then when clustering & assigning we utilize euclidean distance. 

We might benefit from normalizing the centroids (e.g. spherical kmeans) as well for cosine/dot-product similarity during indexing. It may improve recall at lower percentages by allowing a "more correct" cluster to be picked first.

I don't think this will be a significant impact, but it might provide a small measurable improvement.

body_text:
The get async search status API (GET /_async_search/status/{id}) was introduced in 7.11 to support efficient polling of async search progress without the overhead of retrieving full search   
  results. It also served a secondary purpose: allowing monitoring systems to check search status using `cluster:monitor` privileges rather than `indices:data/read`, which is required by the       
  standard get async search API.
                                                                                                                                                                                                 
With the work done in #139828, it is now possible to long-poll on `GET /_async_search/{id}` with `return_intermediate_results=false` and `wait_for_completion_timeout`, which delivers results to the
   client as soon as the search completes — without needing a separate status endpoint. Kibana has already migrated to this approach.
                                                                                                                                                 
Given this, we should deprecate the status API and plan its removal in a future major version.

Open question before removal:

The status API sits under the cluster:monitor privilege scope, while the get async search API requires indices:data/read. This means users with the built-in monitoring_user role can currently poll search status without holding data-read permissions. We need to decide how to handle this before removing the endpoint:
                                                                                                                                                                                                 
  - Do we add a cluster:monitor privilege path to GET /_async_search/{id}?
  - Or do we accept that this use case is no longer supported and document the change?
                                                                                                                                                                                                 
  Proposed steps
                                                                                                                                                                                                 
  1. Deprecate GET /_async_search/status/{id} with a warning header and documentation update.
  2. Resolve the permissions gap above.
  3. Remove the API in the next major version.

body_text:
### Problem

In `SearchService`, the listener chain that handles a shard search response 

```
wrapFailureListener -> 
   wrapListenerForErrorHandling -> 
      releaseCircuitBreakerOnResponse -> 
         user listener -> 
            NetworkPathListener
```

 frees the `ReaderContext` on serialization failure by relying on `NetworkPathListener.onResponse` **throwing**. The exception bubbles up to `AbstractRunnable.run`'s `catch (Exception)`, which then routes through 

```
wrapFailureListener.onFailure -> 
   processFailure -> 
      freeReaderContext.
```

- Listeners aren't generally expected to throw from `onResponse`; failures should propagate via `onFailure`.
- Any wrapper inserted into the chain that doesn't propagate `RuntimeException` from `onResponse` silently breaks the cleanup. Anything backed by `assertOnce` (active when assertions are enabled, i.e. tests) converts a thrown `RuntimeException` into an `AssertionError`, which `AbstractRunnable.run` cannot catch (it only catches `Exception`), so `wrapFailureListener.onFailure` is never invoked and the `ReaderContext` leaks.
- The contract is non-local, split between `SearchTransportService` and `SearchService`, and easy to break by accident.

### Update
Refactor the listener chain so ReaderContext cleanup is triggered through onFailure rather than relying on NetworkPathListener.onResponse throwing.

body_text: ### Problem If a user writes a query like the following `TS metrics-hostmetricsreceiver.otel-default | STATS AVG(metrics.system.cpu.utilization) BY attributes.state` and adds it to a dashboard that autorefreshes every N seconds, then the visualizations will render the series as returned and that generates the following situation: - Kibana - Last 15m refreshing every 5s - Grafana using the ES|QL plugin - Last 15m refreshing every 5s Another example would be when the user runs a query like `TS metrics-hostmetricsreceiver.otel-default | STATS metrics.system.cpu.utilization BY TBUCKET(100)` then the user will get the colours of the series changing every a few refreshes: To solve that the user would have to add `| SORT metrics.system.cpu.utilization` Are users expected to add sort on the queries all the time to avoid those type of issues or is there anything elasticsearch should do to minimize or solve this problem? Relates to: https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/260226

The verifications that we perform on optimized logical plans are very light today, mostly just a check that the overall output types have not changed and that a plan node only references attributes from the child nodes' outputs.

In particular, the optimizer's operators batch runs in a loop but we only verify correctness once, after the whole batch of optimizer rules has run. That's a little light and leads to hard to triage problems - we only get the infamous "... optimized incorrectly due to missing references..." error message.

There are more invariants that we can enforce for earlier discovery of problems (some only during tests for perf reasons):

- After the operator optimization batch is done, all foldable expressions in the plan must be folded, so that we can assume they're Literals. We already assume that a lot, but never enforce it.
- In tests, ensure that each optimizer rule emits a valid plan that does not reference missing attributes (rather than doing this only after the full optimizer run) (ResolveUnionTypes was emitting inconsistent plans for forever, leading to weird workarounds - with this check, we'd have found out immediately!)
- On multiple accounts, we failed to consider that some Project nodes may just not be able to be pulled up to the top of the plan (because new nodes, such as MvExpand or Join cannot (yet) be pushed down past them). We can inject random, no-op Projects during optimization and check that the rule still produces a consistent plan after being applied.
- More generally, we should implement at least a minimal set of pre- and post-condition checks for optimizer rules. For instance, rules that rewrite expressions must not change the overall output data type. That would have been relevant for https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/149752, for instance. If we could add and enforce such conditions (e.g. by applying the rule to random query plans! Maybe our generative tests are sufficient, though), that would be lovely.

...There's probably more

### Elasticsearch Version

9.6.0 (`main`, source build)

### Installed Plugins

_No response_

### Java Version

_bundled_

### OS Version

Linux 6.8.0-84-generic #84-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC x86_64 GNU/Linux (Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS)

### Problem Description

`ROUND(5, -1)` returns **0**. It should return **10**.

When the value has no more digits than the rounding scale, `ROUND` on a whole number returns zero
instead of rounding up to the next power of ten. The same value passed as a double rounds
correctly, so the answer depends on the type of the input:

| expression | integer / long | double | expected |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ROUND(5, -1)` | **0** | 10.0 | 10 |
| `ROUND(9, -1)` | **0** | 10.0 | 10 |
| `ROUND(50, -2)` | **0** | 100.0 | 100 |
| `ROUND(99, -2)` | **0** | 100.0 | 100 |
| `ROUND(999, -3)` | **0** | 1000.0 | 1000 |
| `ROUND(-5, -1)` | **0** | -10.0 | -10 |
| `ROUND(15, -1)` | 20 | 20.0 | 20 |
| `ROUND(4, -1)` | 0 | 0.0 | 0 |

Note it is inconsistent even within whole numbers: `ROUND(15, -1)` is 20, but `ROUND(5, -1)` is 0.

**Expected vs actual**

The documentation states that "if the precision is a negative number, rounds to the number of
digits left of the decimal point". Rounding 5 to the nearest ten is 10. Actual result is 0.

**Root cause**

`Maths#round(long, long)` takes a truncation shortcut before rounding:

```java
long digitsToRound = -precision;
int digits = (int) (Math.log10(Math.abs((double) n)) + 1);
if (digits <= digitsToRound) {
    return 0L;                     // <- assumes "fewer digits than the scale" means zero
}
```

That is valid for truncation, and `TRUNCATE(5, -1)` is legitimately 0. It is not valid for
rounding: a leading digit of 5 or more rounds up to the next power of ten. The double path
(`Maths#round(Number, long)`) has no such shortcut, which is why doubles are correct.

A comparison against `BigDecimal` with `RoundingMode.HALF_UP` over 400,660 value/precision pairs
produced **9,947 mismatches**, all of this shape.

**Two related defects on the same path**

1. `-precision` overflows when `precision` is `Long.MIN_VALUE`, since `-Long.MIN_VALUE` is itself.
   The scale is then left negative, the zero shortcut is skipped, and the result is built from a
   wrapped scale: `ROUND(12345, -9223372036854775808)` returns 12340 instead of 0. `TRUNCATE` on
   the same input drives `tenPower()` to `0.0` and throws `ArithmeticException: / by zero`.

2. Independent of the above, and **not** fixed in my PR: `Round#process(int, long)` calls
   `.intValue()` on a long result, silently truncating on overflow.
   `ROUND(2147483647, -1)` returns **-2147483646** — a positive input yielding a negative output.
   The `Int` evaluator declares no `warnExceptions`, so fixing it means regenerating evaluators;
   I left it out to keep the PR reviewable and am happy to follow up.

**Prior mention**

This is not entirely unreported. In merged PR #119536 the author noted in passing:

> "rounding to a number like 7 to -1 returns 0 instead of 10, which may be considered an error.
> But it's consistent, so I'm leaving it to another PR."

That follow-up PR was never opened and there is no issue tracking it. The reason given for
deferring does not hold: it is **not** consistent, since `ROUND(5.0, -1)` returns 10.0 while
`ROUND(5, -1)` returns 0, and `RoundTests` already asserts `round(999.0, -1) -> 1000.0` for the
double path.

**Scope**

The legacy `x-pack/plugin/ql` copy of `Maths` carries the identical shortcut, so SQL's `ROUND` is
likely affected too. My PR changes only the ES|QL copy.



### Steps to Reproduce

No index or mapping is needed; `ROW` is enough.

```esql
ROW a = ROUND(5, -1), b = ROUND(9, -1), c = ROUND(50, -2), d = ROUND(-5, -1)
```

Actual:

```
a:integer | b:integer | c:integer | d:integer
0         | 0         | 0         | 0
```

Expected:

```
a:integer | b:integer | c:integer | d:integer
10        | 10        | 100       | -10
```

The type dependence is visible in a single row:

```esql
ROW i = ROUND(5, -1), l = ROUND(5::long, -1), d = ROUND(5.0, -1)
```

Actual `0 | 0 | 10.0`, expected `10 | 10 | 10.0`.

At the unit level, against `x-pack/plugin/esql`:

```java
assertEquals(10L, (long) Maths.round(5L, -1));    // fails, returns 0
assertEquals(100L, (long) Maths.round(99L, -2));  // fails, returns 0
assertEquals(-10L, (long) Maths.round(-5L, -1));  // fails, returns 0

// the two related defects
assertEquals(0L, (long) Maths.round(12345L, Long.MIN_VALUE));   // fails, returns 12340
Maths.truncate(12345L, Long.MIN_VALUE);                         // throws ArithmeticException: / by zero
```

The disk usage API reports estimates and not measurements.  For doc values, `IndexDiskUsageAnalyzer#analyzeDocValues `wraps the directory in a `TrackingReadBytesDirectory` that records only the min and max byte offset touched, then probes each field. By doing doing a binary walk via `advance(...)` and if there is a dictionary then invoking lookupOrd(0) / lookupOrd(valueCount - 1) .

Doc values formats internally keep track of file offsets / lengths that can be used to more accurately determine the disk usage of each. More importantly without doing I/O, because most of this information is loaded when opening a segment.

At least for the doc values formats, that are in the Elasticsearch codebase, we should be able to more accurately and cheaply report disk usage.

### Description

Muting an ES|QL function's test class causes the next **local** full ES|QL test-suite run to silently delete that function's generated documentation. The deletions land in the working tree, where they are easy to commit by accident (e.g. `git commit -a`).

This is the same class of bug as #147402, but at file rather than directory granularity — the fix for that issue does not cover it (see below).

### Reproduction

`ReverseTests` is currently muted ([`muted-tests.yml`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/muted-tests.yml), added in 867834375d72 for #158550), so this reproduces on `main` as-is:

```
./gradlew :x-pack:plugin:esql:test
git status --short
```

Result:

```
 D docs/reference/query-languages/esql/_snippets/generated/x-pack-esql/functions/briefSummary/reverse.md
 D docs/reference/query-languages/esql/_snippets/generated/x-pack-esql/functions/description/reverse.md
 D docs/reference/query-languages/esql/_snippets/generated/x-pack-esql/functions/examples/reverse.md
 D docs/reference/query-languages/esql/_snippets/generated/x-pack-esql/functions/layout/reverse.md
 D docs/reference/query-languages/esql/_snippets/generated/x-pack-esql/functions/parameters/reverse.md
 D docs/reference/query-languages/esql/_snippets/generated/x-pack-esql/functions/types/reverse.md
 D docs/reference/query-languages/esql/images/generated/x-pack-esql/functions/reverse.svg
 D docs/reference/query-languages/esql/kibana/generated/x-pack-esql/definition/functions/reverse.json
 D docs/reference/query-languages/esql/kibana/generated/x-pack-esql/docs/functions/reverse.md
```

All three artifact kinds are affected: `_snippets` markdown, the signature SVG, and the Kibana definition JSON/markdown.

### Root cause

Function docs are generated by running each function's `*Tests` class; `EsqlFunctionPlugin` then syncs the generated output back into `docs/`. A fully muted class emits nothing, and the sync treats its absence as "this function no longer exists".

The guard against that is a count threshold, in all three sync methods in [`EsqlFunctionPlugin.java`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/build-tools-internal/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/gradle/internal/esql/EsqlFunctionPlugin.java):

```java
if (countImages <= 100) {
    spec.preserve(preserveSpec -> preserveSpec.include("**/*.svg"));
}
```

- `syncSnippets` — `countTypes <= 100`
- `syncImages` — `countImages <= 100`
- `syncKibana` — `countKibana <= 100`

A **targeted** run (`--tests SomeFunctionTests`) stays under the threshold, so `preserve` applies and nothing is removed. A **full-suite** run exceeds it, `preserve` is skipped, and the sync becomes authoritative — deleting anything not regenerated in that run.

The threshold is presumably meant to distinguish "partial run, don't trust it" from "full run, safe to mirror". But a full run is exactly when muted classes are also absent, so the two cases are not actually distinguishable by count.

### Why the #147402 fix doesn't cover this

`syncKibana` already mitigates the muted-test case via `unpopulatedKibanaSubdirs`, which preserves `definition/<subdir>` entries whose source counterpart produced no files. That works when an entire generating category is muted (the `CommandLicenseTests` case in #147402).

It does not help here: `definition/functions/` *is* populated, by all the other ~200 functions that did run. A single muted function's JSON inside a populated directory is not preserved. `syncSnippets` and `syncImages` have no equivalent mitigation at all.

### Impact

Local only — CI sets `generateDocs=assert` and syncs `docs/` → build output, never back, so CI does not delete anything. The risk is a developer running the full suite locally and committing the deletions along with unrelated work.

### Suggested fix

Preserve per-file rather than per-count. Options, roughly in order of preference:

1. Drive the sync from the set of functions the plugin knows about, and preserve docs for any whose test class produced no output this run — rather than inferring intent from an artifact count.
2. Read `muted-tests.yml` and preserve docs for muted classes explicitly.
3. Fail (or warn loudly) when a function that has existing docs generated nothing, instead of deleting silently.

Dropping the `<= 100` thresholds so `preserve` always applies would stop the deletions, but it would also mean genuinely removed functions keep stale docs forever, so it needs pairing with something like (3).

### Elasticsearch Version

`main` @ `54a7b6680fb6` (`build-tools-internal/version.properties`: `elasticsearch = 9.6.0`)

### Installed Plugins

N/A

### Java Version

_bundled_

### OS Version

N/A — pure string parsing, OS independent.

### Problem Description

`Geohash#longEncode(String)` accepts strings that are not valid geohashes and returns a
long that decodes to a *different, valid* geohash instead of reporting an error.

`BASE_32_STRING.indexOf(c)` returns `-1` for characters outside the base-32 alphabet. `Geohash#longEncode(String, int)`
(`libs/geo/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/geometry/utils/Geohash.java:309`) shifts that
`-1` into the accumulator unchecked, so its sign bits overwrite previously decoded
levels. An empty string encodes to `0`, which `Geohash#stringEncode` then rejects with
`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` rather than a validation error.

The expectation comes from the class's own sibling: `Geohash#mortonEncode(String)`
(`Geohash.java:329`, `:339`) performs the same base-32 parsing and *does* reject both
cases with `IllegalArgumentException`. `ToGeohash` in
ES|QL already declares `@ConvertEvaluator(warnExceptions = { IllegalArgumentException.class })`,
so it is written to expect an exception that this path never throws.

Reachable from ES|QL via `TO_GEOHASH` and implicit `KEYWORD` to `GEOHASH` casting.
Aggregation and mapper call sites pass machine-generated hashes and are unaffected.

### Steps to Reproduce

```sh
curl -XPOST "localhost:9200/_query?pretty" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "query": "ROW g = TO_GEOHASH(\"ai\") | EVAL s = TO_STRING(g) | KEEP s"
}'
# expected: s = null plus a warning ("ai" contains "a" and "i", neither is in the geohash alphabet)
# actual:   s = "zz"   -- a valid geohash denoting a completely different location, no warning
```

Also reproducible as a unit test:

```
Geohash.longEncode("55.5")  // returns -428, decodes to "zzz5"
Geohash.longEncode("")      // returns 0, then stringEncode throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Geohash.mortonEncode("55.5")  // correctly throws IllegalArgumentException
```

### Logs (if relevant)

N/A — no exception is raised; the failure mode is a silently wrong value.

### Problem Description

`Geohash#longEncode(String)` accepts strings that are not valid geohashes and returns a
long that decodes to a *different, valid* geohash instead of reporting an error.

`BASE_32_STRING.indexOf(c)` returns `-1` for characters outside the base-32 alphabet. `Geohash#longEncode(String, int)`

`-1` into the accumulator unchecked, so its sign bits overwrite previously decoded
levels. An empty string encodes to `0`, which `Geohash#stringEncode` then rejects with
`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` rather than a validation error.

The expectation comes from the class's own sibling: `Geohash#mortonEncode(String)`
(`Geohash.java:329`, `:339`) performs the same base-32 parsing and *does* reject both

so it is written to expect an exception that this path never throws.

Aggregation and mapper call sites pass machine-generated hashes and are unaffected.

# actual:   s = "zz"   -- a valid geohash denoting a completely different location, no warning
```

Also reproducible as a unit test:

```

Geohash.longEncode("")      // returns 0, then stringEncode throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Geohash.mortonEncode("55.5")  // correctly throws IllegalArgumentException
```

### Elasticsearch Version
`main @ 54a7b6680fb6` (`build-tools-internal/version.properties`: `elasticsearch = 9.6.0`). Present since the ECS port in #76885 (2021).

### Installed Plugins
N/A

### Java Version
_bundled_

### OS Version
N/A — the failure is in pattern text, so it is OS independent.

### Problem Description
Three built-in ECS v1 patterns in `libs/grok/src/main/resources/patterns/ecs-v1/firewalls` cannot be compiled at all:

- line 51 `CISCOFW106023`
- line 53 `CISCOFW106100_2_3`
- line 55 `CISCOFW106100`

All three end with `\%{DATA:[@metadata.cisco.asa.hashcode1}, %{DATA:@metadata.cisco.asa.hashcode2}\]`. The literal `\[` that should precede the hashcode block was pulled into the following field name during the ECS port. `Grok`'s subname expression accepts `[` in a field name, so parsing succeeds, but the regex handed to joni then contains an unterminated character class and `Grok`'s constructor throws `org.joni.exception.SyntaxException: premature end of char-class`.

Expected: these patterns match the Cisco ASA hashcode block, as the legacy bank does at `patterns/legacy/firewalls` lines 43/45/47, and as the upstream `logstash-patterns-core` `patterns/ecs-v1/firewalls` does at the same lines 51/53/55.

Actual: any pipeline that references one of them fails at creation time. The pattern is unusable, not merely non-matching.

### Steps to Reproduce
```sh
curl -XPUT 'localhost:9200/_ingest/pipeline/cisco' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "processors": [ { "grok": {
    "field": "message",
    "patterns": ["%{CISCOFW106023}"],
    "ecs_compatibility": "v1"
  } } ]
}'
# expected: acknowledged
# actual:   400, [patterns] Invalid regex pattern found in: [%{CISCOFW106023}].
#                premature end of char-class
```
`CISCOFW106100_2_3` and `CISCOFW106100` behave identically. `CISCOFW733100` on line 92 is a separate, already reported defect (#143332) and does compile.

Library level, actually run: `new Grok(GrokBuiltinPatterns.get(true), "%{CISCOFW106023}", logger::warn)` throws from the constructor. `GrokProcessor.Factory` wraps that into the configuration exception above.

### Logs (if relevant)
```
org.joni.exception.SyntaxException: premature end of char-class
	at org.joni.ScannerSupport.newSyntaxException(ScannerSupport.java:163)
```

### Elasticsearch Version
`main` @ 54a7b6680fb6 (`build-tools-internal/version.properties`: `elasticsearch = 9.6.0`)

### Installed Plugins
N/A

### Java Version
_bundled_

### OS Version
N/A — code path defect, OS independent

### Problem Description
`Grok#match(String)` (`libs/grok/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/grok/Grok.java:185`) builds a joni
`Matcher` over the UTF-8 bytes of the input but passes `text.length()`, a character count, as the
search range. The sibling overload `Grok#match(byte[], int, int, GrokCaptureExtracter)` (`:239`) and
`Grok#innerCaptures` (`:217-219`) pass the byte length.

The joni range limits candidate start offsets, not where a match ends, so anchored patterns and
matches starting at offset 0 are unaffected. The defect appears when the first match starts at a byte
offset >= the character count, i.e. when enough multi-byte characters precede the match. `match()`
then returns `false` while `captures()` on the same instance extracts the fields.

This is user visible through `_text_structure/find_message_structure` and `find_structure`:
`FullMatchGrokPatternCandidate#matchesAll` (`.../structurefinder/GrokPatternCreator.java:960`)
validates the supplied `grok_pattern` with `match(String)`, and `GrokPatternCreator:277` rejects the
request — while `processMatch` (`:989`), one step later, uses `captures` and extracts every field.

### Steps to Reproduce
Sample line below is 46 characters / 76 UTF-8 bytes; the timestamp match starts at byte offset 49.

```sh
curl -XPOST "localhost:9200/_text_structure/find_message_structure?format=semi_structured_text&grok_pattern=%25%7BTIMESTAMP_ISO8601:timestamp%7D%20%25%7BLOGLEVEL:level%7D%20%25%7BGREEDYDATA:message%7D&pretty" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "messages": ["인증 서버에서 오류가 발생했습니다 2023-01-01T00:00:00 ERROR x"]
}'
# expected: 200, the three fields are extractable
# actual:   400 "Supplied Grok pattern [...] does not match sample messages"
```

An ASCII line of the same length is accepted.

Library-level reproduction, actually run:

```
./gradlew :libs:grok:test --tests \
  "org.elasticsearch.grok.GrokTests.testMatchAgreesWithCapturesOnMultiByteText"
```
→ `AssertionError: Expected: is <true> but: was <false>` for `%{LOGLEVEL:level}` against
`"가나다라마바사아자차카타파하 ERROR"` (20 characters / 48 bytes, match at byte 43); `captures()`
returns `{level=ERROR}`.

`main` @ 54a7b6680fb6 (`build-tools-internal/version.properties`: `elasticsearch = 9.6.0`)

### Installed Plugins
N/A

### Java Version
_bundled_

### OS Version
N/A — code path defect, OS independent

### Problem Description
`Grok#match(String)` (`libs/grok/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/grok/Grok.java:185`) builds a joni
`Matcher` over the UTF-8 bytes of the input but passes `text.length()`, a character count, as the
search range. The sibling overload `Grok#match(byte[], int, int, GrokCaptureExtracter)` (`:239`) and
`Grok#innerCaptures` (`:217-219`) pass the byte length.

The joni range limits candidate start offsets, not where a match ends, so anchored patterns and
matches starting at offset 0 are unaffected. The defect appears when the first match starts at a byte
offset >= the character count, i.e. when enough multi-byte characters precede the match. `match()`
then returns `false` while `captures()` on the same instance extracts the fields.

This is user visible through `_text_structure/find_message_structure` and `find_structure`:
`FullMatchGrokPatternCandidate#matchesAll` (`.../structurefinder/GrokPatternCreator.java:960`)
validates the supplied `grok_pattern` with `match(String)`, and `GrokPatternCreator:277` rejects the
request — while `processMatch` (`:989`), one step later, uses `captures` and extracts every field.

### Steps to Reproduce
Sample line below is 46 characters / 76 UTF-8 bytes; the timestamp match starts at byte offset 49.

```sh
curl -XPOST "localhost:9200/_text_structure/find_message_structure?format=semi_structured_text&grok_pattern=%25%7BTIMESTAMP_ISO8601:timestamp%7D%20%25%7BLOGLEVEL:level%7D%20%25%7BGREEDYDATA:message%7D&pretty" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "messages": ["인증 서버에서 오류가 발생했습니다 2023-01-01T00:00:00 ERROR x"]
}'
# expected: 200, the three fields are extractable
# actual:   400 "Supplied Grok pattern [...] does not match sample messages"
```

An ASCII line of the same length is accepted.

Library-level reproduction, actually run:

```
./gradlew :libs:grok:test --tests \
  "org.elasticsearch.grok.GrokTests.testMatchAgreesWithCapturesOnMultiByteText"
```
→ `AssertionError: Expected: is <true> but: was <false>` for `%{LOGLEVEL:level}` against
`"가나다라마바사아자차카타파하 ERROR"` (20 characters / 48 bytes, match at byte 43); `captures()`
returns `{level=ERROR}`.

## Summary

Follow-up to #158927. That PR bounds concurrent `find_structure` analyses to `EsExecutors.allocatedProcessors(settings)` and removes per-value `Pattern.compile` from the mapping-guess hot path, but two memory limits remain open.

## Gaps left by #158927

### 1. Unbounded throttle queue

`ThrottledTaskRunner` uses a `LinkedTransferQueue`, i.e. an unbounded queue. `RestController` holds each request body against the in-flight breaker until the *response* completes, so a large enough burst of concurrent requests still accumulates request bodies in heap (e.g. ~200 queued requests × ~2.8 MB body ≈ ~560 MB on top of in-flight analyses).

### 2. Unbounded single-request sample size

`AbstractFindStructureRequest.validate()` places no upper limit on `lines_to_sample`. A single wide, deep sample can still OOM a small node on its own, independent of concurrency.

## Proposed fix

Meter the parse against `indices.breaker.request` so excess or oversized requests receive a 429 instead of risking node OOM. Consider:

- Rejecting or queue-limiting when estimated working-set would exceed breaker budget
- Capping `lines_to_sample` (or total sample bytes) with a sensible default and cluster setting

## Related

- #158927 — concurrency bound (merged/pending)

Follow-up to #157850.

The ids of the default inference endpoints are written as plain strings in more than one file:

- `.multilingual-e5-small-elasticsearch` (E5)
- `.jina-embeddings-v5-text-small` (Jina v5)

The inference plugin already keeps these as constants (`ElasticsearchInternalService.DEFAULT_E5_ID` and `InternalPreconfiguredEndpoints.DEFAULT_JINA_V5_ENDPOINT_ID`).

But ES|QL's `DenseVector` can't use them: ES|QL only depends on the inference plugin in tests, not in main code. So `DenseVector` keeps its own copies (`DEFAULT_INFERENCE_ID` and `EIS_JINA_V5_INFERENCE_ID`), and the same string ends up in several places where it can drift.

### Fix

Put each id in one shared spot both sides already build against 

No behavior change; it just removes the duplicated strings.

Follow-up from the #157850 review.

ES|QL resolves each query's candidate `inference_id`s once, in pre-analysis, via one `GetInferenceModelAction` per unique id. It's a metadata lookup for the endpoint's task type (no model load), run in parallel — so it's cheap today and not urgent.

But it runs on every query that uses inference, so it may be worth optimizing later, e.g. caching resolved task types across queries or a lighter lookup.

Filing so the idea isn't lost

### Elasticsearch Version

main

### Installed Plugins

_No response_

### Java Version

_bundled_

### OS Version

n/a

### Problem Description

Follow-up from https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/157956 (review: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/157956#discussion_r3955976678).

That PR stops nested `CASE` of `DATE_PERIOD` / `TIME_DURATION` from overflowing the stack during constant folding by walking the taken branch in a loop. Those types have no evaluator, so `Case.fold()` has to do that by hand.

The same nested shape with other types can still overflow:

```esql
CASE(true, CASE(true, …, 1), 0)
```

Those types fold through the evaluator (`EvaluatorMapper.fold`), which calls `fold()` on each child. A deep tree of nested `CASE`s is still recursive there.

We cannot reuse the date-period loop inside `Case.fold()` for these types. The evaluator is what emits the warning when a condition is multivalued; walking the taken branch ourselves skips that and the warnings disappear (this failed `CaseTests.testFancyFolding` when we tried it on the PR).

So the date-period/time-duration overflow is fixed in #157956. The remaining overflow for integer (and other evaluator-backed) `CASE` needs a fix on the evaluator fold path, not in `Case.fold()`.

Related: elastic/security#12297.

### Steps to Reproduce

On a tree built in tests (deeper than the parser’s `ExpressionBuilder.MAX_EXPRESSION_DEPTH` of 300), fold:

```text
CASE(true, CASE(true, …, 1), 0)
```

with enough nesting to blow the stack. Parsed queries are capped at 300, but the fold path is still recursive.

During a 9.4->9.5 rolling upgrade, GeoIP enrichment fails on ingest nodes that have been restarted as part of the upgrade while the master is still on 9.4.x. Documents are tagged `_geoip_database_unavailable_* `instead of being enriched, and recover once the master upgrades.

 #145011 introduced IpLocationDownloadConsumers to track which consumers want IP databases.
DatabaseNodeService.checkDatabases treats an absent custom as "preserve existing loaders and skip". 
The custom entry is only written by the master node (via IngestIpLocationPlugin), so while the master is still 9.4.x nobody writes it and all freshly-upgraded ingest nodes skip loading entirely.

body_text:
## Summary

A `_search` with a `significant_terms` aggregation on a floating-point field returns HTTP **500** (`search_phase_execution_exception`) instead of a client error.

Seen on serverless 9.6.0, `POST /logs-*/_search`, Kibana log-rate analysis (`sig_term_p_value_*` agg name, nested under `random_sampler`). Two shards failed during query; the coordinating node then failed fetch/reduce.

## Stack trace (redacted)

```
SearchPhaseExecutionException: Failed to execute phase [fetch]
shardFailures:
  QueryPhaseExecutionException: Query Failed [Failed to execute main query]
  Caused by: UnsupportedOperationException: No support for examining floating point numerics

Caused by: IllegalArgumentException: Merging/Reducing the aggregations failed when computing the aggregation [sig_term_p_value_11] because the field you gave in the aggregation query existed as two different types in two different indices
  at AggregationErrors.reduceTypeMismatch
  at InternalSignificantTerms
  at InternalRandomSampler
  at QueryPhaseResultConsumer.aggregate → FetchSearchPhase
```

## Root cause

`SignificantTermsAggregatorFactory.numericSupplier()` throws a raw `UnsupportedOperationException` when the values source is floating-point:

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/search/aggregations/bucket/terms/SignificantTermsAggregatorFactory.java#L178-L181

```java
if (numericValuesSource.isFloatingPoint()) {
    throw new UnsupportedOperationException("No support for examining floating point numerics");
}
```

The same factory already uses `ElasticsearchStatusException(..., RestStatus.BAD_REQUEST)` for an analogous validation (sampling + `min_doc_count`). The float check should do the same (or `IllegalArgumentException`, matching the regex include/exclude check a few lines above).

The `reduceTypeMismatch` `IllegalArgumentException` is a second, related failure: `logs-*` spans backing indices where the aggregated field is not the same type. That path also surfaces as 500 because it happens during fetch/reduce after the shard-level UOE.

## Expected

- **400** with a clear message that `significant_terms` does not support floating-point fields.
- Mixed field types across indices in the same agg should also be a **400**, not a 500.

## Related

- Same `reduceTypeMismatch` / `sig_term_p_value_11` stack was reported on a suppressed-rest-errors alert on 2026-02-12; no GitHub issue was filed then.
- Pattern match: #154354 (`UnsupportedOperationException` → 500 instead of 400).

`date_diff` throws an HTTP 500 `UnsupportedOperationException` when one of its timestamp
arguments carries the `NULL` data type at planning time. The error message self-reports:
*"there is a bug in DateDiff.resolveType()"*.

## Root cause

`TypeResolutions.isType()` unconditionally accepts `NULL`-typed expressions (intentional —
null propagation is meant to handle null *values* at evaluation time):

```java
if (predicate.test(e.dataType()) || e.dataType() == NULL) {
    return TypeResolution.TYPE_RESOLVED;
}
```

So `DateDiff.resolveType()` passes. But `DateDif factory by
matching known type pairs and throws for anything else:

```java
} else if (startTimestamp.dataType() == DATETIME) == DATE_NANOS) {
    ...
}
throw new UnsupportedOperationException(
    "Invalid types [" + startTimestamp.dataType(taType() + "] "
        + "If you see this error, there is a bug in DateDiff.resolveType()"
);
```

The pair `(DATETIME, NULL)` falls through to the throw, producing an HTTP 500.

The optimizer normally short-circuits `f(x, null_typed_expr)` to `null`, but not when the
non-null argument is itself a computed expressiomp, null)`) — in
that case both arguments reach `toEvaluator`.

## Reproducer

```esql
SET unmapped_fields="nullify";
FROM partial_mapping_sample_data
| EVAL ts = coalesce(@timestamp, null),
       x  = date_diff("day", ts, totally_nonexistent_field)
```

`totally_nonexistent_field` is absent from the i_fields="nullify"`
gives it type `NULL`. `coalesce(@timestamp, null)` is a computed `DATETIME` expression the
optimizer cannot fold away. Both reach `toEvalua.

## Error

```json
{
  "error": {
    "type": "unsupported_operation_exception",
    "reason": "Invalid types [DATETIME, NULL] If is a bug in DateDiff.resolveType()"
  },
  "status": 500
}
```

## Expected behaviour

`date_diff` with a `NULL`-typed argument should ll-propagation
semantics), not HTTP 500.

## Fix direction

`DateDiff.toEvaluator()` needs a guard for when either timestamp argument has `DataType.NULL`,
returning an evaluator that always emits null — ES|QL function does
via null propagation.

body_text:
### Description

Tests that assert on recovery type, shard location, or other placement-sensitive state should disable rebalancing (e.g. `index.routing.rebalance.enable: none` or `cluster.routing.rebalance.enable: none`) unless the test is *intentionally* exercising rebalance/relocation.

Today this is handled ad hoc: each flake gets a one-off fix after CI mutes it. The same class of race keeps recurring because sibling scenarios or related suites omit the setting.

### Why

Rebalancing can start a PEER recovery or move shards between setup and assertion. That races with tests that expect:

- snapshot recovery stats (e.g. `type: SNAPSHOT`, `stage: DONE`)
- a stable shard copy for reads (term vectors, field caps, etc.)
- specific shard allocation (e.g. testing local/non-local specific behavior, specific transport layer interaction)
- no-relocating within a short timeout after the real work is done

### Proposed approach

1. Let an agent go over resent test failures and look for common patterns where the test fix has been to disable relocations.
2. Look for the most common patterns and apply the fix pro-actively where applicable.

Another approach could be to disable relocation as the default for tests and only enable relocation for tests that specifically test relocation behavior. This seems a lot more invasive though and there is a point to be made about keeping integration tests as close as possible to production setup.

### Evidence / related failures

Same snapshot.restore PEER-vs-SNAPSHOT race (recurring):

- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/159161 (open; muted) — restore path missing `rebalance.enable: none` while siblings in the same file already set it
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/157984 (closed duplicate)
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/157065 → fix https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/157424 (setting added on create only; restore gap left #159161)
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/94354 → fix https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/108768 (original pattern: disable rebalance after restore so `_recovery` is not overwritten by PEER)

Related placement/rebalance flakes and fixes:

- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/98746 / https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/95889 — `tsdb/30_snapshot` restore asserts (same PEER/SNAPSHOT class)
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/148096 → https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/153153 — mtermvectors BWC race when creating a second index triggers rebalance mid-test
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/131394 → https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/133036 — `DataStreamLifecycleDownsampleDisruptionIT` `ensureGreen` timeout from post-work rebalancing (Distributed suggested disable rebalance)
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/85169 — disable rebalancing in `IndexDiskUsageAnalyzerIT`
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/61068 — disable rebalancing in searchable snapshot tests

Counterexample (when re-enabling is fine): https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/122889 — ES|QL REST tests re-enabled rebalance once query execution no longer failed under relocation.

In-progress fix for the latest snapshot.restore instance: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/159172
