body_text:
## Observed

No ES|QL function converts an IPv4 address stored as a number to the `ip` type. An IPv4 address is
32 bits, so it can be written as dotted text, `192.168.1.1`, or as the single integer those bits
form, `3232235777`.
`TO_IP` and the `::ip` cast accept only text and the `ip` type itself.

Reproduced on `main` at `fa290247433fe578902f065aa104c66f0776199a`. From an empty cluster, with no
setup:

```
POST _query
{ "query": "ROW src_ip_int = 3232235777 | EVAL src_ip = TO_IP(src_ip_int) | KEEP src_ip" }
```

Result:

```
Found 1 problem
line 1:45: argument of [TO_IP(src_ip_int)] must be [ip or string], found value [src_ip_int] type [long]
```

Expected `192.168.1.1`. `3232235777` is `0xC0A80101`, that address with its first octet in the most
significant byte. Both comparable engines convert it in one call: ClickHouse's
`IPv4NumToString(3232235777)` returns the string `192.168.1.1` and `toIPv4` returns the typed value,
and BigQuery's `NET.IPV4_FROM_INT64` returns the address as `BYTES`, its reference defining the
encoding as "the least significant bit of the IP address is stored in the least significant bit of
the integer … 1 means 0.0.0.1, and 0x1FF means 0.0.1.255".

## Impact

Affects every user whose IPv4 data is stored numerically, on indices and external datasets alike.
Reaching the `ip` type at all requires rebuilding the dotted quad arithmetically and parsing it back
as text:

```
ROW n = 3232235777
| EVAL src_ip = TO_IP(CONCAT(
    TO_STRING(n / 16777216 % 256), ".",
    TO_STRING(n / 65536 % 256), ".",
    TO_STRING(n / 256 % 256), ".",
    TO_STRING(n % 256)))
| KEEP src_ip
```

That query resolves, and `CIDR_MATCH` and `IP_PREFIX` work on its output, so the data is reachable —
at three divisions, four modulos, four string conversions and a seven-argument concatenation per
row, which the user must write correctly for every column holding an address. Scope is the conversion surface
only: the `ip` data type, its storage and its functions are unaffected, and IPv6 does not arise
because it does not fit an integer.

## Structural cause

The conversion functions derive their accepted input types from a map of evaluators keyed by input
`DataType`, and a type absent from that map is rejected during type resolution, before planning. The
`ip` conversions register evaluators for the string-shaped inputs and for `ip` itself. The numeric
encoding of an address therefore has no entry point into the type: the gap is not in the `ip`
representation, which is a fixed binary value, but in the absence of any mapping from a 32-bit
integer onto it.

## Mechanical cause

[`ToIp`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/fa290247433fe578902f065aa104c66f0776199a/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/expression/function/scalar/convert/ToIp.java#L78-L124)
declares `type = { "ip", "keyword", "text" }` on its `field` parameter, and its `resolveType` calls
`isTypeOrUnionType(field, ToIpLeadingZerosRejected.EVALUATORS::containsKey, …)`. That map's keys are
`IP`, `KEYWORD` and `TEXT`, so `INTEGER`, `LONG` and `UNSIGNED_LONG` are all rejected at one site.

The `::ip` cast reaches the same accepted set by a different route: `EsqlDataTypeConverter` maps the
`ip` target to `ToIpLeadingZerosRejected::new`, so the cast builds that function directly rather than
`ToIp`, and inherits the same evaluator keys.

## Structural fix

Give the numeric encoding an entry point into the type where the string shapes and `ip` itself
already have one: an evaluator keyed by the numeric `DataType`, in the maps the `ip` conversions
share. The
declaration that an integer is an address belongs at the point of use, as an explicit conversion the
user writes, rather than as an implicit coercion driven by a declared field type. That is where both
comparable engines put it: ClickHouse exposes `IPv4NumToString` and `toIPv4`, and BigQuery exposes
`NET.IPV4_FROM_INT64`.

## Mechanical fix

- Add the whole-number input types to the evaluator maps the `ip` conversions share
  (`ToIpLeadingZerosRejected`, `ToIpLeadingZerosDecimal`, `ToIpLeadingZerosOctal`), and widen the
  `field` parameter's declared types on `ToIp` to match.
- Read the number as a 32-bit IPv4 address with the first octet in the most significant byte.
- A number that does not represent an address takes the path the function already uses for an
  unparseable string: `null` with a warning header.
- The `leading_zeros` option applies to text parsing only.

## Acceptance

- `ToIpTests` covers each numeric input type, asserting the converted address for representative
  values including the lowest and highest address, and asserting `null` with a warning for a number
  that does not represent one.
- `ip.csv-spec` covers an end-to-end conversion of an indexed numeric column, and a `CIDR_MATCH`
  over the converted column. No existing `ip.csv-spec` fixture carries a numeric column, so the case
  brings its own fixture.

## Related

- elastic/elasticsearch#137172 — added a `base` argument to `TO_LONG` and `TO_INTEGER`. It widened a
  conversion function's surface by adding a parameter rather than a new input type, so it is
  precedent for the shape of the change and not for its mechanism.

body_text:
Explore whether LIMIT BY could be pushed to every individual branch of FORK:

i.e. turning:

```sql
FROM index
| FORK (fork1) (fork2)
| LIMIT N BY a
```

into:

```sql
FROM index
| FORK (fork1 | LIMIT N BY a) (fork2 | LIMIT N BY a) 
| LIMIT N BY a
```

body_text:
### Description

Are there plans to support write high availability in stateless Elasticsearch, so clients can continue successfully writing when an indexing node fails and its shards are being recovered or reassigned?

The goal is continuous write availability during node failures and shard recovery, in addition to durability of previously acknowledged writes. We would like to avoid an ingestion interruption that lasts until shard recovery completes.

We can accept delayed search visibility. For example, one possible approach might be to continue durably accepting writes into a translog or equivalent durable log while the shard is unavailable, then replay them after recovery. This is only an example of an acceptable trade-off, not a request for a specific implementation; other approaches to write high availability would also meet the need.

Is this capability already supported or on the roadmap? If there is an existing tracking issue or public design discussion, could you point us to it?

Thank you!

See: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/150492#issuecomment-5611224118 for full repro and explanation.

An indexing shard captures the routing-table recipients for a new commit at the start of `onCommitCreation`. A search shard can then be allocated and complete recovery before the newest commit becomes visible to recovery. It recovers from the previously available commit, but is absent from the already-captured recipient list when the new commit notification is sent.

The shard therefore remains on the older commit, and refreshes or `IMMEDIATE` / `WAIT_UNTIL` writes waiting for the newer generation can block until another commit notification arrives. The system should eventually converge on a later commit, so this should be low risk, but we should probably fix the race by strengthening coordination between search-shard recovery and commit notification recipient selection.

body_text:
I discovered while investigating a jump in `WARN` logs from `SigtermTerminationHandler` ([ref](https://elastic.slack.com/archives/C05QR7WNXA4/p1789717320632179)) that this isn't really a meaningful thing to look at: some `WARN` messages emitted by `SigtermTerminationHandler` should be at `INFO` while others should be at `ERROR`, and conversely some `INFO` messages look to be deserving of higher log levels. This ticket is to suggest a review of the logging from this class. More details follow.

---

The `Timed out waiting for graceful shutdown` message indicates a problem deserving of some attention and therefore I think it should be at `WARN` and not `INFO`.

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/ee9cc432043ff6c7408187bcae95f04fed6aaeff/x-pack/plugin/stateless-sigterm/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/stateless/shutdown/SigtermTerminationHandler.java#L124

---

There are two log messages which follow an `assert false`, indicating a bug, and therefore should be at `ERROR`. I would also prefer that we log first and assert second, or at least that the assertion message includes the `currentRoles` field from which you could determine the complete details of the log message.

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/ee9cc432043ff6c7408187bcae95f04fed6aaeff/x-pack/plugin/stateless-sigterm/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/stateless/shutdown/SigtermTerminationHandler.java#L206-L207

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/ee9cc432043ff6c7408187bcae95f04fed6aaeff/x-pack/plugin/stateless-sigterm/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/stateless/shutdown/SigtermTerminationHandler.java#L216-L217

---

Should we be logging the informational message about ongoing recoveries at `WARN`? This is emitted every poll interval; it is normal to see some ongoing recoveries at the start of shutdown, and if the response is empty then that definitely doesn't deserve any more attention.

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/ee9cc432043ff6c7408187bcae95f04fed6aaeff/x-pack/plugin/stateless-sigterm/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/stateless/shutdown/SigtermTerminationHandler.java#L426

Likewise does a failure to retrieve the recoveries status deserve to be a (potentially-paging) `ERROR` log?

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/ee9cc432043ff6c7408187bcae95f04fed6aaeff/x-pack/plugin/stateless-sigterm/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/stateless/shutdown/SigtermTerminationHandler.java#L431

---

We attempt to suppress a `NodeClosedException` when warning about failures from `GetShutdownStatusAction`, but we do not account for the fact that this exception might be wrapped (e.g. in a `SendRequestTransportException`):

body_text:
### Description

The Inference API has first-party services for Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Azure AI Studio, Google Vertex AI, Google AI Studio and IBM watsonx, but none for **Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Generative AI**, Oracle's managed model service. It serves Cohere Command and Embed (including `cohere.embed-v4.0` with selectable output dimensions and `cohere.rerank-v4.0-fast`), Meta Llama, OpenAI, xAI Grok and Google Gemini models behind one regional endpoint, on demand or through dedicated AI clusters.

Today an Elasticsearch user on OCI cannot use it from semantic_text, the inference processor or the retrievers at all: OCI authenticates with its own HTTP request-signature scheme (RSA signature over `(request-target) host date x-content-sha256 content-type content-length`), which none of the existing services or the `custom` service can produce. The workaround is to run a separate proxy that re-signs requests, which means another component to operate and secure.

I would like to add an `ocigenai` service supporting `text_embedding`, `completion`, `chat_completion` (streaming and non-streaming) and `rerank`:

- **Authentication** with an OCI API signing key (`tenancy_id`, `user_id`, `fingerprint`, `private_key` PEM) using the OCI request-signature scheme, implemented in the plugin on top of the existing `HttpRequestSender` stack rather than by adding the OCI Java SDK and its Jersey HTTP client, so there are no new dependencies, licenses, entitlements or third-party audit allow-lists. This is the same approach the Vertex AI service takes for its credentials.
- **Service settings**: `region` (or `url` for private endpoints and other OCI realms), `compartment_id`, `model_id`, optional `endpoint_id` for dedicated AI clusters, `rate_limit`; embeddings also `dimensions`, `similarity`, `max_input_tokens`. **Task settings**: `input_type` and `truncate` for embeddings, `top_n` and `return_documents` for rerank.
- **Chat formats**: Cohere Command models use OCI's `COHERE` chat format; every other family uses `GENERIC`, which maps the unified chat request one to one, including image content, function tools and tool choice, with SSE streaming mapped to unified chunks.

I have an implementation ready on a branch, with unit tests for the signer (verified against the public key), PEM parsing, settings serialization, both request formats, streaming and the service itself through `MockWebServer`, and I have verified it live against OCI Generative AI in `us-chicago-1` for embeddings, both chat formats (streaming and not), and rerank, with a tampered signature correctly rejected with 401. I will open the PR referencing this issue.

It serves Cohere Command and Embed (including `cohere.embed-v4.0` with selectable output dimensions and `cohere.rerank-v4.0-fast`), Meta Llama, OpenAI, xAI Grok and Google Gemini models behind one regional endpoint, on demand or through dedicated AI clusters.

Today an Elasticsearch user on OCI cannot use it from semantic_text, the inference processor or the retrievers at all: OCI authenticates with its own HTTP request-signature scheme (RSA signature over `(request-target) host date x-content-sha256 content-type content-length`), which none of the existing services or the `custom` service can produce. The workaround is to run a separate proxy that re-signs requests, which means another component to operate and secure.

I would like to add an `ocigenai` service supporting `text_embedding`, `completion`, `chat_completion` (streaming and non-streaming) and `rerank`:

- **Authentication** with an OCI API signing key (`tenancy_id`, `user_id`, `fingerprint`, `private_key` PEM) using the OCI request-signature scheme, implemented in the plugin on top of the existing `HttpRequestSender` stack rather than by adding the OCI Java SDK and its Jersey HTTP client, so there are no new dependencies, licenses, entitlements or third-party audit allow-lists. This is the same approach the Vertex AI service takes for its credentials.
- **Service settings**: `region` (or `url` for private endpoints and other OCI realms), `compartment_id`, `model_id`, optional `endpoint_id` for dedicated AI clusters, `rate_limit`; embeddings also `dimensions`, `similarity`, `max_input_tokens`. **Task settings**: `input_type` and `truncate` for embeddings, `top_n` and `return_documents` for rerank.
- **Chat formats**: Cohere Command models use OCI's `COHERE` chat format; every other family uses `GENERIC`, which maps the unified chat request one to one, including image content, function tools and tool choice, with SSE streaming mapped to unified chunks.

I have an implementation ready on a branch, with unit tests for the signer (verified against the public key), PEM parsing, settings serialization, both request formats, streaming and the service itself through `MockWebServer`, and I have verified it live against OCI Generative AI in `us-chicago-1` for embeddings, both chat formats (streaming and not), and rerank, with a tampered signature correctly rejected with 401. I will open the PR referencing this issue.

body_text:
It can happen that LOAD_ALL circuit breaks before being assigned an async id. In this case, the query is aborted with an error but there is no way for the user to understand the cause of the query not going through at all.

Let's make sure we still assign an async id in this case so the user can retrive the (error) result and retry at a later time.

C.f. https://github.com/elastic/esql-planning/issues/1778

### Elasticsearch Version

9.6

### Installed Plugins

_No response_

### Java Version

_bundled_

### OS Version

Darwin Kernel Version 25.6.0

### Problem Description

We allow to provide a pattern when requesting METADATA, e.g.
```
FROM index METADATA _in*
```
will translate to 
```
FROM index METADATA _index, _index_mode
```
---
There is an interesting behavior in the errors reported if you provide an invalid metadata attribute or pattern:
```
FROM index METADATA _index, _fake, _ttt*
```
will yield the following errors:
```
unresolved metadata fields: [?_fake, ?_ttt*]
Unresolved metadata pattern [_fake]
Unresolved metadata pattern [_ttt*]
```

The problems:
1. Redundancy - `_ttt*` reported both as an invalid field and an invalid pattern 
2. `_fake` reported as an invalid pattern, while it's not a pattern expression
3. Inconsistent messaging - invalid fields get reported in a list, while each pattern gets it's own error line

### Steps to Reproduce

See description

### Logs (if relevant)

_No response_

### Elasticsearch Version

Elasticsearch `main` (9.6 snapshot).

### Installed Plugins

Not applicable: this concerns merge-policy selection and configuration, independently of plugins, JVM, or OS.

### Java Version

_bundled_

### OS Version

All

### Problem Description

The time-based merge policy can leave substantial deleted data unreclaimed during continued indexing, increasing storage usage relative to live data. The underlying selection behavior is described in Lucene [issue](https://github.com/apache/lucene/issues/16701).

Elasticsearch selects this policy by default for indices with an `@timestamp` field, not just data streams. Unlike `TieredMergePolicy`, it has no explicit deletion budget driving background reclamation. Deletes influence selection indirectly through estimated segment sizes.

Elasticsearch uses `mergeFactor=32`, compared with Lucene's default of 10. This increases the number of segments required at each level before a merge is considered, with a geometric effect across levels.

For illustration, assuming 50 MB flush segments and full merges:

| Merge factor | Level 0 segment | Level 1 segment | Flush data needed to fill level 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 50 MB | 500 MB | 5 GB |
| 32 | 50 MB | 1.6 GB | 51.2 GB |

This simplified model assumes no reduction from deletes or compression changes. Lucene's bare default would cap merges at 2 GB, but Elasticsearch configures 100 GB for the time-based policy, so merges at this scale are permitted.

With `mergeFactor=32`, filling level 1 requires about ten times as much flush data as with `mergeFactor=10`. At a constant flush rate, this means a correspondingly longer wait in this model.

Meanwhile, 31 segments of 1.6 GB already occupy almost 50 GB while remaining below the segment-count threshold. If they accumulate deletes without becoming eligible for a merge, that space remains unreclaimed. Continued indexing may eventually trigger reclamation, but does not ensure it happens promptly.

Current mitigations are switching `index.merge.policy.type` to `tiered`, which restores delete-budget-based selection but gives up adjacency-only merging, or explicitly invoking force merge with `only_expunge_deletes=true`. The latter is a one-off operation, waits for completion by default, and can incur substantial merge I/O.

On an index that has already accumulated a large number of deleted documents, switching to `tiered` makes many segments eligible for merging at once, and the resulting merge activity can be disruptive. The transition can be staged by setting `index.merge.policy.deletes_pct_allowed` to a high value alongside the policy change and then lowering it gradually as merging stabilizes. Note that `index.merge.policy.max_merged_segment` does apply under the time-based policy, and its default there is larger than for the tiered policy, so segments can grow considerably before any size limit applies.


### Steps to Reproduce

The Lucene [issue](https://github.com/apache/lucene/issues/16701) describes isolated merge-selection tests. The relevant workload in Elasticsearch is:

1. Use an index with the time-based merge policy (an index with mappings including a timestamp field is enough) and the default `mergeFactor=32`.
2. Index data until a level contains multiple segments but fewer than 32 (index in batches with a refresh between each, producing fewer than 32 segments).
3. Apply updates or deletes affecting those segments.
4. Observe background merge selection and deleted-document counts while insufficient new segments reach that level.

Once those merges complete, no further merges occur until enough new segments arrive at that level, regardless of how many documents are deleted.

**Actual behavior:** Heavily deleted segments can remain unmerged because the normal merge-selection conditions are not met.

**Expected behavior:** Background merging should account for substantial reclaimable deletes without requiring the level to fill, while retaining safeguards against excessive write amplification.

Follow-up questions for Elasticsearch:

- Is `mergeFactor=32` still the right default given its effect on reclamation latency?
- Should automatic policy selection depend on data-stream membership rather than the presence of an `@timestamp` field?
- Could existing settings expose any new reclamation controls? `index.merge.policy.deletes_pct_allowed` and `index.merge.policy.expunge_deletes_allowed` currently apply only to the tiered policy. Reusing them where their semantics match would give operators familiar controls.

### Logs (if relevant)

See the Lucene issue for merge-selection results: https://github.com/apache/lucene/issues/16701

### Description

Currently, the logic that selects the merge policy, if none is set, and the index has `@timestamp` in the mapping defaults to `LogByteSizeMergePolicy`. This merge policy works well with append only data.

However, `LogsByteSizeMergePolicy` works well with append data. We observed that a standalone index that receives a lot of updates can accumulate a significant number of deleted documents and the `LogsByteSizeMergePolicy` will not be efficient at merging them because it tries to preserve the `@timestmap` ordering.

We want to investigate making the criteria for picking `LogsByteSizeMergePolicy` stricter, for example, check if the index belongs to a data stream, to avoid this situations.

body_text:
Follow-up from https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/159905.

`SearchDirectory#mergeMetadata` pins the first-seen BCC for each generational file and, for a relocated PIT, ends up pinning every BCC referenced by the PIT's generational files. This is necessary today because when the PIT is opened on a not yet uploaded BCC, the handoff builds the PIT metadata from the metadata present in the source `SearchDirectory` and the target re-acquires each of them when opening the PIT.

This is asymmetric with recovery, which opens generational files from a single BCC. A PIT is anchored on a single commit, so ideally it should be able to reference each generational file from that commit's latest BCC only instead of holding references to several older BCCs.

As suggested in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/159905#discussion_r4072910095 we could give the search node enough information to know the latest unuploaded copies of generational files locations so it can override the blob-file-ranges timestamp and transmit a single-BCC PIT metadata. 

Options discussed on the PR: 
- read the unuploaded VBCC from the indexing shard (e.g. via the get-VBCC-chunk action), or
- maintain/track the VBCC's unuploaded `StatelessCompoundCommit`s on the search node.

Then `mergeMetadata` would only need to pin the PIT commit's latest BCC (as long as it has generational files), making the PIT path symmetric with recovery.

Note that there is a TODO in the code (`SearchDirectory#mergeMetadata`).

body_text:
## Description

When an ES|QL `COMPLETION` command calls an inference connector that uses Anthropic's extended-thinking feature, the request fails with a 400 error. Extended thinking causes the model to return `choices[0].message.content` as an **array of blocks** (a `thinking` block followed by a `text` block) rather than a plain string. The EIS `CompletionResult`/`Choice` deserialiser expects `content` to be a required string field and cannot handle the array form.

## Error

```
status_exception: Failed to send Elastic Inference Service chat completions request.
  Cause: [1:1302] [CompletionResult] failed to parse field [choices]
    Caused by: x_content_parse_exception: [1:1302] [Choice] failed to parse field [message]
      Caused by: illegal_argument_exception: Required [content]
```

`[1:1302]` is the character offset in the raw EIS response body where the array value is encountered. EIS successfully receives a complete, well-formed response from the model — it fails only at deserialisation of the `content` field.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an Anthropic inference endpoint that supports extended thinking (e.g. Claude Fable / claude-3-7-sonnet with `thinking` enabled).
2. Use `COMPLETION` in an ES|QL query with a prompt complex enough to trigger extended thinking in the model.
3. Observe the `status_exception` 400 returned from Elasticsearch.

The error is deterministic for prompts that reliably trigger extended thinking. Simpler prompts that do not trigger extended thinking succeed on the same connector.

## Root Cause

Anthropic's extended-thinking API returns `message.content` as a structured array:

```json
{
  "choices": [{
    "message": {
      "content": [
        { "type": "thinking", "thinking": "<internal reasoning>" },
        { "type": "text",     "text": "<actual model response>" }
      ]
    }
  }]
}
```

EIS's `CompletionResult` / `Choice` parser treats `content` as a required `string` field. When it encounters the array, it cannot find the string value and throws `Required [content]`.

Possible fixes:
- Detect when `content` is an array; concatenate or extract the `text`-type block's `.text` value.
- Make `content` nullable/optional and fall back to reading from the first `text`-typed block.
- Handle the extended-thinking response schema as a distinct `Choice` variant alongside the standard one.

## Environment

- Elastic 9.5.4 (self-managed)
- ES|QL `COMPLETION` command with an Anthropic inference connector

## Expected behaviour

When an ES|QL `COMPLETION` command calls an inference connector that uses Anthropic's extended-thinking feature, the request fails with a 400 error. Extended thinking causes the model to return `choices[0].message.content` as an **array of blocks** (a `thinking` block followed by a `text` block) rather than a plain string. The EIS `CompletionResult`/`Choice` deserialiser expects `content` to be a required string field and cannot handle the array form.

## Error

```
status_exception: Failed to send Elastic Inference Service chat completions request.
  Cause: [1:1302] [CompletionResult] failed to parse field [choices]
    Caused by: x_content_parse_exception: [1:1302] [Choice] failed to parse field [message]
      Caused by: illegal_argument_exception: Required [content]
```

`[1:1302]` is the character offset in the raw EIS response body where the array value is encountered. EIS successfully receives a complete, well-formed response from the model — it fails only at deserialisation of the `content` field.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an Anthropic inference endpoint that supports extended thinking (e.g. Claude Fable / claude-3-7-sonnet with `thinking` enabled).
2. Use `COMPLETION` in an ES|QL query with a prompt complex enough to trigger extended thinking in the model.
3. Observe the `status_exception` 400 returned from Elasticsearch.

The error is deterministic for prompts that reliably trigger extended thinking. Simpler prompts that do not trigger extended thinking succeed on the same connector.

## Root Cause

Anthropic's extended-thinking API returns `message.content` as a structured array:

```json
{
  "choices": [{
    "message": {
      "content": [
        { "type": "thinking", "thinking": "<internal reasoning>" },
        { "type": "text",     "text": "<actual model response>" }
      ]
    }
  }]
}
```

EIS's `CompletionResult` / `Choice` parser treats `content` as a required `string` field. When it encounters the array, it cannot find the string value and throws `Required [content]`.

Possible fixes:
- Detect when `content` is an array; concatenate or extract the `text`-type block's `.text` value.
- Make `content` nullable/optional and fall back to reading from the first `text`-typed block.
- Handle the extended-thinking response schema as a distinct `Choice` variant alongside the standard one.

### Description

**Context**
Users running automation against the transform APIs need to distinguish continuous from batch transforms — for example, to alert when a *continuous* transform is in a stopped state.

**Current behavior**
The transform type is only explicit in the `_cat/transforms` API, which is not well suited to automated/programmatic workflows. In the `GET _transform` response the distinction can only be inferred from the presence or absence of the `sync` field, and the `GET _transform/_stats` response does not return `sync` at all — so from stats alone the type cannot be determined.

**Prior art (the exact field already exists in `_cat`)**
`_cat/transforms` already exposes a `transform_type` column (alias `tt`) with values `batch` / `continuous`, derived as `config.getSyncConfig() == null ? "batch" : "continuous"` (`RestCatTransformAction`). This request is simply to surface that same field in the JSON API responses.

**Request**
Add an explicit `transform_type` field (values `continuous` / `batch`) to the responses of:
- `GET _transform` — https://www.elastic.co/docs/api/doc/elasticsearch/operation/operation-transform-get-transform
- `GET _transform/_stats` — https://www.elastic.co/docs/api/doc/elasticsearch/operation/operation-transform-get-transform-stats

This provides parity with `_cat/transforms`, simplifies documentation, and makes automation more reliable.

**Workaround today**
Infer the type from the presence of the `sync` field in `GET _transform`. This works but is error-prone for automated consumers and is unavailable in `_transform/_stats`.

**Reproduced on**
`main` (9.6.0). `TransformConfig.toXContent` emits no `transform_type`, and `TransformStats.toXContent` emits neither `transform_type` nor `sync`.

### Description

An ES|QL query that does not name its output columns returns every field mapped in every matched index. In cross-cluster search, this produced about **2GB** of request bodies, made up almost entirely of column names.

Query:

```esql
FROM index*
| LIMIT 3
```

With no `KEEP` or other projection, the output schema is the union of every field in every matched index. Across many indices with different mappings, that can be hundreds of thousands to millions of columns. The coordinator serializes the physical plan into the `ClusterComputeRequest` it sends to each remote cluster, and the plan carries an attribute (name, type, id) for every one of those columns. So the size of the request grows with the number of columns, not with anything the query asked for. The remote cluster then fans the plan out again to its data nodes.

The same shape also costs a lot on a single cluster. Reproduced with an internal cluster test, where each index maps 1000 distinct `keyword` fields (the default `index.mapping.total_fields.limit`) and holds one document.


### Proposal

Add a dynamic cluster setting that caps how many **unreferenced** columns a query carries. An unreferenced column is one the query does not name anywhere (`KEEP`, `EVAL`, `WHERE`, `STATS`, `SORT`, and so on). It is only in the output because of the implicit "all fields" projection.

- Suggested name: `esql.query.max_unreferenced_columns`.
- Default: `1000`.
- Users who really want very wide results can raise it, e.g., to `1000000`.
- Columns the query references explicitly are always kept and do not count toward the limit.
- Apply the cap during analysis, before the plan is serialized to remote clusters or data nodes, so the plans sent over the wire stay bounded too.
- When the limit truncates the output, add a response warning saying how many columns were dropped and naming the setting, so the result is never silently narrower than expected.

### Open questions

- Do wildcard projections such as `KEEP foo*` count as references (always kept), or as unreferenced (capped)?
- Which columns survive truncation? Stable ordering (for example, by name) keeps results reproducible, including across clusters in cross-cluster search.
- Should a per-request query setting also be able to override the cluster setting?

body_text:
### Description

In cross-cluster search, the coordinator resolves the field mappings of all matched clusters, merges them into one schema, and sends **the same physical plan** to every remote cluster. When the query has no projection (no `KEEP`), the plan carries an attribute for every column in that merged schema, including columns that no index on the receiving cluster maps. Those columns can only ever be `null` in the rows that cluster returns, but they are still serialized to the cluster and then again to each of its data nodes.

We saw this in a production heap dump. A CCS query over a log index pattern (`LIMIT 3`, no `KEEP`) produced a plan with **532,109 columns**. The receiving cluster maps only **about 35k** of those fields across all of its matching indices; **497k (93%)** exist only on other clusters. Column names dominate the serialized plan, and they are all unique, so the string cache in `PlanStreamOutput` doesn't help.

| | Columns in plan | Per data-node request body | 48 concurrent serializations | Fan-out of 50 data-node requests |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Today (merged schema) | 532,109 | ~65–70 MB | ~2.2 GB of buffers seen in-flight (partially serialized) | ~3.3–3.5 GB |
| Pruned to the cluster's own fields | ~34.6k | ~4.4 MB | ~210 MB | ~220 MB |

Sizes are estimates. They were computed from the actual attribute names in the dump and the serialization code (names written once each, cached parent and leaf names, about 25 B of fixed overhead per attribute). The 2.2 GB in-flight figure was measured.

The receiving cluster's coordinator re-serializes that plan separately for each local data node, on the search pool. In the observed case this tied up 48 of the 49 search threads and was the final push into an OOM.

### Proposal

On the coordinator, build a **per-cluster remote plan** that drops output-only field attributes the target cluster doesn't map, and fill them back in as null blocks when that cluster's pages arrive.

- **Which fields a cluster has:** `IndexResolver.mergedMappings` already iterates per-index field-caps responses whose index names carry the cluster alias (`RemoteClusterAware.splitIndexName`), and it already groups concrete indices by cluster. Record the set of mapped field names per cluster alias alongside that.
- **Prune:** in `ClusterComputeHandler`, today `new RemoteClusterPlan(plan, cluster.concreteIndices, cluster.originalIndices)` uses the same `plan` for every cluster. Instead, derive a copy per cluster. Remove from the sink output and from the `EsRelation` output any `FieldAttribute` that isn't mapped on that cluster and isn't referenced anywhere else in the plan.
- **Pad:** wrap that cluster's `RemoteSink` before `exchangeSource.addRemoteSink(...)` so that each incoming page gets constant-null blocks inserted at the pruned positions. The coordinator keeps seeing the global layout, and nothing downstream changes.
- **Compatibility:** the remote receives an ordinary, smaller plan, so there is no wire-format change and it works against older remotes.

### Constraints

- **Keep referenced attributes.** Only drop columns that are in the output purely because of the implicit "all fields" projection. Fields used in `WHERE`, `SORT`, `STATS`, `EVAL` and so on stay; data nodes already turn fields that are missing locally into nulls.
- **Metadata attributes (`_index` etc.) are always kept.**
- **Behaviour change:** a field added to a remote mapping between field resolution and execution would come back as `null` instead of its value. The resolved schema already decides the columns and types, so this seems acceptable.

### Limits of this fix

- The bound is each cluster's own field union. A cluster with its own mapping explosion still gets a large plan.
- The coordinator and the response still carry the full merged schema. Capping unreferenced columns (#160235) addresses that.
- Within the remote cluster, the plan is still serialized once per data node. Serializing it once and reusing the bytes would remove that multiplier; that's a separate improvement.

Sorry for the AI-generated text - it's based on an investigation made with Claude. I reviewed it, it makes sense so I want to keep it.

Alex' minion speaking:

`SET unmapped_fields="LOAD_ALL"` has no test coverage for the `_source` load counters that #152762 added to `ValuesSourceReaderOperatorStatus` (`source_docs_loaded`, `source_field_reads`, `source_bytes_loaded`), nor for the `profile.unmapped_fields` field that PR also added.

## The counters do work today

Verified manually against a single-node `9.6.0-SNAPSHOT` cluster (1 shard, `dynamic: false` mapping so the extra fields live only in `_source`).

LOAD_ALL does route through `ValuesSourceReaderOperator`: `UnmappedFieldsBlockLoader.rowStrideStoredFieldSpec()` returns `new StoredFieldsSpec(true, false, Set.of())`, so `requiresSource == true` — the predicate the counters key on (`ValuesReader.java:166`, `ValuesFromSingleReader.java:224`). `columnAtATimeReader()` returns `null`, so it is always row-stride, which is the only path that calls `trackSourceFieldReads` / `trackSourceBytesAndRelease`.

5000 docs x 100 fully-unmapped fields:

| query | `source_bytes_loaded` |
|---|---|
| `LOAD_ALL`, `KEEP mapped_kw, u099*` (wildcard -> synthetic `$$unmapped_fields` column) | 33,443,000 |
| `LOAD_ALL`, `KEEP mapped_kw, u099` (concrete -> per-field `UnmappedKeywordBlockLoader`) | 328,890 |

Identical output, 100x difference in `_source` read, correctly reported. `source_bytes_loaded` is therefore the counter that exposes the LOAD_ALL cliff: a wildcard stops `DetermineUnmappedFieldsToKeep` from resolving a concrete field set, so the whole `_source` is read per doc.

## The gap

Nothing asserts any of this.

- `ValuesSourceReaderOperatorTests.testSourceLoadProfileCounters` / `testSourceLoadProfileCountersForUnmappedField` (both added by #152762) drive the operator with a plain `KeywordFieldMapper.KeywordFieldType`. Neither `UnmappedFieldsBlockLoader` nor `UnmappedKeywordBlockLoader` is exercised.
- `RestEsqlIT` asserts shape only, not value:
  ```java
  .entry("source_docs_loaded", greaterThanOrEqualTo(0))
  .entry("source_field_reads", greaterThanOrEqualTo(0))
  .entry("source_bytes_loaded", greaterThanOrEqualTo(0));
  ```
  This passes if every counter is permanently 0.
- The LOAD_ALL functional suites (`unmapped-load-all.csv-spec`, `294_unmapped_load_all_valueless_fields.yml`, `295_unmapped_load_all_type_conflict.yml`, `297_unmapped_load_object_from_synthetic_source.yml`, `298_unmapped_load_all_columnar.yml`) never request `"profile": true`.

So if the synthetic column stopped being source-backed, all three counters would silently report 0 and CI would stay green.

## Concrete regression risks

1. `UnmappedFieldsBlockLoader.rowStrideStoredFieldSpec()` changing away from `requiresSource == true`.
2. A column-at-a-time reader being added to `UnmappedFieldsBlockLoader` (currently `null`). That path never calls the tracking 

## Suggested coverage

- A `ValuesSourceReaderOperatorTests` case built on the real `UnmappedFieldsBlockLoader`, asserting `sourceDocsLoaded == docCount`, `sourceFieldReads == docCount`, and `sourceBytesLoaded > 0`.
- An end-to-end assertion that LOAD_ALL over an index with fully-unmapped `_source` fields reports `source_bytes_loaded > 0`, and that the wildcard-`KEEP` form reads materially more than the concrete-`KEEP` form. The 100x separation measured above is stable enough to assert with a wide margin.
- While we're at it, make sure that LOAD also has a similar end-to-end assertion
- Pin `profile.unmapped_fields == "load_all"`, which currently has no test either.

## What should *not* be asserted

`source_field_reads` and `values_loaded` stay at `docs x 1` under LOAD_ALL regardless of how many fields are materialized, because `$$unmapped_fields` is a single block. That is the truthful count — LOAD_ALL performs one `_source` read per doc and filters it, rather than N per-field reads — so tests should lock that in rather than expect it to scale with field count.

This is a serverless suppressed error, the query text is not logged, the reproducer below is reverse engineered according to the plan logged.

```
simplified query
TS k8s
| FORK
    (WHERE cluster != "staging" | EVAL cluster = TO_STRING(cluster))
    (WHERE cluster == "staging" | EVAL cluster = "Other")
| STATS max_bytes = MAX(TO_LONG(network.total_bytes_in)) BY cluster
| SORT CASE(cluster == "Other", -1.0, max_bytes::double) DESC
;

line 5:3: Plan [TimeSeriesAggregate[[_tsid{m}#107],[LASTOVERTIME($$TO_LONG(network>$LASTOVERTIME$0{r$}#110,@timestamp{r}#103,true[BOOLEAN],PT0S[TIME_DURATION]) AS LASTOVERTIME_$1#108, VALUES(cluster{r}#105,true[BOOLEAN],PT0S[TIME_DURATION]) AS cluster#105] ,null,@timestamp{r}#103,TS_COMMAND]] optimized incorrectly due to missing references [_tsid{m}#107]

closer to the original query in serverless log
TS k8s
| FORK
    (WHERE cluster NOT IN (
        TS k8s
        | STATS max_bytes = MAX(TO_LONG(network.total_bytes_in)) BY cluster
        | SORT max_bytes DESC
        | LIMIT 2
        | KEEP cluster
     )
     | EVAL cluster = "Other"
    )
    (WHERE cluster IN (
        TS k8s
        | STATS max_bytes = MAX(TO_LONG(network.total_bytes_in)) BY cluster
        | SORT max_bytes DESC
        | LIMIT 2
        | KEEP cluster
     )
     | EVAL cluster = TO_STRING(cluster)
    )
| STATS max_bytes = MAX(TO_LONG(network.total_bytes_in)) BY cluster
| SORT CASE(cluster == "Other", -1.0, max_bytes::double) DESC
;
line 21:3: Plan [TimeSeriesAggregate[[_tsid{m}#69],[LASTOVERTIME($$TO_LONG(network>$LASTOVERTIME$0{r$}#72,@timestamp{r}#55,true[BOOLEAN],PT0S[TIME_DURATION]) AS LASTOVERTIME_$1#70, VALUES(cluster{r}#57,true[BOOLEAN],PT0S[TIME_DURATION]) AS cluster#57],null, @timestamp{r}#55,TS_COMMAND]] optimized incorrectly due to missing references [_tsid{m}#69]
```

**Root Cause**

In TranslateTimeSeriesAggregate (an Analyzer "Finish Analysis" rule that runs AFTER resolveMergePlan):

1. findTimeSeriesSourceTsid walks the plan tree, iterating all children of a Fork. When it visits Branch 1's EsRelation it sets tsid = _tsid#A; then Branch 2's EsRelation overwrites it with tsid = _tsid#B. The last branch wins.
2. The first-phase TimeSeriesAggregate is created with firstPassGroupings = [_tsid#B].
3. But resolveMergePlan (which ran earlier in "Resolution") already fixed the Fork's output to _tsid#A (from outputUnion, first branch wins). The Fork's output and the TimeSeriesAggregate's grouping now reference different NameIds.
4. During Optimization, PruneColumns sees _tsid#B in used (from the TimeSeriesAggregate), but the Fork's output has _tsid#A. Since _tsid#A ≠ _tsid#B (different NameId), it prunes _tsid#A from the Fork's output.
5. Post-optimization verifier fires: TimeSeriesAggregate references _tsid#B, Fork output has neither → "optimized incorrectly due to missing references [_tsid]".

This affects any Fork with 2+ branches below a TS STATS, regardless of whether branches use IN subqueries.

**Fix — two changes in TranslateTimeSeriesAggregate.java**

Change 1: findTimeSeriesSourceTsid — stop at a MergePlan, use its output

When the plan being walked is a MergePlan (Fork), don't descend into branches (which have per-branch EsRelation instances with per-branch NameIds). Instead, read _tsid from the Fork's own output(), which already holds the canonical attribute established by outputUnion during resolution.
```
// Add before the generic "for children" loop:
if (plan instanceof MergePlan) {
    for (Attribute attr : plan.output()) {
        if (attr.name().equals(MetadataAttribute.TSID_FIELD)) {
            tsid.set(attr);
            return;
        }
    }
    return;  // _tsid not in Fork output — leave holder unchanged
}
```
After this change, tsid = _tsid#A, consistent with the Fork's output.

Change 2: addTsidToTimeSeriesSource — replace a same-named but different-NameId _tsid instead of duplicating

The transformer lambda currently checks relation.output().contains(tsid) (NameId equality). When a Fork branch's EsRelation already has a _tsid by a different NameId, contains returns false and the code adds the canonical _tsid#A alongside the existing _tsid#B, producing a duplicate. **Root Cause**

In TranslateTimeSeriesAggregate (an Analyzer "Finish Analysis" rule that runs AFTER resolveMergePlan):

1. findTimeSeriesSourceTsid walks the plan tree, iterating all children of a Fork. When it visits Branch 1's EsRelation it sets tsid = _tsid#A; then Branch 2's EsRelation overwrites it with tsid = _tsid#B. The last branch wins.
2. The first-phase TimeSeriesAggregate is created with firstPassGroupings = [_tsid#B].
3. But resolveMergePlan (which ran earlier in "Resolution") already fixed the Fork's output to _tsid#A (from outputUnion, first branch wins). The Fork's output and the TimeSeriesAggregate's grouping now reference different NameIds.
4. During Optimization, PruneColumns sees _tsid#B in used (from the TimeSeriesAggregate), but the Fork's output has _tsid#A. Since _tsid#A ≠ _tsid#B (different NameId), it prunes _tsid#A from the Fork's output.
5. Post-optimization verifier fires: TimeSeriesAggregate references _tsid#B, Fork output has neither → "optimized incorrectly due to missing references [_tsid]".

This affects any Fork with 2+ branches below a TS STATS, regardless of whether branches use IN subqueries.

**Fix — two changes in TranslateTimeSeriesAggregate.java**

Change 1: findTimeSeriesSourceTsid — stop at a MergePlan, use its output

When the plan being walked is a MergePlan (Fork), don't descend into branches (which have per-branch EsRelation instances with per-branch NameIds). Instead, read _tsid from the Fork's own output(), which already holds the canonical attribute established by outputUnion during resolution.
```
// Add before the generic "for children" loop:
if (plan instanceof MergePlan) {
    for (Attribute attr : plan.output()) {
        if (attr.name().equals(MetadataAttribute.TSID_FIELD)) {
            tsid.set(attr);
            return;
        }
    }
    return;  // _tsid not in Fork output — leave holder unchanged
}
```
After this change, tsid = _tsid#A, consistent with the Fork's output.

Change 2: addTsidToTimeSeriesSource — replace a same-named but different-NameId _tsid instead of duplicating

The transformer lambda currently checks relation.output().contains(tsid) (NameId equality). When a Fork branch's EsRelation already has a _tsid by a different NameId, contains returns false and the code adds the canonical _tsid#A alongside the existing _tsid#B, producing a duplicate. Instead, replace the existing attribute:
```
private static LogicalPlan addTsidToTimeSeriesSource(LogicalPlan plan, Attribute tsid, boolean requiredTimeSeriesSource) {
    return TranslateTimeSeriesUtils.transformTimeSeriesSource(plan, relation -> {
        IndexMode indexMode = requiredTimeSeriesSource ? relation.indexMode() : IndexMode.STANDARD;
        if (relation.output().contains(tsid)) {
            return relation.withIndexMode(indexMode);
        }
        // Branch EsRelation may already have _tsid under a different NameId (e.g. a FORK where
        // each branch has its own EsRelation instance). Replace rather than duplicating.
        List<Attribute> output = relation.output();
        for (int i = 0; i < output.size(); i++) {
            if (output.get(i).name().equals(tsid.name())) {
                List<Attribute> newOutput = new ArrayList<>(output);
                newOutput.set(i, tsid);
                return relation.withIndexMode(indexMode).withAttributes(newOutput);
            }
        }
        return relation.withIndexMode(indexMode).withAttributes(CollectionUtils.combine(output, tsid));
    });
}
```
After both changes, Branch 2's EsRelation outputs _tsid#A (replaced), Fork output has _tsid#A, TimeSeriesAggregate groups by _tsid#A — all consistent, verifier passes.

body_text:
Following Felix's suggestion after #159234: can we retire the `scrape_interval` parameter for `PROMQL`, and document the new behavior of rate and related aggregations?

## Context

#159234 links the nearest populated buckets for each time series, allowing rate/increase calculations to interpolate across empty buckets within a five-minute lookback/lookahead. This includes exponential histogram increases. Zooming into sparse counter data can therefore retain results even when the immediately preceding bucket is empty.

The [PROMQL command documentation](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/docs/reference/query-languages/esql/_snippets/commands/layout/promql.md) still defines `scrape_interval` (default `1m`) as an input to implicit range selection: `max(step, scrape_interval)`. The interpolation improvement does not by itself establish that this separate role is redundant.

## Follow-up

- [ ] Evaluate whether `scrape_interval` is still needed after #159234. Check its role in implicit range selectors across affected functions, including queries where `step` is smaller than the collection interval. Keep explicitly supplied range selectors distinct from interpolation lookback/lookahead.
- [ ] Record the decision. If retiring the parameter, define replacement implicit-window behavior and a compatibility/deprecation path for existing queries. If retaining it, explain when users still need it.
- [ ] Update the documentation for affected aggregations, including `rate`, `increase`, and applicable histogram variants. Explain interpolation across sparse buckets, the five-minute bounds, midpoint handling of gaps, and when insufficient surrounding samples can still yield no result. Clarify which behavior applies to ES|QL and PROMQL.
- [ ] Add a zoomed-in sparse-counter example and regression coverage for the chosen implicit-window behavior, explicit ranges, and gaps beyond the interpolation bounds.

The outcome should make it clear whether users still need to configure a collection interval and what results to expect when zooming below that interval.

### Description

Follow-up from the "graceful termination under load" testing of `LOAD_ALL` (see [esql-planning#1778 comment](https://github.com/elastic/esql-planning/issues/1778#issuecomment-5488032092)) and the cancellation fix in #160053 (issue #159914).

An async ES|QL query (`POST /_query/async`) that is rejected by the circuit breaker **before** it is stored is indistinguishable, from the client's point of view, from a query that was never submitted. In the report's **T3** scenario, wide `LOAD_ALL` queries hit the breaker while `ExpandUnmappedFieldsPostProcessor` allocated builders for a very large number of columns. The `circuit_breaking_exception` was returned synchronously, before an async ID was stored, so:

- `is_running` is never observable as `false` for these queries.
- A subsequent `GET /_query/async/{id}` cannot retrieve the failure by ID (there is no ID).

This is distinct from cancellation (now handled by #160053): a circuit-broken query is already dead and there is nothing to cancel — but a client that submitted it with `wait_for_completion_timeout: 0ms` still has no ID to poll and no stored error to read back.

### Proposal

Allocate the async query ID (and store a placeholder/`is_running` entry) **before** the expensive coordinator work — in particular before the `ExpandUnmappedFieldsPostProcessor` expansion phase — so that a failure occurring during expansion (circuit breaking or otherwise) is retrievable by ID via `GET /_query/async/{id}` rather than only surfacing as a synchronous error on submission.

### Notes

- Scope is the **async** query lifecycle / storage ordering, not the expansion loop itself.
- Original recommendation #2 from the T-series report; recommendation #1 (cancellation checkpoints in `ExpandUnmappedFieldsPostProcessor`) is addressed by #160053.

Follow-up from the "graceful termination under load" testing of `LOAD_ALL` (see [esql-planning#1778 comment](https://github.com/elastic/esql-planning/issues/1778#issuecomment-5488032092)) and the cancellation fix in #160053 (issue #159914).

An async ES|QL query (`POST /_query/async`) that is rejected by the circuit breaker **before** it is stored is indistinguishable, from the client's point of view, from a query that was never submitted. In the report's **T3** scenario, wide `LOAD_ALL` queries hit the breaker while `ExpandUnmappedFieldsPostProcessor` allocated builders for a very large number of columns. The `circuit_breaking_exception` was returned synchronously, before an async ID was stored, so:

- `is_running` is never observable as `false` for these queries.
- A subsequent `GET /_query/async/{id}` cannot retrieve the failure by ID (there is no ID).

This is distinct from cancellation (now handled by #160053): a circuit-broken query is already dead and there is nothing to cancel — but a client that submitted it with `wait_for_completion_timeout: 0ms` still has no ID to poll and no stored error to read back.

### Proposal

Allocate the async query ID (and store a placeholder/`is_running` entry) **before** the expensive coordinator work — in particular before the `ExpandUnmappedFieldsPostProcessor` expansion phase — so that a failure occurring during expansion (circuit breaking or otherwise) is retrievable by ID via `GET /_query/async/{id}` rather than only surfacing as a synchronous error on submission.

### Notes

- Scope is the **async** query lifecycle / storage ordering, not the expansion loop itself.
- Original recommendation #2 from the T-series report; recommendation #1 (cancellation checkpoints in `ExpandUnmappedFieldsPostProcessor`) is addressed by #160053.

JSON_EXTRACT differentiates between `{"foo": {"bar": ...}}` and `{"foo.bar": ...}`. The former requires `JSON_EXTRACT(json, "foo.bar")`, the latter `JSON_EXTRACT(json, "['foo.bar']")`.

This is correct for JSON, but can be an obstacle when users don't care about the distinction (dirty data), or when `JSON_EXTRACT` is used to work on `_source`: using synthetic source will generally lose the distinction between `"foo": {"bar": ...}` and `"foo.bar":`, so a  query may stop working if we point it at an otherwise identical index but flip the source from synthetic to stored (or vice versa); this is posing a migration obstacle.

Let's consider a way to make the `JSON_EXTRACT`'s path argument more lenient to dots in the path. This could be e.g. a query SETting.

## Description

Part of the `validation/logsdb` workstream in #155883.

### Problem

The nightly duels on `elastic/logs` and `textbench` compare ColumNAR against `ES819` inside `logsdb_columnar`. The contender arm opts into the codec through a track parameter and the baseline arm sets nothing.

#159646 makes the codec default to on. The baseline arm would inherit that default, so both arms would run ColumNAR and the comparison would no longer measure `ES819` against ColumNAR.

### Proposal

Add an index-mode comparison for both workloads: `logsdb` against `logsdb_columnar`, each at its defaults. This measures what a user experiences when switching modes.

The `logsdb` baseline still uses `ES819` doc values. The modes also differ in whether keyword fields are indexed by default, and both tracks leave `index` unset on effectively every keyword field, so that difference applies across both workloads. Results therefore combine the indexing change with the codec change, and the codec's contribution cannot be isolated.

> [!NOTE]
> `event.original` sets `index` explicitly in `elastic/logs` and so is unaffected by the mode default.

I propose replacing the existing codec duels with this comparison, because migration impact is the question users face when adopting `logsdb_columnar`.

### Decision

Whether the dedicated codec duels remain:

1. **Fix and retain them, and add the mode comparisons separately.** Keeps controlled `ES819` against ColumNAR coverage, at the cost of more benchmark runs and more to maintain. The track must emit an explicit `false` on the baseline arm, since omitting the setting is what causes the problem above.
2. **Replace them with the mode comparisons.** Fewer runs, and the adoption question is answered directly, but no controlled `ES819` against ColumNAR comparison remains.

The companion `clickbench` issue faces the same choice with a different mode comparison, and the two should be settled consistently.

## Description

Part of the `validation/logsdb` workstream in #155883.

### Problem

The `clickbench` nightly duel compares ColumNAR against `ES819` inside the `doc-values-only` scenario, which uses `index.mode: columnar`. The contender arm opts into the codec through a track parameter and the baseline arm sets nothing.

#159646 makes the codec default to on. The baseline arm would inherit that default, so both arms would run ColumNAR and the comparison would no longer measure `ES819` against ColumNAR.

### Proposal

Add an index-mode comparison: `standard` against `columnar`. This measures what a user experiences when moving a ClickBench-shaped workload to `columnar`.

`standard` uses stock Lucene doc values rather than `ES819`, so replacing the codec duel would remove the dedicated `ES819` comparison for this workload entirely. `standard` also stores `_source` where `columnar` uses synthetic source, and leaves inverted indexes on by default where `columnar` leaves them off.

I propose replacing the codec duel with this comparison, because migration impact is the question users face when adopting `columnar`.

### Decision

Whether the dedicated codec duel remains:

1. **Fix and retain it, and add the mode comparison separately.** Keeps the only controlled `ES819` against ColumNAR coverage this workload has, at the cost of more benchmark runs and more to maintain. The track must emit an explicit `false` on the baseline arm, since omitting the setting is what causes the problem above.
2. **Replace it with the mode comparison.** Fewer runs, and the adoption question is answered directly, but this workload is left with no `ES819` comparison.

Secondary: should the mode comparison use `standard` at its defaults, or set synthetic source on the baseline? Source storage could otherwise dominate the storage difference.

The companion `elastic/logs` and `textbench` issue faces the same choice with a different mode comparison, and the two should be settled consistently.

Part of the `validation/logsdb` workstream in #155883.

### Problem

The `clickbench` nightly duel compares ColumNAR against `ES819` inside the `doc-values-only` scenario, which uses `index.mode: columnar`. The contender arm opts into the codec through a track parameter and the baseline arm sets nothing.

#159646 makes the codec default to on. The baseline arm would inherit that default, so both arms would run ColumNAR and the comparison would no longer measure `ES819` against ColumNAR.

### Proposal

Add an index-mode comparison: `standard` against `columnar`. This measures what a user experiences when moving a ClickBench-shaped workload to `columnar`.

`standard` uses stock Lucene doc values rather than `ES819`, so replacing the codec duel would remove the dedicated `ES819` comparison for this workload entirely. `standard` also stores `_source` where `columnar` uses synthetic source, and leaves inverted indexes on by default where `columnar` leaves them off.

I propose replacing the codec duel with this comparison, because migration impact is the question users face when adopting `columnar`.

### Decision

Whether the dedicated codec duel remains:

1. **Fix and retain it, and add the mode comparison separately.** Keeps the only controlled `ES819` against ColumNAR coverage this workload has, at the cost of more benchmark runs and more to maintain. The track must emit an explicit `false` on the baseline arm, since omitting the setting is what causes the problem above.
2. **Replace it with the mode comparison.** Fewer runs, and the adoption question is answered directly, but this workload is left with no `ES819` comparison.

Secondary: should the mode comparison use `standard` at its defaults, or set synthetic source on the baseline? Source storage could otherwise dominate the storage difference.

The companion `elastic/logs` and `textbench` issue faces the same choice with a different mode comparison, and the two should be settled consistently.

## Description

`text` and `match_only_text` use ColumNAR in `columnar` and `logsdb_columnar` (#159508, #159739), but some query behavior is not explicitly covered by tests.

The remaining gaps are:

- **Index modes:** `AbstractColumnarBinaryLayoutTestCase` only exercises `columnar`, not `logsdb_columnar`.
- **Phrase queries:** The existing tests do not cover unindexed phrase behavior or `text` phrase queries.
- **Unsupported queries:** Expected rejections for phrase, intervals, span prefix, and fuzzy queries on unindexed `text` fields are not asserted.

### Work items

- [x] Extend the shared query tests to cover both columnar index modes.
- [x] Verify phrase behavior with and without postings for `text` and `match_only_text`.
- [x] Assert expected failures for unsupported queries instead of silently accepting empty results.
- [x] Cover representative single-valued, multi-valued, and missing-value cases.

DSL equivalence testing against ES819 is tracked separately in #160326.

Related to #155883.

## Description

Part of the `validation/logsdb` workstream in #155883.

### Problem

In `elastic/logs`, the [`logging-querying` challenge](https://github.com/elastic/rally-tracks/blob/master/elastic/logs/challenges/logging-querying.json) queries `message`, a `match_only_text` field, with four ES|QL `MATCH` operations and three `MATCH_PHRASE` operations. In the benchmarks inspected, that is all the text query coverage in a columnar index mode.

No benchmark queries a `text` field, although the `logs-k8-application.log` data stream contains populated `text` fields. `textbench` does not cover this either: its only text-family field is `Body`, mapped as `pattern_text`.

With ColumNAR storage and query support for text (#159508, #159739), we need performance coverage beyond those existing operations. Functional coverage is being extended separately in #160313.

### Proposal

Extend the text operations used by the `elastic/logs` columnar comparison in #160305.

| Field type | Existing coverage | Proposed additions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `match_only_text` (`message`) | ES\|QL `MATCH` and `MATCH_PHRASE` | Query-string queries with a phrase clause, ES\|QL `LIKE` or `RLIKE`, and highlighting |
| `text` | No query operations found in the inspected benchmarks | Analyzed matching, phrase matching, query-string queries, ES\|QL `LIKE` or `RLIKE`, and highlighting |

- [ ] Select a populated `text` field from `logs-k8-application.log`
- [ ] Add representative operations for the missing query families, reusing existing coverage where it already applies
- [ ] Verify the operations return meaningful results on the benchmark data
- [ ] Identify which operations exercise ColumNAR value loading, since matching uses postings by default
- [ ] Add the operations to the comparison dashboard

Direct column matching with postings disabled belongs to #160315 rather than here.

Done when each proposed addition has an operation in the chosen challenge and a panel on the comparison dashboard.

### Recommendation

Start with one representative operation per missing query family and field type, then agree which of them should run nightly.

### Open decision

Should we extend the shared `logging-querying` challenge, or add a separate challenge for this comparison? The existing challenge is shared by eight nightly benchmarks, so extending it adds runtime to all eight and may affect comparisons with earlier runs. A separate challenge would let us add these operations only to the columnar comparison.

## Description

Part of the `validation/logsdb` workstream in #155883.

### Problem

What does a user gain and lose by disabling postings on text fields in a columnar index?

`text` and `match_only_text` keep postings by default in columnar modes. Setting `index: false` makes supported queries fall back to ColumNAR doc values (#159508, #159739), but we have no measurements of the storage, indexing throughput and query latency tradeoff.

### Proposal

Compare `elastic/logs` in `logsdb_columnar` with postings enabled versus disabled on the targeted `text` and `match_only_text` fields, with no other change to settings or mappings.

- Measure storage, indexing throughput and query latency.
- Reuse queries from #160314 that #160313 establishes as supported without postings.
- Add at least one DSL `prefix`, `wildcard` or `regexp` query, verifying postings execution on one arm and column execution on the other. With postings enabled these run off the inverted index, so the unindexed arm is the only place that path runs.
- Include selective and broad queries, to see how the tradeoff changes with the number of matching documents.
- Check equivalent results before comparing performance. An unsupported query that returns nothing would otherwise look like a large speedup.

Record the results and what they imply for users considering `index: false`. Unlike #160305 and #160306, this comparison changes the text mapping rather than the index mode.

### Recommendation

Run this as an optional one-off experiment, starting with queries already known to work in both configurations. Use the results to decide whether recurring coverage is worthwhile.

### Open decision

Is this experiment worth scheduling alongside the planned benchmark work?

## Description

Part of the `validation/logsdb` workstream in #155883.

### Problem

Keyword has a DSL behavior duel (#158283): one corpus into an `ES819` baseline and a ColumNAR contender, asserting both expose the same behavior. There is no text counterpart in the suites I looked at.

`text` and `match_only_text` write ColumNAR columns under the same gates (#159508, #159739). The DSL coverage they do have runs over six single-word documents built in one pass, so no long multi-word values and no merge. ES|QL is covered separately by `CsvColumnarIT` and `CsvColumnarCodecIT`, which are two corpus runs rather than a paired comparison.

### Proposal

Same index mode and mappings on both arms, `index.columnar_codec.enabled` false on the baseline and true on the contender. Cover `text` and `match_only_text`, in `columnar` and `logsdb_columnar`, with `index` at its default and with `index: false`.

With `index: false` the queries match the whole stored value rather than analyzed tokens, so the unindexed query set needs non-empty whole-value matches or it compares zero against zero. Expected outcomes come from #160313; the two codecs agreeing does not make the behavior correct.

- [x] Set the codec setting explicitly on both arms and assert the resulting codec before comparing
- [x] Duel the baseline against a copy of itself first, as #158283 does, so corpus or check bugs fail as baseline failures
- [x] Corpus with long multi-word values, dense and sparse, missing fields, arrays and inline nulls, unicode, multi-valued
- [x] Compare matching doc ids and retrieved values, plus scores and order where the arms should agree
- [x] Compare results before and after merging segments
- [x] Record which paths each run exercised, for a representative subset
- [x] Reuse or extend the #158283 harness, keyword-typed today

### Open decision

Run both postings configurations every time, or draw one per run from the seed. Running both is what I would propose; sampling only if the runtime turns out to matter.

body_text:
### Description

With the addition of the `dense_vector` query in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/147820, we added a new reliance on the `VectorScorer.Bulk` scoring path. Similarly, https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/152158 exposes additional usage of the bulk path. We should simplify vector rescore prefetching while also improving `dense_vector` performance for larger-than-memory deployments by adding prefetch logic to the `VectorScorer.Bulk` scoring iterator. It might look something like the `PrefetchingCentroidIterator`, though it doesn't need to.

One key detail for the `RescoreKnnVectorQuery` prefetch implementation is that it operates over a sparse collection of vectors from each segment until it has prefetched sufficiently many vectors before calling the bulk score method. This might mean that cannot simply copy the `PrefetchingCentroidIterator`, though in a separate issue, I've already argued for additional feedback loops where the downstream consumer should be able to hint that some number of elements is likely to be needed in the future https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/151343.

### Problem Description

I think the `elasticsearch-node` tool has some bug since version 9.5. Kibana is doing something that the tool cannot interpret. If I execute for example `/usr/share/elasticsearch/bin/elasticsearch-node remove-index-settings index.hidden` I get:

### Description

Follow-up from #159914 / #160053, prompted by [@dnhatn's review comment](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/160053#pullrequestreview-5324916562):

> Unrelated to this PR, but `ExpandUnmappedFieldsPostProcessor` seems like an operator to me, running with the final driver. I haven't looked into it long enough to understand the constraints, but if it ran as an operator in the final driver, we could have task descriptions, profiling, yielding, and cancellation built in. These would be helpful for debugging and diagnosing production issues.

Today the `SET unmapped_fields="LOAD_ALL"` expansion runs as a static coordinator-side step (`ExpandUnmappedFieldsPostProcessor.expand(...)` called from `EsqlSession`) **after** all compute drivers finish and pages are collected into a `Result`. Because it lives outside the driver runner, it does not participate in any of the compute framework's built-in machinery:

- **No profiling** — expansion time never appears in the `"final"` driver profile.
- **No task descriptions** — the work is invisible to task-level introspection.
- **No driver-native cancellation** — #160053 had to bolt on manual `BooleanSupplier` polling every 1024 rows.
- **No yielding / fair scheduling** — see #160286; a large expansion can monopolize the completing thread.

### Proposal

Convert `ExpandUnmappedFieldsPostProcessor` into a compute `Operator` inserted into the coordinator's final driver (before the `OutputOperator`), so expansion inherits profiling, task descriptions, cancellation, and cooperative yielding for free.

### Relationship to existing issues

- **Supersedes the approach in #160286** ("avoid monopolizing the coordinator thread"). #160286 proposes a coordinator-side chunked re-dispatch (`AbstractRunnable` re-queuing itself) that keeps expansion *outside* the driver. Running expansion as a driver operator addresses the same thread-monopolization concern more holistically (driver time-slicing/yielding) while also delivering profiling + task descriptions + cancellation. If this issue is taken up, #160286 should be closed as superseded; otherwise #160286 remains the lighter-weight fallback.
- **Independent of #160278** (async-query ID storage ordering vs. circuit breaker) — that concerns the async lifecycle, not where expansion runs.

### Constraints / why this is not a mechanical refactor

The per-row transform (`rewritePage`, JSON leaf flattening, `UnmappedKeywordValues`, circuit-breaker reservations) ports almost verbatim. The non-trivial work is pipeline integration:

1. **Finish-gated emission.** The output columns are not known until *every* page has been seen — expansion computes a global union of unmapped leaf field names across all rows and fixes column order via `UnmappedFieldsOrdering`. So it cannot be a simple 1-page-in/1-page-out `AbstractPageMappingOperator`; it must buffer input and emit on `finish()` (aggregation-style). Pages are already fully buffered before expansion today, so the memory footprint does not regress.
2. **Dynamic output schema (biggest gap).** `OutputOperator`'s columns and `Result.schema` are fixed at plan time from `outputExec.output()`, which still contains the synthetic `UnmappedFieldsAttribute`. 3. **Cancellation semantics change.** Expansion would abort via driver/task cancellation rather than the current post-compute listener polling; `LoadAllCancellationIT` depends on the current ordering and would need reworking.
4. **Batch-only.** `LOAD_ALL` is already incompatible with `streaming=true`; global buffering + schema discovery is fundamentally at odds with streaming, so this stays a batch-only path.

Column-expansion is 1→1 (wider) page, not row-expansion, so no new driver-yielding infrastructure is needed for page splitting.

- Planner wiring in `LocalExecutionPlanner` to insert the operator before `OutputExec` when the plan output contains `UnmappedFieldsAttribute`.
- Dynamic schema propagation from the final driver to `Result` (`ComputeService` / `EsqlSession`).

### Description

#### **Feature Request**
Add native support in Elasticsearch for tabular foundation transformer models such as **[TabFM (Google Research)](https://github.com/google-research/tabfm)** and **[TabPFN (Prior-Labs)](https://huggingface.co/Prior-Labs/tabpfn_3)** to enable zero-shot and few-shot classification directly inside Elasticsearch without requiring external supervised training pipelines for every classification task.

---

#### **Context & Use Case (Story)**
We classify and enrich security-relevant string and entity fields to add threat context, specifically focusing on fields like:
- `user_agent.original` (e.g., suspicious/anomalous client identification)
- `dns.question.name` (e.g., DGA detection, suspicious or tunneling domains)
- `url.original` (e.g., malicious URL categorization)

In the past, adding classification context for each of these distinct targets required building custom supervised models from scratch:
1. Manually gathering and cleaning labeled datasets for each specific task (domains, user agents, URLs).
2. Using **AutoGluon** externally to train tabular/tree-based models (such as XGBoost).
3. Exporting the trained models and uploading them into Elasticsearch via `eland` / the Trained Models API.

This workflow is time-consuming and labor-intensive because every new classification task requires repeating the data collection, cleaning, and training pipeline externally before we can produce classifications. Having a tabular foundation model that supports zero-shot or few-shot in-context learning would eliminate this per-task training overhead.

---

#### **What We Had to Do Instead (Current Workaround & Pain Points)**
Without native tabular foundation model support, our workflow is constrained to:
- **Heavy Data Preparation Overhead:** Spending significant manual effort sourcing, labeling, and sanitizing datasets for every single field we want to classify.
- **External Training Loops:** Relying on external Python/AutoGluon environments to train XGBoost models, convert them, and import them into Elasticsearch.
- **Rigid Model Lifecycles:** When new threat vectors or variations appear, we cannot simply provide a few reference examples; we have to re-gather data and re-run the full AutoGluon training loop.

---

#### **Proposed Execution & Workflow Ideas**
1. **Execution Environments:**
   - **Ingest Pipelines:** Run zero-shot / few-shot tabular inference via an `inference` processor to enrich documents as they are ingested.
   - **ES|QL / Query-Time:** Evaluate classifications on the fly within ES|QL queries or search workflows.
2. **In-Context / Reference Data via Elasticsearch Indices:**
   - Tabular foundation models (like TabPFN) excel at learning from a small set of prompt/reference examples. Elasticsearch could supply this context directly using a lookup index or dedicated reference index queried via KQL or ES|QL.
3. **End-to-End In-Cluster ML Pathway:**
   - This opens a path to configuring custom classification tasks entirely inside Elasticsearch—potentially leveraging tools like Agent Builder for automated dataset gathering and cleaning, with no need to leave Elasticsearch for external model training.

### Description

Allow a default reasoning effort to be stored on an `openai` `chat_completion` inference endpoint in `task_settings.reasoning`, the same way `service: elastic` already can.

A caller can send `reasoning.effort` on `_stream` today. Elasticsearch maps it to OpenAI `reasoning_effort`. That was added in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/156505. The same PR deferred persist: "Do not persist reasoning in OpenAI task_settings for now (that work is deferred)."

PUT or `_update` with `task_settings.reasoning` on `service: openai` fails at schema time:

Configuration contains settings [{reasoning={effort=low}}] unknown to the [openai] service

`openai` `task_settings` only accept `user` and `headers`: https://www.elastic.co/docs/api/doc/elasticsearch/operation/operation-inference-put-openai

If the request omits `reasoning`, Elasticsearch does not inject `reasoning_effort`. The gateway or model then applies its own default.

Kibana also has no connector-level default. Agent Builder UI and Observability / Security AI Assistant omit `reasoning`, so callers that do not send it on each request cannot set a default on the endpoint.

Workaround is to pass `reasoning.effort` on `_stream`, or `reasoning_level` on https://www.elastic.co/docs/api/doc/kibana/operation/operation-post-agent-builder-converse. Neither covers the Agent Builder UI.

Suggested store and merge: use the stored default when the request omits `reasoning`. Per-request `reasoning.effort` wins.

Related: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/148909

body_text:
This seems like docs / spec fix only. The product errors are expected as per output.

https://www.elastic.co/docs/api/doc/elasticsearch/operation/operation-inference-update lists `service` (string, Required) and `service_settings` (object, Required) on the `_update` body. The example and all language snippets also send `"service": "example-service"`.

The same page intro says `_update` can change `task_settings`, secrets (within `service_settings`), or `num_allocations`. That matches the product.

`_update` only accepts mutable `task_settings` and secrets. `service` cannot be updated. Create-time `service_settings` such as `model_id` / `url` are not updatable. This is not a Kibana issue.

Lab on ES 9.5.2, `service: openai`:

```
_update with service: Request contained fields which cannot be updated, remove these fields and try again [{service=openai}]

_update with openai service_settings.model_id / url: Configuration contains settings [{url=..., model_id=gpt-5.4-nano}] unknown to the [openai] service
```


`_update` of `task_settings.user` works. A secret in `service_settings` (`api_key`) is the kind of `service_settings` `_update` is meant to take.

Fix needed
* Stop marking `service` and `service_settings` as required on `_update`
* Drop `service` from the example and client snippets
