{"repository": "facebook/pyrefly", "task_candidate_id": 4605, "repository_id": 94, "issue_number": 5012, "github_issue_id": 5559286126, "html_url": "https://github.com/facebook/pyrefly/issues/5012", "created_at": "2026-09-23T20:44:20+00:00", "author_association": "CONTRIBUTOR", "title": "LSP: after an on-disk edit to the module defining a generic class, an unchanged importer sees `__getitem__` return the unsolved `T`", "body_text": "### Describe the Bug A generic class and a second class live in the same module. When that module is edited on disk (reported through `workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles`), an open file that uses the generic class through another module gets `Indexer[Item].__getitem__` typed as returning the bare type parameter `T` instead of `Item`. Attribute access on the result then fails with `Object of class 'object' has no attribute …`. A fresh `pyrefly check` of the same files reports no error. Restarting the language server clears it. We hit this in VS Code after a `git pull` fast-forwarded the checkout under a running server: a file nobody had touched showed a new error until the server was restarted. #### Reproduction The script below is self-contained (standard library only). It writes four small modules and an empty `pyrefly.toml` to a temp directory, starts `pyrefly lsp`, opens `app.py`, edits `indexing.py` on disk, reports the change through `workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles`, and prints `app.py`'s diagnostics before and after. It then runs a fresh `pyrefly check` on the edited files. ``` python repro.py [path/to/pyrefly] ```
repro.py ```python """Pyrefly LSP: after an on-disk edit to the module that defines a generic class, an unchanged, open importer sees `Indexer[Item].__getitem__` return the unsolved `T` (reported as `object`). Usage: python repro.py [path/to/pyrefly] stdlib only; the default is `pyrefly` on PATH """ import json import subprocess import sys import tempfile import threading import time from pathlib import Path PYREFLY = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "pyrefly" FILES = { "pyrefly.toml": "", "indexing.py": """\ class Indexer[T]: def __getitem__(self, idx: int) -> T: raise NotImplementedError class Provider: size: int = 0 """, "holder.py": """\ from indexing import Indexer class Item: day: int = 0 class Holder: items: Indexer[Item] """, "user.py": """\ from indexing import Provider def use(provider: Provider) -> None: pass """, "app.py": """\ from typing import reveal_type from holder import Holder from user import use def first_day(holder: Holder, provider) -> int: day = holder.items[0].day reveal_type(holder.items.__getitem__) use(provider) return day """, } # One line added above `Indexer`, and `Provider` loses its attribute. Either change alone does not reproduce. EDITED_INDEXING = """\ class Indexer[T]: def __getitem__(self, idx: int) -> T: raise NotImplementedError class Provider: pass """ class Client: def __init__(self, cwd: Path) -> None: self.proc = subprocess.Popen([PYREFLY, "lsp"], stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, cwd=cwd) self.lock = threading.Lock() self.pending: dict[int, threading.Event] = {} self.next_id = 1 self.last_message = time.time() self.diagnostics: dict[str, list] = {} threading.Thread(target=self._read, daemon=True).start() def _send(self, msg: dict) -> None: body = json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", **msg}).encode() with self.lock: self.proc.stdin.write(b"Content-Length: %d\r\n\r\n" % len(body) + body) self.proc.stdin.flush() def request(self, method: str, params: dict) -> None: done = self.pending[self.next_id] = threading.Event() self._send({"id": self.next_id, "method": method, "params": params}) self.next_id += 1 done.wait(60) def notify(self, method: str, params: dict) -> None: self._send({"method": method, "params": params}) def _read(self) -> None: out = self.proc.stdout while True: length = 0 while line := out.readline().strip(): if line.lower().startswith(b"content-length"): length = int(line.split(b":")[1]) if not length: return msg = json.loads(out.read(length)) self.last_message = time.time() if "id" in msg and "method" in msg: # a server request: defaults for configuration, null otherwise items = msg["params"].get("items") if msg["method"] == "workspace/configuration" else None self._send({"id": msg["id"], "result": [{}] * len(items) if items is not None else None}) elif "id" in msg: self.pending.pop(msg["id"]).set() elif msg.get("method") == "textDocument/publishDiagnostics": self.diagnostics[msg["params"]["uri"]] = msg["params"]["diagnostics"] def settle(self) -> None: """Wait until the server has been quiet for two seconds.""" while True: time.sleep(0.25) if time.time() - self.last_message > 2: return root = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()).resolve() for rel, text in FILES.items(): (root / rel).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) (root / rel).write_text(text) app, indexing = root / "app.py", root / "indexing.py" def show(client: Client, label: str) -> None: print(label) for d in client.diagnostics.get(app.as_uri(), []): print(f" app.py:{d['range']['start']['line'] + 1}: [{d.get('code')}] {d['message']}") client = Client(cwd=root) client.request("initialize", { "processId": None, "rootUri": root.as_uri(), "workspaceFolders": [{"uri": root.as_uri(), "name": "repro"}], "capabilities": {"workspace": {"configuration": True, "workspaceFolders": True, "didChangeWatchedFiles": {"dynamicRegistration": True}}}, }) client.notify("initialized", {}) client.notify("textDocument/didOpen", {"textDocument": { "uri": app.as_uri(), "languageId": "python", "version": 1, "text": app.read_text()}}) client.settle() show(client, "before the edit:") indexing.write_text(EDITED_INDEXING) # on disk, as `git pull` or a branch switch would client.notify("workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles", {"changes": [{"uri": indexing.as_uri(), "type": 2}]}) client.settle() show(client, "after the edit, incremental:") client.proc.kill() fresh = subprocess.run([PYREFLY, "check", "--output-format", "min-text", "app.py"], cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True) print("fresh `pyrefly check` of the edited files:") print(" " + ("\n ".join(fresh.stdout.split("\n")).strip() or "no errors")) ```
The modules: ```python # indexing.py class Indexer[T]: def __getitem__(self, idx: int) -> T: raise NotImplementedError class Provider: size: int = 0 ``` ```python # holder.py from indexing import Indexer class Item: day: int = 0 class Holder: items: Indexer[Item] ``` ```python # user.py from indexing import Provider def use(provider: Provider) -> None: pass ``` ```python # app.py (open in the editor, never changed) from typing import reveal_type from holder import Holder from user import use def first_day(holder: Holder, provider) -> int: day = holder.items[0].day reveal_type(holder.items.__getitem__) use(provider) return day ``` The edit to `indexing.py` adds a blank line above `Indexer` and removes `Provider`'s attribute: ```python class Indexer[T]: def __getitem__(self, idx: int) -> T: raise NotImplementedError class Provider: pass ``` #### Output (1.3.1 and 1.4.0-dev.1 print the same) ``` before the edit: app.py:9: [reveal-type] revealed type: (idx: int) -> Item after the edit, incremental: app.py:8: [missing-attribute] Object of class `object` has no attribute `day` app.py:9: [reveal-type] revealed type: (idx: int) -> T fresh `pyrefly check` of the edited files: INFO app.py:9:16-42: revealed type: (idx: int) -> Item [reveal-type] ``` **Expected:** after the edit, `__getitem__` is still `(idx: int) -> Item`, and there is no `missing-attribute` error, matching the fresh check. #### What is needed to trigger it Deterministic in our runs. Each of these is required; removing any one makes the error disappear: - **Both parts of the edit.** Only shifting `Indexer` down a line, or only changing `Provider`, does not reproduce. - **`app.py` calling a function whose signature mentions `Provider`** (`use(provider)` here), from a module other than `indexing.py`. - **A config file.** An empty `pyrefly.toml` is enough. Without one, it does not reproduce. It does not depend on the interpreter or on the attribute's name. It also reproduces with the modules in a package under `src/`. #### Possibly related #4216 and #4171 also describe incremental rechecks that end in a different state from a fresh check. We could not tell whether the cause is shared. ### Sandbox Link Not possible: the bug needs an on-disk edit under a running language server. The self-contained script above reproduces it instead. ### (Only applicable for extension issues) IDE Information - Pyrefly VS Code extension 1.3.1, with `pyrefly.lspPath` pointing at a pinned `pyrefly` 1.3.1 binary. The script reproduces it without the editor, against 1.3.1 and 1.4.0-dev.1. - macOS 15, arm64. - The output pane shows no panic or error around the recheck; the only warnings are unrelated config-migration messages. - The workspace is multi-root, but one folder is enough to reproduce. ### Describe the Bug

A method whose decorator comes from a module imported through a `try: import X` / `except ModuleNotFoundError: import shim as X` fallback is not bound as a method when `X` is not installed. The decorated method's type becomes `((self: C, ...) -> R) | Unknown`, and accessing it passes the first argument where `self` should go.

SQLAlchemy 2.1 uses exactly this pattern in `sqlalchemy/engine/_row_cy.py`: `try: import cython` / `except ModuleNotFoundError: from sqlalchemy.util import cython`, with `BaseRow.__getattribute__` decorated by `@cython.annotation_typing(False)`. Without Cython installed, pyrefly reports every `row.<column>` access on a SQLAlchemy 2.1.1 `Row` (`missing-argument` plus `bad-argument-type` on `BaseRow.__getattribute__`). In our codebase that is about 270 false positives. pyright and mypy accept the same code.

### Reproduction (no SQLAlchemy needed)

`pyrefly.toml`

```toml
python-version = "3.14.0"
```

`pkg/__init__.py` is empty.

`pkg/cyshim.py`

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import TypeVar

_T = TypeVar("_T")
_NO_OP = Callable[[_T], _T]

compiled = False


def _no_op(fn: _T) -> _T:
    return fn


cclass = _no_op


def annotation_typing(_: bool) -> _NO_OP[_T]:
    return _no_op
```

`pkg/row.py`

```python
from typing import Any

try:
    import cython
except ModuleNotFoundError:
    from pkg import cyshim as cython


@cython.cclass
class BaseRow:
    if cython.compiled:

        @cython.annotation_typing(False)
        def __getattribute__(self, name: str) -> Any:
            return object.__getattribute__(self, name)

    @cython.annotation_typing(False)
    def __getattr__(self, name: str) -> Any:
        return name
```

`use.py`

```python
from pkg.row import BaseRow


def read(row: BaseRow) -> str:
    return row.name
```

### Output

pyrefly 1.3.1 (1.4.0.dev1 reports the same four errors):

```
ERROR Cannot find module `cython` [missing-import]
 --> pkg/row.py:4:12
ERROR Class member `BaseRow.__getattribute__` overrides parent class `object` in an inconsistent manner [bad-override-mutable-attribute]
  --> pkg/row.py:14:13
  `BaseRow.__getattribute__` has type `((self: BaseRow, name: str) -> Any) | Unknown`, which is not consistent with `(name: str, /) -> Any` in `object.__getattribute__` (the type of read-write attributes cannot be changed)
ERROR Argument `Literal['name']` is not assignable to parameter `self` with type `BaseRow` in function `pkg.row.BaseRow.__getattribute__` [bad-argument-type]
 --> use.py:5:12
ERROR Missing argument `name` in function `pkg.row.BaseRow.__getattribute__` [missing-argument]
 --> use.py:5:12
 INFO 4 errors
```

- pyright 1.1.414: `0 errors`.
- mypy 2.3.1: only `import-not-found` for `cython`; `row.name` is accepted.

### Observations

- Replacing the `try/except` with a direct `from pkg import cyshim as cython` gives 0 errors.
- Installing the real `cython` package gives 0 errors, both in this repro and for SQLAlchemy 2.1.1.
- Only the missing-import half of the fallback is `Unknown`. The union with it seems to stop pyrefly from treating the attribute as a bindable method.
- Expected: when one member of a union is `Unknown`, the attribute should still bind like the known function (or the whole thing should degrade to `Unknown`), not be called unbound.

### Versions

pyrefly 1.3.1 and 1.4.0.dev1, Python 3.14, macOS (arm64); SQLAlchemy 2.1.1 for the real-world case.

### Describe the Bug

Extract Function/Method currently declines selections containing `return`, `break`, or `continue`.

This was an intentional limitation in the original Extract Function implementation (#1786 / `39ec3446b2f5eeebbef4c6d4d6a99377b6295aaf`), but I couldn't find a follow-up issue tracking support for these cases.

For example:

```python
def find(items):
    for item in items:
        if matches(item):
            return item
    return None
```

Selecting the `if` block cannot currently be extracted because it contains `return`.

Similarly, selections containing `break` or `continue` are rejected even where the control flow could potentially be preserved by the generated helper/call-site transformation.

It would be useful to track support for these control-flow cases separately from the already-implemented basic Extract Function/Method refactoring.

Relevant implementations:

- Extract Function: #1786 / `39ec3446b2f5eeebbef4c6d4d6a99377b6295aaf`
- Extract Method: #1831 / `c7a1d52feaef3f93bab7a32c86857c32d92d75b7`

### Sandbox Link

N/A — the sandbox does not expose LSP refactoring code actions.

### (Only applicable for extension issues) IDE Information

Not IDE-specific.

### Describe the Bug

When matching a union type against a `Protocol`, `pyrefly` incorrectly thinks matching is impossible. 
The warning doesn't get triggered when a non-union type is used.

```python
from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable

@runtime_checkable
class SupportsMethod(Protocol):
    def method(self) -> None: ...


class Foo: ...

def check(arg: Foo) -> None:
    match arg:
        case SupportsMethod():  # OK
            pass

def check_union(arg: Foo | None) -> None:
    match arg:
        case SupportsMethod():  # WARNING: case pattern can never match
            pass
```

```

```

### Describe the Bug

Observed on 1.4.0.dev2

When a sort key's return type does not satisfy `SupportsRichComparison`, Pyrefly's top-level overload diagnostic displays the callback as `(value: Unknown) -> Unknown`. The detailed overload analysis still knows the concrete parameter and return types. This makes the error misleading and obscures the actual comparison-protocol mismatch.

```
class Key:
    def __lt__(self, other: object) -> object:
        return object()

def sort_values(values: list[Key]) -> None:
    values.sort(key=lambda value: value)
```


Output:
```
ERROR sandbox.py:6:16-41: No matching overload found for function `list.sort` called with arguments: (key=(value: Unknown) -> Unknown) [no-matching-overload]
  Possible overloads:
    (*, key: None = None, ...) -> None
    (*, key: (Key) -> SupportsRichComparison, ...) -> None [closest match]
  Argument `(value: Key) -> Key` is not assignable to parameter `key` with type `(Key) -> SupportsRichComparison` in function `list.sort`
```


The top-level diagnostic should preserve the known callback type, such as `(value: Key) -> Key`, instead of displaying `Unknown`.

This was seen when sorting records by NumPy (1.26.4) `np.float32` values, whose comparison methods return `np.bool_` rather than builtin `bool`

body_text: ### Describe the Bug When I rename a function that has `@overload` signatures, Pyrefly renames only the implementation and the call sites. The `@overload` stubs keep the old name, so the code is left in an invalid state. Repro file `c.py`: ```python from typing import overload @overload def g(x: int) -> int: ... @overload def g(x: str) -> str: ... def g(x): return x g(1) ``` Steps: 1. Put the cursor on `g` in `def g(x):` (line 7). 2. Rename it to `zz` (F2 in VS Code). Actual result: ```python @overload def g(x: int) -> int: ... @overload def g(x: str) -> str: ... def zz(x): return x zz(1) ``` Only 2 edits are made (the implementation and the call). Both `@overload` stubs are left as `g`. Expected result: all three `def` lines and the call are renamed, because they are the same symbol. After the rename, `pyrefly check --preset default c.py` reports: ``` ERROR Overloaded function must have an implementation [invalid-overload] --> c.py:4:5 ``` so the rename turns valid code into code with a type error. (With no config, the `basic` preset does not enable this check, so the editor shows no diagnostic.) For comparison, I sent the same `textDocument/rename` request (new name `zz`, at the implementation `def g`) to other servers. Pyright 1.1.414 and ty 0.0.84 both return 4 edits, renaming both stubs, the implementation and the call. Related but a different case: #4350 / astral-sh/ty#3350 (renaming a parameter of an overloaded method should rename it in all overloads). This issue is about renaming the function name itself, where the @overload stubs are skipped. Screenshots of the file after the rename and of the check output are attached below. ### Sandbox Link https://pyrefly.org/sandbox/?project=v2.I6HIhJU44KyI4IAiO12jwgoYG5AkDqStFPT09LCrAiUykCogDVUFkqqq0qiApT1ouqsA2QMUN9TEDGllhQCIgALU0cAyBhhF6aXAkgwY9EBDlYGFWKpCRklJQbGVvj5Me35Run5qnn5KfnKxPooOfQVQokosS8wEl4-oxinkg1NGMdBYSqJYHRLD6vgiWB0Uv0AVeOMMAA ### (Only applicable for extension issues) IDE Information VS Code, Pyrefly extension 1.3.2 (meta.pyrefly-1.3.2-darwin-arm64), macOS (Apple Silicon)

### Describe the Bug

Polars supports creating dataframes from records that are dataclasses, TypedDicts, or NamedTuples. This is a common usecase. In these cases, it is possible to infer the schema of the dataframe statically and Pyrefly should support this.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import NamedTuple, TypedDict, reveal_type

import polars as pl


@dataclass
class DCProduct:
    item_id: int
    product: str


class NTProduct(NamedTuple):
    item_id: int
    product: str


class TDProduct(TypedDict):
    item_id: int
    product: str


dc_records = [DCProduct(101, 'Laptop'), DCProduct(102, 'Mouse')]
reveal_type(dc_records)  # list[DCProduct]
nt_records = [NTProduct(101, 'Laptop'), NTProduct(102, 'Mouse')]
reveal_type(nt_records)  # list[NTProduct]
td_records = [TDProduct(item_id=101, product='Laptop'), TDProduct(item_id=102, product='Mouse')]
reveal_type(td_records)  # list[TDProduct]

dc_df = pl.DataFrame(dc_records)
nt_df = pl.DataFrame(nt_records)
td_df = pl.DataFrame(td_records)

reveal_type(dc_df)  # just DataFrame, no inferred schema
reveal_type(nt_df)  # just DataFrame, no inferred schema
reveal_type(td_df)  # just DataFrame, no inferred schema
```

### Describe the Bug

`pyrefly` ignores the _invariant_ `self` restriction (`self: ElementOpsMixin[int]`) when matching a
protocol's overloaded method, so `bool` leaks through `bool <: int` and the invalid
`Series[bool] - bool` resolves to `Series[int]` instead of erroring. Same false-negative as
python/mypy#20061.

```python
from typing import Generic, Protocol, TypeVar, reveal_type

T = TypeVar("T")
T_contra = TypeVar("T_contra", contravariant=True)
S2 = TypeVar("S2")


class ElementOpsMixin(Generic[S2]):
    def _proto_sub(self: ElementOpsMixin[int], other: int) -> ElementOpsMixin[int]: ...  # invariant


class Supports_ProtoSub(Protocol[T_contra, S2]):
    def _proto_sub(self, other: T_contra, /) -> ElementOpsMixin[S2]: ...


class Series(ElementOpsMixin[T]):
    def __sub__(self: Supports_ProtoSub[T_contra, S2], other: T_contra, /) -> Series[S2]: ...


reveal_type(Series[bool]() - True)  # Series[int], where it should raise
```

`pyrefly` ignores the _invariant_ `self` restriction (`self: ElementOpsMixin[int]`) when matching a
protocol's overloaded method, so `bool` leaks through `bool <: int` and the invalid
`Series[bool] - bool` resolves to `Series[int]` instead of erroring. Same false-negative as
python/mypy#20061.

```python
from typing import Generic, Protocol, TypeVar, reveal_type

T = TypeVar("T")
T_contra = TypeVar("T_contra", contravariant=True)
S2 = TypeVar("S2")


class ElementOpsMixin(Generic[S2]):
    def _proto_sub(self: ElementOpsMixin[int], other: int) -> ElementOpsMixin[int]: ...  # invariant


class Supports_ProtoSub(Protocol[T_contra, S2]):
    def _proto_sub(self, other: T_contra, /) -> ElementOpsMixin[S2]: ...


class Series(ElementOpsMixin[T]):
    def __sub__(self: Supports_ProtoSub[T_contra, S2], other: T_contra, /) -> Series[S2]: ...


reveal_type(Series[bool]() - True)  # Series[int], where it should raise
```

body_text:
### Summary

`workspace/symbol` currently returns symbols from third-party libraries as well as project code. I'd like a server-side way to choose between project-only and project + libraries.

### Motivation

The LSP spec describes `workspace/symbol` as listing project-wide symbols matching a query. It doesn't say whether dependencies count as part of the project, and the request has no parameter to choose, so servers behave differently. Pyright, basedpyright and ty return project symbols only. lua_ls includes libraries only when they're listed in its `workspace.library` setting. Pyrefly appears to include libraries by default.

Both modes are useful. Project-only search is the common case when navigating your own code. Library search is valuable when exploring a dependency's API. PyCharm offers both, and I'd like the same from Pyrefly.

### Problem with client-side filtering

I currently filter results in the editor (Neovim, via a picker transform) by dropping files outside the project root and anything under `site-packages`/`venv`. ### Describe the Bug

## Summary

When a project file imports a package from site-packages, Pyrefly runs the "unconfigured project" resolver for that package's directory. That resolver searches upward for `mypy.ini`, `pyrightconfig.json` or `pyproject.toml`, so a `mypy.ini` that happens to be packaged in a wheel is found and migrated in memory. Its warnings are then printed during an unrelated `pyrefly check`.

## Minimal repro

Version: pyrefly 1.3.1 (also reproduced with 1.3.2).

```
repro/
  sp/fakepkg/__init__.py     # def f() -> int: return 1
  sp/fakepkg/mypy.ini        # [mypy]
                             # mypy_path = fakepkg/stubs
                             # disable_error_code = annotation-unchecked
  proj/pyproject.toml        # [tool.pyrefly]
                             # site-package-path = ["../sp"]
  proj/main.py               # import fakepkg
                             # x: int = fakepkg.f()
```

```
cd repro/proj
pyrefly check main.py
```

Output:

```
 WARN Cannot migrate unsupported or unrecognized mypy error code `annotation-unchecked`; audit the generated [errors] table
 WARN Invalid search-path: `<repro>/sp/fakepkg/fakepkg/stubs` does not exist
 INFO 0 errors
```

Passing `--preset basic` makes the warnings go away.

*EDIT*:
This requires site-packages to be outside the project directory, as in the layout above (or with a pyenv / virtualenv environment outside the project). With the venv inside the project (e.g. `proj/.venv`), the warnings do not appear; the project's own `[tool.pyrefly]` config is found first by the upward search.

## Expected vs actual

- Expected: any type checker configuration file, mypy or pyrefly, shipped inside a dependency has no effect on how Pyrefly performs the type check.
- Actual: `litellm` 1.75.3 ships `site-packages/litellm/mypy.ini`, which contains `mypy_path = litellm/stubs` and `disable_error_code = valid-type, annotation-unchecked`. With it installed, running pyrefly 1.3.1 `pyrefly check` on a project file that imports `litellm` (in a project with `[tool.pyrefly]` in `pyproject.toml`) prints:

  ```
   WARN Cannot migrate unsupported or unrecognized mypy error code `annotation-unchecked`; audit the generated [errors] table
   WARN Invalid search-path: `<venv>/lib/python3.12/site-packages/litellm/litellm/stubs` does not exist
  ```

## Where this happens

Permalinks at 0e44796d6b53b3a84cb6ae1bcab9a48af628e796:

- `pyrefly/lib/commands/config_finder.rs` L267-L334: the fallback closure of `standard_config_finder`, used when no config is found for a file. For a non-fallback module, `path.root_of(name)` is used as the root (L273-L283), and `configure2.configure(...)` is called. Nothing here checks whether the path is under a `site-package-path` entry.
- `pyrefly/lib/commands/config_finder.rs` L77-L92 and L111-L137: `DefaultConfigConfigurer::configure` calls `apply_unconfigured_resolver_if_applicable`, which only skips configs from a real file or with a preset already set.
- `crates/pyrefly_config/src/resolve_unconfigured.rs` L91-L101: `resolve_unconfigured_config` calls `find_and_migrate_in_memory(start)` unless an explicit preset override is given.
- `crates/pyrefly_config/src/migration/run.rs` L98 and L176-L192: `find_and_migrate_in_memory` / `find_upward_config` walk upward from `start` with `UpwardSearch` for `mypy.ini`, `pyrightconfig.json`, `pyproject.toml`, with no boundary.

I did not find any reference to `site_package_path` or site-packages in these code paths outside tests. I have not traced exactly why the root ends up at `site-packages/<pkg>` rather than `site-packages` in this case, so that part is a guess.

## Suggested behavior

Either of these would give the expected behavior:

1. Do not run config discovery / in-memory migration for files that resolve under a `site-package-path` entry (use the existing synthesized default config instead).
2. Stop the upward search at a site-packages boundary.

## Related

I looked at #3614, which also mentions an `Invalid search-path ... site-packages/pandas/typings` warning, but it is about pandas-stubs test coverage and was closed as not a Pyrefly problem. It does not discuss config discovery.

```py
    return _bar()

# private utils:
def _bar(): # error: unannotated-return
    return 1
class _Baz:
    def fn(self): # error: unannotated-return
        return 1
```

### Describe the Bug

```py
# ./foo/a.py

a = 1
```
```py
# ./foo/__init__.py

from foo.a import a
```
```py
# ./sandbox.py

from foo import a # error
```

```
ERROR sandbox.py:1:17-18: `a` is not exported from module `foo` [[implicit-reexport](https://pyrefly.org/en/docs/error-kinds/#implicit-reexport)]
  `a` is imported by `foo` but not re-exported (via `import ... as a`, `__all__`, or a wildcard import)
```

in this case, it seems to be impossible to import `foo/a.py` from `sandbox.py` just because the `__init__.py` happens to use it without re-exporting it.

i could go `from foo.a import a` instead, but that doesn't work in my case because i need to import the module itself (i need to mutate an attribute in it unfortunately).

(basedpyright's `reportPrivateLocalImportUsage` rule has the same problem btw)

```python
def pprint(arg: object, /, *, options: dict) -> str:
    return "dummy"

class Foo: ...

Bar.__repr__ = partialmethod(pprint, options={})  # ERROR
```

### Describe the Bug

In the example below, narrowing with just `isinstance(arg, type)` works as expected, but if we use `isinstance(arg, type) and issubclass(arg, Foo)` suddenly `pyrefly` widens the type to its original value.

```python
from collections.abc import Sequence

class Foo: ...

def check(arg: type[Foo] | Sequence[type[Foo]]):
    g1: tuple[type[Foo], ...] = (
        (Foo,)
        if isinstance(arg, type)
        else tuple(arg)  # OK
    )

    g2: tuple[type[Foo], ...] = (
        (Foo,)
        if isinstance(arg, type) and issubclass(arg, Foo)
        else tuple(arg)  # ERROR
    )
```

```
ERROR sandbox.py:15:20-23: Argument `Sequence[type[Foo]] | type[Foo]` is not assignable to parameter `iterable` with type `Iterable[type[Foo]]` in function `tuple.__new__` [bad-argument-type]
  Protocol `Iterable` requires attribute `__iter__`
```

body_text:
### Describe the Bug

When python constructs enum members it checks (using `==` comparison) whether the member already exists. In this case, it creates a unique object with shared `id` for both aliases:

```python
from enum import Enum
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Foo: ...

class E(Enum):
    A = Foo()
    B = Foo()

assert Foo() == Foo()
assert E.A is E.B  # always succeeds
```

```
 WARN sandbox.py:12:15-18: Identity comparison `E.A is E.B` is always False [unnecessary-comparison]
```

Of course, this depends on the `__eq__` method of the base class. For example, without the `@dataclass` decorator then indeed `E.A` would indeed be a different instance than `E.B`.

```python
from enum import Enum

class Foo: ...

class E(Enum):
    A = Foo()
    B = Foo()

assert Foo() != Foo()
assert E.A is not E.B
```

### Describe the Bug

Encountered odd behavior while fixing baseline errors. We have the following custom `save` method on a model:

```python
class Alert(AbstractDateTimeModel):
    ...

    secret_key = models.CharField(
        verbose_name=...,
        max_length=40,
    )

    ...

    def save(self, *args, **kwargs):
        """Ensure we get a token when we save the first time."""
        if self.pk is None:
            self.secret_key = get_random_string(length=40)
        super().save(*args, **kwargs)
```

Pyrefly believes the type of `self.pk` is `int` so (correctly) infers `self: Never` in the branch, causing a type error when we try to assign to an attribute.

This is incorrect because Django model pk's are `T | None` with the `None` case representing a model that hasn't been saved to the database yet.

body_text:
### Describe the Bug

When a subclass of `Enum` is created with the functional API (`BaseClass(name, members)`), the resulting class is typed as `Enum` rather than as the subclass, so methods defined on the base class are reported as missing.

### Repro

```python
from enum import Enum

class Base(Enum):
    @classmethod
    def helper(cls) -> int:
        return 42

Dynamic = Base("Dynamic", {"A": "a"})
Dynamic.helper()  # ERROR: Class `Enum` has no class attribute `helper` [missing-attribute]
```

### Actual output (pyrefly 1.3.2 and 1.4.0-dev.3)

```
ERROR ...:9:1-15: Class `Enum` has no class attribute `helper` [missing-attribute]
```

### Expected

No error. `Base("Dynamic", {...})` returns a new `Enum` subclass that inherits from `Base`, so classmethods and other members defined on `Base` should be accessible on the result.

### Notes

This affects Django's `TextChoices` / `IntegerChoices` functional-API pattern:

```python
from django.db import models
X = models.TextChoices("X", [("A", "a")])
X.choices  # flagged missing-attribute
```

`TextChoices.choices` is a classmethod defined on `TextChoices`, but because `TextChoices("X", ...)` is typed as returning plain `Enum`, the attribute is not found.

### Environment

- pyrefly 1.3.2, also 1.4.0-dev.3
- Python 3.14

When a subclass of `Enum` is created with the functional API (`BaseClass(name, members)`), the resulting class is typed as `Enum` rather than as the subclass, so methods defined on the base class are reported as missing.

### Repro

```python
from enum import Enum

class Base(Enum):
    @classmethod
    def helper(cls) -> int:
        return 42

Dynamic = Base("Dynamic", {"A": "a"})
Dynamic.helper()  # ERROR: Class `Enum` has no class attribute `helper` [missing-attribute]
```

### Actual output (pyrefly 1.3.2 and 1.4.0-dev.3)

```
ERROR ...:9:1-15: Class `Enum` has no class attribute `helper` [missing-attribute]
```

### Expected

No error. `Base("Dynamic", {...})` returns a new `Enum` subclass that inherits from `Base`, so classmethods and other members defined on `Base` should be accessible on the result.

### Notes

This affects Django's `TextChoices` / `IntegerChoices` functional-API pattern:

```python
from django.db import models
X = models.TextChoices("X", [("A", "a")])
X.choices  # flagged missing-attribute
```

`TextChoices.choices` is a classmethod defined on `TextChoices`, but because `TextChoices("X", ...)` is typed as returning plain `Enum`, the attribute is not found.

### Describe the Bug

When a generic function `f[T](xs: Iterable[T | None]) -> list[T]` is called with a list literal that includes a `None` element (e.g. `[*s, "x", None]`), pyrefly solves `T` as `str | None` instead of `str`. This causes two errors: the return value cannot be assigned to `list[str]`, and the argument is reported as not assignable to the parameter. Passing a variable with the same type instead of a literal works without errors.

### Repro

```python
from typing import Iterable

def f[T](xs: Iterable[T | None]) -> list[T]: ...

s: list[str] = ["a", "b"]
result: list[str] = f([*s, "x", None])  # two errors
```

### Actual output (pyrefly 1.3.2 and 1.4.0-dev.3)

```
ERROR ...:6:21-39: `list[str | None]` is not assignable to `list[str]` [bad-assignment]
ERROR ...:6:23-38: Argument `list[str | None]` is not assignable to parameter `xs` with type `Iterable[str | None]` in function `f` [bad-argument-type]
```

### Expected

No errors. `T` should be solved as `str`: the `None` element in the literal fills the `None` slot in `T | None`, so `T = str` and the return type is `list[str]`, which matches the assignment target.

### Workaround

Assigning the literal to a variable first avoids the errors:
```python
items: list[str | None] = [*s, "x", None]
result: list[str] = f(items)  # no errors
```

```python
from typing import final


@final
class Foo:
    def __init__(self, bar: str) -> None:
        self.bar = bar
```

```
> pyrefly coverage check coverage.py

 --> coverage.py:7:14

ERROR type coverage 50.00% (1 of 2 typable) is below the 100.00% threshold
```
Since a final class can not be subclassed should self.bar be implicitly typed from the \_\_init\_\_ types?  Why do I need an explicit type?

### Summary

The tutorial says constructor parameters that set tensor dimensions should be `Int[X]`, not `int`
([Tensor shapes tutorial](https://pyrefly.org/en/docs/tensor-shapes-tutorial-basics/)). With
`Int[C]`, a channel mismatch is reported at the call site. With a plain `int`, which is what most

diagnostic. So this is expected under the documented rules. The question is whether Pyrefly could
make that loss of tracking visible, since otherwise a clean run doesn't show how much was actually
checked.

- Python 3.12.8, macOS; `pyrefly==1.3.2`, `pyrefly-torch-stubs==1.3.2`, `pyrefly-shape-extensions==1.3.2`, all installed in one venv

```python
    def forward[B: IntVar](self, a: Tensor[[B, 128, 8, 8]], b: Tensor[[B, 128, 8, 8]]) -> Tensor[[B, 128, 8, 8]]:

class FuseLiteral(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(192, 128, 3, padding=1)

    def forward[B: IntVar](self, a: Tensor[[B, 128, 8, 8]], b: Tensor[[B, 128, 8, 8]]) -> Tensor[[B, 128, 8, 8]]:

    m = FuseTyped(192)
    reveal_type(m)
    m(x)                            # C: wrong size, called through forward
```

```
ERROR Argument `Tensor[IntTuple[B, 256, 8, 8]]` is not assignable to parameter `input` with type `Tensor[IntTuple[B, 192, @_, @_]]` in function `torch.nn.Conv2d.forward` [bad-argument-type]   # B
```

Could Pyrefly report when channel information is lost, so that A isn't silently skipped? For
example:

- a hint at the constructor (`nn.Conv2d(in_ch, …)` where `in_ch: int`) suggesting `Int[...]`, along
  the lines of the tutorial's advice.

them at the documented fix.

> **Note:** Claude (an AI assistant) wrote this issue and the repro below, and a human reviewed it before filing.

### Describe the Bug

`implicit-import` reports an error when a file imports a submodule explicitly, but then uses the submodule through an alias of its parent package.

```python
import sqlalchemy as sa
import sqlalchemy.exc

x = sa.exc.OperationalError  # implicit-import
```

```
ERROR repro.py:4:5-11: Module `sqlalchemy.exc` exists, but was not imported explicitly. You are relying on other modules to load it. [implicit-import]
```

The same error occurs if the submodule import comes first (`import sqlalchemy.exc as _` and then `import sqlalchemy as sa`).

Without the alias, there is no error:

```python
import sqlalchemy
import sqlalchemy.exc

x = sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError  # OK
```

### Expected behavior

No error. `import sqlalchemy.exc` loads the submodule and sets it as an attribute on the `sqlalchemy` module object. `sa` is the same module object, so `sa.exc` is always available at runtime.

### Relation to #2541

#2541 reports `import matplotlib as mpl` followed by `mpl.ticker`, with no import of `matplotlib.ticker`. That error is correct, because nothing guarantees that the submodule is loaded. This issue is different: the file imports the submodule explicitly, so the error is a false positive.

### Version

pyrefly 1.3.2, with `implicit-import = "error"` in the config.

### Describe the Bug

When a callable's signature has explicit parameters followed by both `*args` and `**kwargs` typed `Any` (explicitly, or implicitly by leaving them unannotated), pyrefly treats the whole signature as the gradual `...` form and no longer checks the explicit parameters when assigning it to a `Callable[...]` type. The spec only makes a bare `(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any)` equivalent to `...`; with a leading parameter the signature is `Concatenate[str, ...]`, whose first parameter must still be compatible (parameters are contravariant, so a `str` parameter cannot satisfy `Callable[[int], None]`).

```python
from typing import Any, Callable, Protocol

class P1(Protocol):
    def __call__(self, a: str, /, *args, **kwargs) -> None: ...            # unannotated variadics

class P2(Protocol):
    def __call__(self, a: str, /, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None: ...  # explicit Any

class P3(Protocol):
    def __call__(self, a: str, /, *args: object, **kwargs: object) -> None: ...

class P4(Protocol):
    def __call__(self, a: str, /, *args) -> None: ...                      # only *args

class P5(Protocol):
    def __call__(self, a: str, /) -> None: ...

def f(p1: P1, p2: P2, p3: P3, p4: P4, p5: P5) -> None:
    b1: Callable[[int], None] = p1   # expected error  -> pyrefly: no error
    b2: Callable[[int], None] = p2   # expected error  -> pyrefly: no error
    b3: Callable[[int], None] = p3   # expected error  -> reported
    b4: Callable[[int], None] = p4   # expected error  -> reported
    b5: Callable[[int], None] = p5   # expected error  -> reported

def g(a: str, /, *args, **kwargs) -> None: ...
b6: Callable[[int], None] = g        # expected error  -> pyrefly: no error (plain function, same pattern)
```

```
$ pyrefly check repro.py --output-format min-text --summary=none
repro.py:21:33-35: `P3` is not assignable to `(int) -> None` [bad-assignment]
repro.py:22:33-35: `P4` is not assignable to `(int) -> None` [bad-assignment]
repro.py:23:33-35: `P5` is not assignable to `(int) -> None` [bad-assignment]
```

mypy 2.4.0, pyright 1.1.414, ty 0.0.86 and zuban 0.10.0 report all six assignments (b1–b6). Call checking in pyrefly is fine (`p1(1)` is reported as `int` not assignable to `str`), so this is specific to the assignability relation between the signature and a `Callable` type.

Originally found via the typing conformance test `callables_annotation.py` (`Proto2.__call__(self, a: str, /, *args, **kwargs)` assigned to `Callable[Concatenate[int, ...], None]`), where pyrefly is the only checker that stays silent.

Environment: pyrefly 1.3.2 (PyPI), Python 3.12.15, macOS arm64, empty `pyrefly.toml`.

Code following a `match` (or `if`/`elif` chain) that is exhaustive by type narrowing, and whose every path raises or calls a `NoReturn` function, is never reported by the `unreachable` check. The same code after a syntactically terminating statement, or after an `if`/`else` whose arms both call `NoReturn`, is reported.

### Repro

With `unreachable = "warn"` enabled (it is on in the `default` preset, off in `basic`):

```python
from typing import NoReturn, assert_never

class Dog: ...
class Cat: ...

def never() -> NoReturn: ...

def after_exhaustive_match(pet: Dog | Cat) -> None:
    match pet:
        case Dog():
            raise ValueError()
        case Cat():
            raise ValueError()
    print("unexpectedly unreachable")   # expected: This code is unreachable [unreachable]

def after_noreturn_if_else() -> None:
    if bool():
        never()
    else:
        never()
    print("reported")                   # WARN This code is unreachable [unreachable]

def idiom(pet: Dog | Cat) -> None:
    if isinstance(pet, Dog):
        return
    if isinstance(pet, Cat):
        return
    assert_never(pet)                   # correctly not reported
```

Reproduces on 1.4.0-dev.2 and on a build from `main`.

Sandbox: [repro](https://pyrefly.org/sandbox/?project=v2.pZVRT4MwFIX_ys14ABND4-vejD4bY4w-uIQgdKOJrgSKmf_ec1sILYy5ZbwVzi1t7zlfl5DpJ-8IPn08jcl61DB7mqbD-CE3_dg5O9-CNZk8VHnX8nrQYlNUSS0hQy0sjoqpZ6yGWDM6DwiUXJH4fh0t-caWtZ5kwwRF-MHZRc5Pm1UHk9TolCy_fqnbw0dFxezcrG6gimj4uqbXCukrdGlT6CnpwxtYFI3HwV3noGVqm3HAZqFBND5BymDZ6EsqD8okd_1aJ9GcfR_20khnPrf26RPR-_3L04XbUKXS3_80MeQNtLesndNmUc1zLqh9L7L4-MYK3XDa0EHEC_XuGOYhjujZvaA-D6hE-ncdLkmkGl6OcD9Kqoyp27UQQ7ludkLuRamLVgQVgphX-U-u7NUbTkfaQqfFtNfQI3bwiE-xI2Z0QHESB38)

### Actual Behavior

Only the `print` in `after_noreturn_if_else` is reported.

### Expected Behavior

The `print` in `after_exhaustive_match` is reported as well. `assert_never(pet)` in `idiom` stays unreported.

### Why this is the current behavior

As far as I can tell this is deliberate rather than a gap: the compound-statement gate added in f3ddb9067 ("Propagate divergence through compound statements") refuses any path whose divergence comes from exhaustiveness, with the rationale that reporting it would flag the `assert_never` idiom (see `test_no_compound_gate_for_environment_or_exhaustiveness`). I'd like to make the case that the exemption is broader than the idiom needs.

### Argument

1. **This is the case the warning exists for.** The typing spec's [unreachable code guide](https://typing.python.org/en/latest/guides/unreachable.html) distinguishes *intentionally* unreachable code (`assert_never`, which the checker must *prove* unreachable) from *unexpectedly* unreachable code, for which it recommends a warning such as mypy's `--warn-unreachable`. Code after an all-raising exhaustive `match` is the textbook instance of the second kind, and the guide's own exhaustiveness example is a `match` that is exhaustive by narrowing. Pyrefly already proves the exhaustiveness here (that is what makes the function's implicit return `Never` and what the `Key::Exhaustive` binding computes); it just declines to act on it for reachability.

2. **The idiom can be exempted per statement instead of per mechanism.** mypy 2.4 with `--warn-unreachable` reports the `print` in `after_exhaustive_match` and does *not* report `assert_never(pet)` in either the `if`-chain or the `case _:` form. It does this by skipping statements that are themselves divergence markers (a `raise`, `assert False`, or a call returning `Never`), not by ignoring exhaustiveness altogether. Pyright's `reportUnreachable` reports all three lines, including both `assert_never` calls, which is presumably why it ships off by default; that is the outcome the current exemption guards against, and mypy shows it is avoidable.

3. **The current split is hard to predict from the outside.** The rule in practice is "divergence from `raise`/`NoReturn` is reported, divergence from narrowing is not", except that dead `match` cases *are* reported (`unreachable-match-case`). From a user's perspective the two functions above are the same situation: the type checker has proven that nothing after the statement runs. In the `match` case the proof is arguably stronger, since every arm's divergence is syntactic and only the exhaustiveness is type-based.

### Proposal

Keep the compound gate, but replace the blanket exhaustiveness refusal with a per-statement exemption: do not report a statement that is itself a divergence marker (a `raise`, `assert False`, or an expression statement that is a call returning `Never`, which covers `assert_never` and custom helpers). Everything else after a type-exhaustive statement whose paths all diverge gets the existing `unreachable` warning. No new flag or error kind is needed.

If the concern is rather that union annotations are less trustworthy than `NoReturn` annotations, I'd be interested in that reasoning, since the same trust is already placed in them for `missing-return` and `unreachable-match-case`.

### Related

#5069 (false `unbound-name` after a nested exhaustive `match`) mentions this as a secondary symptom; I'm splitting it out since it is a design question rather than a bug in the flow merge.

Happy to work on this if there's agreement on the approach.

body_text:
### Describe the Bug

Pyrefly 1.3.2 and 1.4.0.dev3 select the first specialised-self overload for `Container[Any]`, but infer `Unknown` for the equivalent ordinary function. This reproduces with and without `--spec-compliant-overloads=true`.

```python
from typing import Any, Generic, TypeVar, overload, reveal_type

T = TypeVar("T")


class Container(Generic[T]):
    @overload
    def scalar(self: "Container[int]") -> int: ...
    @overload
    def scalar(self: "Container[str]") -> str: ...
    def scalar(self) -> int | str:
        raise NotImplementedError

@overload
def scalar(value: Container[int]) -> int: ...
@overload
def scalar(value: Container[str]) -> str: ...
def scalar(value: Container[Any]) -> int | str:
    raise NotImplementedError


def probe(gradual: Container[Any]) -> None:
    reveal_type(gradual.scalar())  # int
    reveal_type(scalar(gradual))   # Unknown
```

Python: 3.12

**Expected:** handle receiver ambiguity consistently with explicit arguments,
per overload Step 5: https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/overload.html#step-5

Reversing the method overloads changes its result to `str`; concrete receivers remain precise.

- Nightly mypy 2.5.0+dev (python/mypy#22011) and Pyright 1.1.414 infer `Any` for both calls
- Ty 0.0.85 infers `Unknown` (astral-sh/ty#4055)

### Describe the Bug

Not sure how to best describe it so I'll just show with an example:

```python
from typing import assert_type
class A: ...

def as_singleton(elem: A | None)-> None:
    match elem:
        case None:
            assert_type(elem, None) # OK!
        case _:
            assert_type(elem, A) # OK!
            
def as_tuple(elem: A | None)-> None:
    match (elem,):
        case (None,):
            assert_type(elem, None) # OK!
        case _:
            assert_type(elem, A) # FAIL! A | None
```

I'd except the `as_tuple` to work the same as the `as_singleton` here. (I get the same error if I match on `(_,)` instead of `_` in the last case)

For reference [ty does the same](https://play.ty.dev/5889c474-eced-4b5a-93f7-c6173104a6cb), Pyright correctly inferes it (can't link to the pyright playground as it's down for me right now)

Not sure it's related but I originally hit it when I had something like:

```python
class A: ...

def merge(left: A | None, right: A | None) -> A:
    match left, right:
        case None, None:
            return A()
        case None, _:
            return right # FAIL! A() | None
        case _, None:
            return left # FAIL! A() | None
        case _, _:
            return right # FAIL! A() | None
```

Which seems exhaustive to me? When I reduced it I found the smaller example, let me know if I should file this as a separate issue. I'm not sure about the semantics of a wildcard here

## Import resolution re-walks every search root for each module that shares a prefix

### Summary

`LoaderFindCache` caches the final result per module name, but the intermediate `find_one_part(name, roots)` lookups in `crates/pyrefly_build/src/module_resolver.rs` are not memoized. Every distinct module `a.b.c` resolves its prefixes from scratch: `a` across all search roots, then `a-stubs` across all roots, then `b` across the namespace roots of `a`, and so on.

With many search roots and a namespace package spread across them, this dominates import resolution. On apache/airflow (232 search roots after the automatic `[tool.mypy]` migration; `airflow` is a namespace package split across provider `src` directories), indexing the project performs ~32M existence probes.

### Repro

- apache/airflow @ `823381c1dc`, no pyrefly config (root `pyproject.toml` with `[tool.mypy]` is migrated automatically), venv with `apache-airflow-core` and `apache-airflow-task-sdk`.
- Run `pyrefly check` in the repo root, or `pyrefly lsp` and open `airflow-core/src/airflow/models/dagrun.py` (this triggers project indexing).
- Read `TelemetryTransactionStats` for the indexing transaction: `total_stat_count` ≈ 31.8M for ~8.8k modules, `find_import_time` 18–22 s of CPU.

### Proposed fix

Memoize `find_one_part` in `DirEntryCache`, keyed by `(part name, root list, style filter)`, when phantom paths are not being collected. The memo has the same lifetime and invalidation as the existing directory-listing cache in `DirEntryCache`, so it adds no new staleness. A prototype is about 40 lines in `module_resolver.rs`: the existing function becomes `find_one_part_uncached`, and a wrapper checks the memo first.

Possible refinements:
- Intern root lists (or key by an id of the config's search path) instead of hashing the root list on every call.
- Memoize by module prefix in `continue_find_module`, which also covers the walk through namespace roots.

Separately, `total_stat_count` counts every `timed_stat` probe, including those served by `DirEntryCache`. A name like `total_exists_probe_count`, or counting only real filesystem calls, would make the telemetry less misleading.

### Measurements (prototype behind an env flag, same binary)

Windows 11, Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX, 24 threads, release build.

| | apache/airflow | home-assistant/core |
|---|---|---|
| Probes while indexing the project | 31.8–32.0M → 1.1–1.9M | 2.0–2.5M → 0.23M |
| CPU in `find_import` while indexing | 18.4–21.9 s → 1.5–2.0 s | 12–36 s → 1.8 s |
| `pyrefly check` wall time | 3.9 s → 2.6 s | 11.2 s → 9.3 s |
| `pyrefly check` output | identical (3,521 lines) | identical (69,068 lines) |
| First `textDocument/references` on a class | 2.9–3.7 s → 0.16–0.52 s | noisy |

Two LSP runs per mode and one `check` run per mode, so treat the timings as indicative. Run-to-run noise on Home Assistant was dominated by file reads.

### Describe the Bug

Pyrefly says the type of Pydantic's `FieldInfo.annotation` is `type[Any] | None`, while the type listed on [Pydantic's documentation](https://pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/api/pydantic/fields/#pydantic.fields.FieldInfo) is `TypeForm[Any] | None`.

I ran into this on a Python 3.13 codebase, so `TypeForm` being 3.15 may be the root cause, but I also ran into the following odd behavior:

```python
import typing
from typing import reveal_type

from pydantic import BaseModel


class Test(BaseModel):
    whatevs: list[int]


info = Test.model_fields["whatevs"]


if (annotation := info.annotation) is not None:
    if isinstance(annotation, type):
        ...
    else:
        reveal_type(annotation)  # revealed type: Never
        container = typing.get_origin(annotation)
        reveal_type(container)  # revealed type: ParamSpec
        print(container)  # <class 'list'>
```

### Describe the Bug

I had a case where the types of a 3rd party lib (in a pyi file) listed the signature of one method as the same as one on another class. Pyrefly will then flag `self` as incorrect which I believe is the right thing to do.

However the error was very confusing to me as a consumer of that third party lib, since it listed a million overloads before writing the actual error.

Here's an example:

```python
from typing import overload

class A:
    @overload
    def meth(self, a: int) -> None: ...
    @overload
    def meth(self, a: str) -> None: ...
    def meth(self, a: int | str) -> None: ...


class B:
    meth = A.meth


x: A | B = A()

x.meth(a=1) # Produces the following error.
# I find it confusing that it
# - lists it as [no-matching-overload] when the actual issue is [bad-argument-type] like below
# - lists all the overloads
# - tags one of them as "closest match"
# - mentions "Argument B" which I don't know anything about at the call site 

# ERROR sandbox.py:18:7-12: No matching overload found for function `A.meth` called with arguments: (a=Literal[1]) [no-matching-overload]
#   Possible overloads:
#     (a: int) -> None [closest match]
#     (a: str) -> None
#   Argument `B` is not assignable to parameter `self` with type `A` in function `A.meth`


class SimpleA:
    def meth(self) -> None: ...


class SimpleB:
    meth = SimpleA.meth


y: SimpleA | SimpleB = SimpleA()

y.meth()
# ERROR sandbox.py:36:7-9: Argument `SimpleB` is not assignable to parameter `self` with type `SimpleA` in function `SimpleA.meth` [bad-argument-type]
```

### Describe the Bug

When sending the `hover` lsp command on a property with a setter that is being assigned to it doesn't show anything. When not assigning it correctly shows the type and similarly for non-property values it shows it

```python
class A:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._x: int | None = None

    @property
    def x(self) -> int | None:
        return self._x

    @x.setter
    def x(self, value: int | None) -> None:
        self._x = value

    def meth(self) -> None:
        self.x = 1 # ERR! Hover on `x` returns nothing ("no information available" in neovim). Should show `int | None`
        self.x # OK! Hover correctly show int | None
        self._x = 1 # OK! Hover on `_x` correctly shows Literal[1]

a = A()
a.x = 1 # ERR! Hover on `x` returns nothing ("no information available" in neovim). Should show `int | None`
a.x # OK! Hover correctly show int | None
a._x = 1 # OK! Hover on `_x` correctly shows Literal[1]
```

### Describe the Bug

When using the result of `cast` with a quoted type as argument in a subscription that is the target of an augmented assignment statement it will complain about the type of the quoted type with `bad-argument-type`.

Quite a mouthful, but it seems like it needs all those specific components to be trigged.
This was actually triggered by real code while migrating to pyrefly, but I get that it might look like I fuzzed it.

```python
from typing import cast
a = 0
lst = [1]


lst[cast("int", a)] += 1 # ERROR sandbox.py:6:9-19: First argument to `typing.cast` must be a type [bad-argument-type]
lst[cast("int", a)] -= 1 # ERROR sandbox.py:7:9-19: First argument to `typing.cast` must be a type [bad-argument-type]
lst[cast("int", a)] *= 1 # ERROR sandbox.py:8:9-19: First argument to `typing.cast` must be a type [bad-argument-type]
lst[cast("int", a)] **= 1 # ERROR sandbox.py:9:9-19: First argument to `typing.cast` must be a type [bad-argument-type]
lst[cast("int", a)] //= 1 # ERROR sandbox.py:10:9-19: First argument to `typing.cast` must be a type [bad-argument-type]
lst[cast("int", a)] %= 1 # ERROR sandbox.py:11:9-19: First argument to `typing.cast` must be a type [bad-argument-type]
lst[cast("int", a)] >>= 1 # ERROR sandbox.py:12:9-19: First argument to `typing.cast` must be a type [bad-argument-type]
lst[cast("int", a)] <<= 1 # ERROR sandbox.py:13:9-19: First argument to `typing.cast` must be a type [bad-argument-type]
lst[cast("int", a)] ^= 1 # ERROR sandbox.py:14:9-19: First argument to `typing.cast` must be a type [bad-argument-type]
lst[cast("int", a)] |= 1 # ERROR sandbox.py:15:9-19: First argument to `typing.cast` must be a type [bad-argument-type]


lst[cast("int", a)] # Works
lst[cast("int", a)] = 1 # Works
lst[cast(int, a)] += 1 # works
level = cast("int", a)
lst[level] -= 1 # works
```

For reference, both ty and pyright correctly does not flag anything

### Describe the Bug

When a package's `__init__.py` defines a class and then does `from .b import *`, and `b` imports that class back from the package, every use of the class through `b` becomes `Unknown`. No error is reported, so all downstream checking of those values is silently disabled.

`pkg/__init__.py`:
```python
class A:
    x: int = 1


from .b import *
```

`pkg/b.py`:
```python
from pkg import A

def make() -> A:
    return A()
```

`main.py`:
```python
from typing import reveal_type
from pkg.b import make

reveal_type(make())  # Pyrefly: Unknown. Expected: A
make().nope          # Pyrefly: no error. Expected: missing-attribute
```

The code runs fine (`type(make())` is `pkg.A`), and basedpyright reveals `A` and reports the missing attribute.

The trigger is narrow:
- Defining `A` *after* the `from .b import *` line makes the bug go away.
- Replacing `from .b import *` with `from .b import make` also makes it go away.

So it looks specific to resolving a star import that is part of an import cycle, after earlier definitions in the same module.

Impact: on [xdslproject/xdsl](https://github.com/xdslproject/xdsl), this pattern produced about 530 false positives (`unknown-*` and downstream errors), roughly half of all Pyrefly output there. Fixing 3 imports dropped the total from 1103 to 573.

Reproduces on pyrefly 1.2.0 and on trunk (1.4.0-dev.3).

### Describe the Bug

A parent-relative import fails when the importing file's name starts with a digit. This breaks every Django migration file that uses one, since migration files are named `0001_initial.py`, `0002_...py`, etc.

```
pkg/__init__.py
pkg/models.py              # x = 1
pkg/migrations/__init__.py
pkg/migrations/0001_initial.py   # from .. import models
pkg/migrations/initial.py        # from .. import models
```

```
$ pyrefly check
ERROR pkg/migrations/0001_initial.py:1:1-22: Could not resolve relative import `..` [missing-import]
```

The identical import in `initial.py` resolves, and `from . import x` from the digit-named file also works. basedpyright resolves both files with no errors.

A guess: the module name derived from the file path isn't a valid identifier (`pkg.migrations.0001_initial`), and the code that walks up the parent package for `..` rejects or mis-parses it. Such modules can't be imported with a plain `import` statement, but Django loads them through `importlib`, and their own relative imports are valid at runtime.

Impact: on [procrastinate-org/procrastinate](https://github.com/procrastinate-org/procrastinate), this produced 38 false `missing-import` errors, one per migration file. That was 41% of all Pyrefly output there.

Reproduces on pyrefly 1.2.0 and on trunk (1.4.0-dev.3).

### Describe the Bug

Question is about this case. Behavior difference between Pyright and Pyrefly. 

```python
@overload
def overloaded(value: list[int]) -> list[int]: ...

@overload
def overloaded(value: list[str]) -> list[str]: ...

def check(value: list[Any]) -> None:
    reveal_type(overloaded(value), expected_text="?")
```


I believe the type spec says the typechecker has to not show an error when accessing any of the possible values for the returned value. 

Pyrefly handles this by just marking all ambiguous matches as Any. 

Pyright was handling this by just picking the first match (which is not conformant because it shows errors for the other matches) but is in the process of representing the result as a kind of intersection of list[int] and list[str]. 

See this Pyright issue:
https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/issues/11731

body_text:
### Describe the Bug

Pyrefly accepts `bytes` in a `RootModel[str]` constructor even with `strict=True`.

Save as `example.py`:

```python
from typing import reveal_type

from pydantic import ConfigDict, RootModel


class Text(RootModel[str]):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)


reveal_type(Text.__init__)
Text(b"hello")
```

Run:

```sh
uv run --no-project --python 3.12 --with 'pyrefly==1.4.0.dev4' --with 'pydantic==2.11.9' pyrefly check example.py
uv run --no-project --python 3.12 --with 'pydantic==2.11.9' python example.py
```

**Expected:** a type error on `Text(b"hello")`, since strict mode requires `str`.

**Actual:** Pyrefly reveals `(self: Text, root: Any) -> None` and reports `0 errors`. Running the snippet raises `ValidationError: Input should be a valid string` (`string_type`).

Without strict configuration, `RootModel[str](b"hello")` succeeds at runtime and produces `root='hello'`.

Reproduced on Linux with Python 3.12.3, Pydantic 2.11.9, and Pyrefly 1.3.2 / 1.4.0.dev4.

### Related issues

- #1230 addressed a RootModel-typed field in an enclosing `BaseModel`. This example calls the strict RootModel subclass directly.
- #2182 was explained by default lax coercion. This example explicitly enables strict mode, which rejects that coercion at runtime.

body_text:
pandera models configure themselves with a nested `class Config:`, the same way marshmallow and Django use `class Meta:`. pyrefly reports `bad-override` on every such class.

```python
import pandera.pandas as pa
from pandera.typing import Series


class BaseSchema(pa.DataFrameModel):
    class Config:
        strict = "filter"


class Child(BaseSchema):
    x: Series[int]

    class Config:
        coerce = True
```

```
ERROR Class member `BaseSchema.Config` overrides parent class `DataFrameModel` in an inconsistent manner [bad-override]
  `BaseSchema.Config` is a ClassVar, but `DataFrameModel.Config` is not
ERROR Class member `Child.Config` overrides parent class `BaseSchema` in an inconsistent manner [bad-override]
  `Child.Config` has type `type[Child.Config]`, which is not assignable to `type[BaseSchema.Config]`
```

This is the documented pandera pattern (https://pandera.readthedocs.io/en/stable/dataframe_models.html#config): `Config` does not need to subclass anything, and pandera's metaclass merges the options from every class in the MRO at runtime. mypy (with the pandera plugin) and ty both accept this code.

## Why the existing exemption does not help

#2054 (marshmallow) and #3933 (DRF) were fixed by skipping the check when the attribute is named `Meta` **and** the class derives from a Django, marshmallow or DRF base. pandera calls the class `Config`, so neither condition matches.

The problem is not pandera-specific. This version with no imports gives the same two errors:

```python
class BaseConfig:
    coerce = False


class Model:
    Config: type[BaseConfig] = BaseConfig


class A(Model):
    class Config:
        strict = "filter"


class B(A):
    class Config:
        coerce = True
```

## Suggested fix

Skip the `bad-override` check when both the parent and the child member are nested class definitions with the same name, or when the parent is a class attribute of type `type[X]` and the child is a nested class. That covers pandera, marshmallow, Django and DRF without a per-framework list. ty's maintainers reached the same conclusion for the `ClassVar` half of this in https://github.com/astral-sh/ty/issues/4660.

Alternatively adding `pandera.api.dataframe.model.DataFrameModel` with attribute name `Config` to the existing list would also work.

## Environment

- pyrefly 1.3.2, pandera 0.33.1, Python 3.14
- `preset = "legacy"` (the default `basic` preset does not enable `bad-override`)

pyrefly 1.4.0 output (python-version = "3.15") ``` ERROR assert_type(list[*Unknown], list[int]) failed [assert-type] --> repro.py:8:12 | 8 | assert_type([*x for x in lists], list[int]) | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ERROR Expected a type form, got instance of `list[int]` [not-a-type] --> repro.py:8:15 | 8 | assert_type([*x for x in lists], list[int]) | ^ ERROR assert_type(set[*Unknown], set[int]) failed [assert-type] --> repro.py:9:12 | 9 | assert_type({*x for x in lists}, set[int]) | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ERROR Expected a type form, got instance of `list[int]` [not-a-type] --> repro.py:9:15 | 9 | assert_type({*x for x in lists}, set[int]) | ^ ERROR assert_type(Generator[*Unknown], Generator[int]) failed [assert-type] --> repro.py:10:12 | 10 | assert_type((*x for x in lists), Generator[int, None, None]) | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ERROR Expected a type form, got instance of `list[int]` [not-a-type] --> repro.py:10:15 | 10 | assert_type((*x for x in lists), Generator[int, None, None]) | ^ ERROR assert_type(dict[Unknown, dict[str, int]], dict[str, int]) failed [assert-type] --> repro.py:11:12 | 11 | assert_type({**d for d in dicts}, dict[str, int]) | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ INFO 7 errors ```

**pyrefly 1.4.0**

```python
from unittest import mock

def patched():
    return mock.patch("os.getcwd")
```

After `pyrefly infer repro.py`:

```python
from unittest.mock import _patch_pass_arg
from unittest.mock import MagicMock
from unittest.mock import AsyncMock
from unittest import mock

def patched() -> _patch_pass_arg[AsyncMock | MagicMock]:
    return mock.patch("os.getcwd")
```

Importing the file now raises:

```
ImportError: cannot import name '_patch_pass_arg' from 'unittest.mock'
```

`_patch_pass_arg` exists only in typeshed's stub for `unittest.mock`, not in the runtime module, so the inferred annotation breaks a module that imported fine before.

**Expected:** no runtime import of a stub-only name. For example, the import under `if TYPE_CHECKING:` with the annotation quoted, or no annotation for that function.

Reproduced with Python 3.14; 1.2.0 behaves the same. Related: #578.

### Describe the Bug

_AI-assisted report; reproduction and output verified locally._

## Current

In `pyrefly==1.3.2` and `pyrefly==1.4.0`, conditionally assigning an attribute after initializing it to `None` loses the assigned type after the `if`:

```python
from typing import assert_type

class Foo:
    pass

class Bar:
    def __init__(self, flag: bool) -> None:
        self.x: Foo | None = None
        if flag:
            self.x = Foo()
        assert_type(self.x, Foo | None)
        assert self.x is not None
        assert_type(self.x, Foo)
```

Running `pyrefly check` reports:

```text
assert_type(None, Foo | None) failed [assert-type]
assert_type(Never, Foo) failed [assert-type]
```

The attribute remains narrowed to `None` after the conditional assignment. The subsequent assertion narrows it to `Never`.

## Expected

`self.x` should have type `Foo | None` after the `if`, and `Foo` after `assert self.x is not None`. Both `assert_type` checks should pass.

### Describe the Bug

Pyrefly 1.3.2 and 1.4.0.

`Field()` alone correctly evaluates to `Field[str, int]` through its TypeVar defaults. Passed directly as an argument whose parameter type is `Field[U1, U2]`, those defaults no longer reach `U1`/`U2`, which fall back to their own default. mypy, pyright and ty all infer `Wrapper[str, int]`.

```python
from typing import Any, Generic, assert_type
from typing_extensions import TypeVar

T1 = TypeVar("T1", default=str)
T2 = TypeVar("T2", default=int)


class Field(Generic[T1, T2]):
    def __init__(self, name: str | None = None) -> None: ...


U1 = TypeVar("U1", default=Any)
U2 = TypeVar("U2", default=Any)


class Wrapper(Generic[U1, U2]):
    def __init__(self, base: Field[U1, U2]) -> None: ...


assert_type(Field(), Field[str, int])  # ok
assert_type(Wrapper(Field()), Wrapper[str, int])  # error: assert_type(Wrapper, Wrapper[str, int]) failed
assert_type(Wrapper(Field()), Wrapper[Any, Any])  # no error, but too loose

f = Field()
assert_type(Wrapper(f), Wrapper[str, int])  # ok
```

`Wrapper[str, int]` is expected but pyrefly infers `Wrapper[Any, Any]`. Binding the argument to a variable first gives the expected result, so the bidirectional expected type seems to suppress the defaults.

Context: django-stubs types `ArrayField(base_field=IntegerField())` this way and reads back `list[Any]` instead of `list[int]`.

### Describe the bug

`Enum` initializes `_value_` when constructing its members. An explicit `_value_` annotation should not require a handwritten initializer.

Reproduced with Pyrefly 1.4.0 and CPython 3.14.8 on macOS. Pyrefly 1.3.2 accepts the same example under `--preset all`.

### Reproducer

```python
from enum import Enum

class Format(Enum):
    _value_: str
    TEXT = "text"

    def render(self) -> str:
        return self._value_

assert Format.TEXT.render() == "text"
```

### Commands

```console
uvx --from pyrefly==1.3.2 pyrefly check --preset all enum_payload.py
uvx --from pyrefly==1.4.0 pyrefly check --preset all enum_payload.py
python enum_payload.py
```

The runtime assertion passes. The configuration only sets `preset = "all"` and `python-version = "3.14"`.

### Pyrefly 1.4.0 output

```text
Instance attribute `_value_` is declared but never initialized [uninitialized-instance-variable]
```

Mypy 2.4.0 (strict, without project plugins) and Pyright 1.1.414 accept this example.

### Describe the bug

The keyword form `member(value=decimal)` is valid and works at runtime. In 1.4.0, replacing it with `member(decimal)` makes the diagnostic disappear. The annotation is a normal callable payload contract; no suppression is needed with 1.3.2.

Reproduced with Pyrefly 1.4.0 and CPython 3.14.8 on macOS. Pyrefly 1.3.2 accepts the same example under `--preset all`.

### Reproducer

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from enum import Enum, member

def decimal(value: int, /) -> str:
    return str(value)

class Format(Enum):
    DECIMAL = member(value=decimal)

    def render(self, value: int, /) -> str:
        formatter: Callable[[int], str] = self.value
        return formatter(value)

assert Format.DECIMAL.render(42) == "42"
```

### Commands

```console
uvx --from pyrefly==1.3.2 pyrefly check --preset all callable_member.py
uvx --from pyrefly==1.4.0 pyrefly check --preset all callable_member.py
python callable_member.py
```

The runtime assertion passes. The configuration only sets `preset = "all"` and `python-version = "3.14"`.

### Pyrefly 1.4.0 output

```text
`member[(value: int, /) -> str]` is not assignable to `(int) -> str` [bad-assignment]
```

### Describe the bug

The annotated slot is assigned before `__new__` returns, and every normal construction supplies the required metadata. Reading `Label("text", flag=True).flag` succeeds. Pyrefly 1.4.0 still reports `uninitialized-instance-variable`; 1.3.2 accepts it under the same all-rules preset. This also prevents replacing factory-initialized string metadata with the standard `__new__` pattern while adopting the new check.

Reproduced with Pyrefly 1.4.0 and CPython 3.14.8 on macOS. Pyrefly 1.3.2 accepts this example with the same configuration. Mypy 2.4.0 (strict, without project plugins) and Pyright 1.1.414 also accept it.

### Reproducer

```python
from typing import Self

class Label(str):
    __slots__ = ("_flag",)
    _flag: bool

    def __new__(cls, text: str, /, *, flag: bool) -> Self:
        result = super().__new__(cls, object=text)
        result._flag = flag
        return result

    @property
    def flag(self) -> bool:
        return self._flag

assert Label("text", flag=True).flag
```

```toml

python-version = "3.14"
```

### Describe the bug

The bundled typeshed declares `Enum.value -> Any` explicitly ([1.4.0 stub](https://github.com/facebook/pyrefly/blob/1.4.0/crates/pyrefly_bundled/third_party/typeshed/stdlib/enum.pyi)). Reading it through the base `Enum` produces `unknown-attribute-access`, even when assigning it to `object`. The [error-kind documentation](https://pyrefly.org/en/docs/error-kinds/#unknown-attribute-access) says explicit `Any` accesses are intentional and not reported. I expected the explicit stub fallback to retain that distinction; I am not asking Pyrefly to infer a concrete payload from a bare `Enum`.

Reproduced with Pyrefly 1.4.0 and CPython 3.14.8 on macOS. Pyrefly 1.3.2 accepts this example with the same configuration. Mypy 2.4.0 (strict, without project plugins) and Pyright 1.1.414 also accept it.

### Reproducer

```python

def read_value(option: Enum) -> object:
    value: object = option.value
    return value
```

Save this as `pyrefly.toml`:


### Describe the bug

After `isinstance(cls, Metadata)`, the metaclass declares a known `int | None` attribute. Pyrefly loses that type when the class also came from `type(shape)` for a protocol with a property of the same name. The same attribute accessed through a parameter annotated directly as `Metadata` is known. The metaclass attribute has a default here to avoid the separate initialization issue in #5278. This is related to, but narrower than, the previously closed #4168.

Reproduced with Pyrefly 1.4.0 and CPython 3.14.8 on macOS. Pyrefly 1.3.2 accepts this example with the same configuration. Mypy 2.4.0 (strict, without project plugins) and Pyright 1.1.414 also accept it.

### Reproducer

```python
from typing import Protocol

class Metadata(type):
    limit: int | None = 1

class Shape(Protocol):
    @property
    def limit(self) -> int | None: ...

def check_limit(shape: Shape) -> None:
    cls = type(shape)
    if not isinstance(cls, Metadata):
        raise TypeError
    if cls.limit is not None:
        print("bounded")
```

body_text:
When an attrs field is annotated (e.g. x: int) and converter=None is passed explicitly, Pyrefly treats the field / synthesized `__init__` parameter as Unknown instead of int.

Expected behavior:
converter=None means “no converter” (same as omitting converter, default argument), so the init parameter should still be typed from the field annotation (int).


Minimal Repro
```python
from attrs import define, field

@define
class A:
    x: int = field(converter=None)
p = A("asd")  # should be a type error; currently accepted (field typed as Unknown)
```

Environment
Pyrefly 1.4
attrs 25.3.0

The cause: converter=None reaches get_converter_param in pyrefly/lib/alt/class/dataclass.rs, which finds no callable signature and falls back to implicit Any.

A second spot in pyrefly/lib/alt/solve.rs skips the check that a default matches the annotation whenever a converter= keyword is present, even when it’s None. Example: x: int = field(default="nope", converter=None) gives no error.

### Describe the Bug

This bug is easier to explain with a code example:
```python
from typing import reveal_type, Any

class Variadic[*Ts](tuple[*Ts]): ...

def f(t: Variadic[str, int | None, *tuple[Any, ...]]):
    a, b, c = t
    reveal_type(a)  # Expected str. Got int | str | Any | None.
    reveal_type(b)  # Expected int | None. Got int | str | Any | None.
```

It affects the types of the result-columns of queries executed with SQLAlchemy and results are fetched using `fetchone()`, so it's very easy to encounter. Rather than each value in a `Row` having its correct type, all types are Unioned, which causes further typing errors where the values are used.

### Describe the Bug

```python
# Mutable list is invariant
list1: list[int] = [10]
list2: list[int | None] = list1 # Error

# Immutable list (tuple) is covariant
tuple1: tuple[int, ...] = (10, )
tuple2: tuple[int | None, ...] = tuple1 # No Error

# Mutable dict is invariant
dict1: dict[str, int] = {"a": 10}
dict2: dict[str, int | None] = dict1 # Error 

# Immutable dict is also invariant????
fdict1: frozendict[str, int] = frozendict(*{"a": 10})
fdict2: frozendict[str, int | None] = fdict1 # Error
# But I think this should not be an error
# I think Key and Value should booth be covariant
```

Python: 3.15

I think a frozen dict should be covariant the same as a tuple is.
If the datatype is readonly, it should always be save to widen the generic Parameters?
As far as i understand, the bundled typeshed types do not declare the Generic Parameters to be covariant.

### Describe the Bug

This issue may need further discussion. Currently Pyrefly reports no error for the case below, but there is a clear error:

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
df["c"] # no error
```

The reason, as suggested in docs, is:

> In contrast, pandas permits direct column assignment and other open-ended mutation on an existing DataFrame. A column can be added through df[name] = values, including when name is only known at runtime. Pyrefly therefore treats every inferred pandas schema as partial, keeping columns defined at construction while allowing untracked columns to exist. This is why an unrecognized column name is an error on a Polars frame but not on a pandas one.

But I think we can mark the schema as complete if possible, and downgrade it to partial if needed later. If all schemas are treated as partial, we cannot report any missing column error to the user and the schema tracking is not useful enough imo.

body_text:
### Describe the Bug

Assigning an attribute on the class object (`cls.attr = ...`, here in `__init_subclass__`) is reported as an attribute missing from `__slots__`. But `__slots__` restricts the attributes of instances, not of the class: the assignment works at runtime, and the same code without `__slots__` passes.

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any


def wrap(call: Callable[..., Any]) -> Callable[..., Any]:
    return call


class Base:
    __slots__ = ()

    def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        call = cls.__dict__.get("__call__")
        if call is not None:
            cls.__call__ = wrap(call)  # error


class Plain:
    def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        call = cls.__dict__.get("__call__")
        if call is not None:
            cls.__call__ = wrap(call)  # no error
```

### Describe the Bug

In some build and test systems, users need to set PYTHONPATH. Currently, pyrefly produces a spurious warning in these cases, and it can be quite long if the PYTHONPATH is long, distracting from legitimate problems.

Proposal 1: add a flag to entirely disable the PYTHONPATH check, available on the CLI, in pyproject.toml, etc.

Proposal 2: support an optional entry in pyproject.toml, etc. that gives the expected PYTHONPATH. If the runtime path differs, warn or error out.

body_text:
Reproduced with pyrefly 1.4.0 (latest), `pyrefly stubgen --search-path . -o out <file>`.

## Describe the Bug

When stubgen writes an inferred type, it adds imports only for `typing` names
(`Literal`, `Self`, `Callable`) and `_typeshed.Incomplete`. Any other class in the
rendered type is written by bare name with no import, so the stub has undefined
names. A consumer resolves them to `Unknown` without any error.

## Minimal repro

```python
# pkg/dep.py
class Widget: ...

def make() -> Widget:
    return Widget()
```

```python
# pkg/input.py
import logging
import re

from pkg.dep import make

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
PAT = re.compile("a+")
widget = make()
```

### Expected output

```python
import logging
import re
from pkg.dep import make

logger: logging.Logger
PAT: re.Pattern[str]
widget: Widget  # plus `from pkg.dep import Widget`
```

Either qualify through a module the source already imports, or add the import.

### Actual output

```python
import logging
import re
from pkg.dep import make

logger: Logger
PAT: Pattern[str]
widget: Widget
```

`ruff check --select F821` reports `Logger`, `Pattern` and `Widget` as undefined.
In a project that imports this stub, `reveal_type(logger)` is `Unknown`, against
`Logger` from the source.

## Notes

- `test_stubgen_dependency_types_survive_eviction` in `pyrefly/lib/stubgen.rs` asserts
  `widget: Widget` but does not check that `Widget` is imported.
- `pyrefly infer` already adds imports for the types it inserts (see #5253), so that
  code might be reusable here.
- On a 101-module real package, 48 of the generated stubs have undefined names
